Contents
  1. The short version
  2. The challenge brief
  3. The two slides
  4. What BMW's PM told us
  5. The M350 film
  6. BMW history
  7. Values, DNA, quotes
  8. Ultimate Driving Machine
  9. What they're looking for
  10. Rules & pitch
  11. Questions for BMW
  12. Glossary
  13. Sources
EHL Hackathon · Munich · 10–11 October 2026 · Research briefing

BMW challenge: AI for product decision making

Everything we know about the challenge, the company behind it, and what "The Ultimate Driving Machine" means, explained in plain language. Each fact taken from outside material links to its source, marked like this S1.

1,000,000,000customer findings
1,000requirements
1car, sold for 7–8 years
01

The short version

BMW wants a tool that helps its product managers decide what the next generation of a car should offer customers. Those managers face an ocean of information: complaints, reviews, sales numbers, competitor launches, market trends. They have to turn all of it into a short list of clear requirements for the engineers, and defend every choice.

Today that work is manual, slow, and hard to trace afterwards. BMW wants AI to do the heavy lifting: reading, sorting, grouping and suggesting. The human must stay in charge of every decision, and anyone looking later must be able to see why each one was made.

The idea to hold on to

BMW's slogan is "The Ultimate Driving Machine". In this challenge the product manager is the driver and our tool is the machine: powerful, precise, responsive, but it never takes the wheel. BMW's own design rule for its cars is "Hands on the wheel, eyes on the road" S14. For our tool that means the manager approves everything, and the evidence is always in view.

What the judges will reward, in BMW's own words: trustworthy sources, transparent reasoning, thoughtful prioritization, and a clear understanding of uncertainty and conflicting evidence. They care about what customers value, not about engineering specifications, regulation or detailed business cases.

02

The challenge brief, explained

The official two-page brief is titled "AI for Product Decision Making". It asks one question: What should the next generation of a BMW vehicle offer its customers?

What we have to build

An AI-powered application that helps product managers derive (find), justify (explain) and prioritize (rank) customer requirements for a successor vehicle, meaning the next generation of a car that already exists. Every proposal must be grounded in customer feedback, BMW's product and sales data, and research from the web.

The scope we can choose from

ChoiceOptionsWhat it means
VehicleBMW 1 Series, 5 Series, 7 Series, or a mixThe 1 Series is the small entry car, the 5 Series the mid-size business sedan, the 7 Series the luxury flagship.
MarketsEurope, China, USA, or any subsetCustomers differ strongly between these regions, so a market view matters.
Time horizon3 to 5 years aheadWe must guess what customers will want when the new car launches, not only what they want today.
Honesty ruleMark evidence vs assumptionsShow clearly which conclusions come from real data and which are forecasts about the future.

The data

For each vehicle BMW provides customer feedback, equipment data (which options people buy), sales volumes and a customer study. We may add outside sources such as competitor information, reviews, and market or technology trends.

"We are interested in how your solution turns diverse information into actionable product-management insights and makes its reasoning transparent, not in a specific workflow or technical architecture."
BMW briefing, page 1

In other words, they will not judge our tech stack. They will judge whether a product manager makes better decisions with our tool.

What we must show in the demo

  1. A working prototype where AI helps identify, formulate and prioritize customer-facing requirements using their data and outside sources.
  2. A set of example requirements, each backed by clear evidence and reasoning, showing how feedback, data, market signals and competitor insights turn into a requirement and why it ranks where it does.
  3. A transparent decision experience where the manager can review, challenge, modify, approve or reject each AI proposal, while evidence, assumptions, uncertainties and decisions stay visible and traceable.

"Make it yours"

We don't have to build everything equally well. We should pick the area where we can add the most value (customer insights, combining BMW and outside data, writing strong requirements, prioritization, or the human-in-the-loop experience) and go deep there. We should also show how the idea could scale to other car lines, markets and future decisions.

03

The two slides, explained

Slide 1: "From billions of findings to one BMW vehicle"

At the bottom of the slide is BMW's working definition:

Customer Requirement = Customer Relevant Attribute of a Car. A requirement is anything about the car that a customer would notice and care about, written in the customer's language.

The left column shows raw customer quotes. They are messy on purpose, and some contradict each other:

  • "Charging takes too long."
  • "The app should just work."
  • "Too many menus."
  • "Too much plastic."
  • "Ugly kidney grille."
  • "I love the design."
  • "Uncomfortable seats."
  • "More rear space, please."
  • "Very nice exterior colors."
  • "The NEW XPENG."
  • "Tesla and GROK"

Two things stand out. First, the direct contradiction (in red): one customer hates the grille, another loves the design. Our tool must show such conflicts, not average them away. Second, customers name XPeng and Tesla/Grok as reference points. These are software-first electric car brands from China and the US, not the traditional rivals Mercedes and Audi.

The middle of the slide is a word cloud of themes. Some words are bright and bold, others are faded, which seems to signal different importance:

Prominent
Intuitive UXPremium feelRangeFast chargingLong battery lifeIconic designSafetyEasy charging
Medium
Joy of drivingReliable softwareClear displaysComfortable seatsSmooth rideFast app responsePhysical controlsRoom for familyEasy child seat fitData privacyEasy updatesGreat soundHome chargingPersonalized…
Faded
AffordableEfficiencyEveryday spaceSeat ventilationReal-world rangeDynamicSustainableElectricLow running costs

What this tells us: feedback arrives unstructured, duplicated, emotional, contradictory and market-specific. The job is to turn it into a clean list of customer-relevant attributes, then weigh them. Software, user experience and charging seem to be where BMW feels the pressure.

Slide 2: "The Process"

This is how BMW's product managers work today. The icons on the slide show who does what. Here is the same process in plain words:

Stage 1

Situation analysis

Start from the baseline: the current model, the rest of BMW's range, and how many cars sell. Then gather competition, customer and public feedback, and global trends.

AI + human
Stage 2

Structure & context

AI classifies and clusters the findings, removes duplicates, groups themes and links insights. The output is a list of possible requirements as yes/no items, e.g. "electric powertrain?", "cooler?", "seat ventilation?"

AI
Stage 3

Requirements definition

Turn each yes/no into a measurable target: "Range: 600 or 700 miles?", "A cooler for how many bottles?", "Is the seat ventilation fast enough?" Sorted by area: exterior, interior, powertrain, driver assistance.

AI + human
Stage 4

Prioritization

Rank the requirements along at least two axes: customer value and business value.

AI + human
Stage 5

Documentation

Requirements tracking. The icon is a loop: the record is kept alive and revisited, not filed away.

AI

Where the hard decisions happen: the jump from stage 2 to stage 3 (from "yes, electric" to "exactly how much range, at what cost") and stage 4 (where what customers want and what the business can afford pull against each other).

04

What BMW's product manager told us

A BMW product manager introduced the challenge on stage. This is a cleaned-up summary of the transcript in our Notion page.

"It's about emotions. But there are humans who are in charge of building this emotion, pressed into steel and a product, and that's called product management."

The product manager's "universe"

Every decision is pulled in five directions at once. The speaker described them as planets circling the product:

ForceWhat they saidWhat it means
Brand & legacy"Sheer driving pleasure. You want to build on that."The brand both limits and enables what a new BMW can be.
Markets"If you ask five markets, five times out of five you will hear: oh yes, but my market is different."Each region has its own culture and needs.
Engineering"They can do everything and anything, but sometimes at a price we [don't] want to pay."Cost forces choices.
CustomerEach customer has a single need: small car, big car, fast car.Different buyers want different things.
Competition"Formerly known as Mercedes or Audi, quite recently Xiaomi… XPeng."The new threat is Chinese tech companies.

The job is to find an equilibrium between these forces and condense "billions, gazillions of information pieces" into a set of requirements handed to engineering. The stakes are high because one car stays on the market for seven to eight years.

The example everyone should remember

"This car is going to be electric. How electric? Fully electric. How fully? 1,000 km. How long to recharge? Ten minutes. How much does it cost? …OK, going back: 900 km."

Requirements get negotiated against cost, back and forth. A tool that helps with this trade-off, even in a simple "what if" form, speaks directly to their daily work. (Interesting detail: BMW's newest electric 3 Series has exactly 900 km of range and adds 400 km in 10 minutes of charging S15.)

Why documentation matters so much

"At some point in the market, three years [in], things happen and then you need to reconsider some decisions. So this is why you need to document your decisions and the context at the time you take the decision."

It is not enough to record what was decided. We must record what was known and assumed at that moment, so a later reviewer can tell whether the decision is still valid.

05

The M350 film, analysed

The presentation opened with a 54-second film: "The new BMW M350 xDrive Sedan" S35, published by BMW M on 5 October 2026. We downloaded it and studied it frame by frame.

The car: the sportiest petrol version of the new 3 Series. A 3.0-litre six-cylinder engine with mild-hybrid support, 443 hp, 0–100 km/h in 4.1 seconds, new yellow "M lights", painted Fire Red. It also has a new "Drift Moment" mode that sends all power to the rear wheels S16.

The sound: music and engine noise only. There is no voice-over; we confirmed this by running the audio through a speech-recognition model. The film is meant to be felt, not explained.

A detail that matters: the film states that its animal scenes were generated using artificial intelligence. BMW already uses AI in its own creative work.

What the images mean

This is our interpretation; the film itself explains nothing.

  • The panther stands for controlled power: instinct, precision and calm, not chaos. The film cuts from the panther's eyes to the car's yellow headlights, so the car becomes a creature with intent.
  • The kayaker stands for a person mastering a wild force through skill. The river is powerful and unpredictable; the paddler reads it, commits and steers. The kayak is the same red as the car, a visual hint that the machine is an extension of the human.
  • The interior shots show the cockpit as a calm, crafted space built around the driver.
  • The ending is the slogan "The Ultimate Driving Machine". No specs, only feeling.
Why it matters for our challenge

The product manager is the kayaker. The billion findings are the white water. Our tool is the boat and the paddle: it gives power and precision, but the person reads the river and makes the calls.

06

BMW history: the parts that matter

BMW (Bayerische Motoren Werke, "Bavarian Motor Works") is more than 100 years old. Its history repeats one pattern: it nearly fails, then survives by finding what customers really want. The right-hand column explains why each moment matters for our challenge.

WhenWhat happenedWhy it matters for us
1913Karl Rapp founds an aircraft-engine company in Munich. S20The roots are in aviation.
7 Mar 1916Bayerische Flugzeugwerke is founded. BMW counts this as its official birthday. S4 S9
1917Rapp's company is renamed Bayerische Motoren Werke. Austrian engineer Franz Josef Popp takes charge. Designer Max Friz builds the BMW IIIa, a six-cylinder aircraft engine "soon regarded as the world's best". S9 S21Precision engineering and the straight-six engine are in BMW's DNA from day one. The M350 in the film still uses a straight-six.
10 Dec 1917The round blue-and-white logo is registered. The popular "spinning propeller" story only appeared in advertising in the late 1920s. S9A useful reminder that brand myths and facts differ.
1923After the First World War, Germany is banned from making aircraft engines. BMW pivots to motorcycles: the R32. S20The first of many pivots to survive.
1928–33BMW buys a car factory in Eisenach and starts making cars. The BMW 303 (1933) brings the first six-cylinder BMW car and the first kidney grille. Its light frame proved that a car didn't need to be heavy to handle well. S9 S11The same grille that a customer on the slide calls "ugly" is 93 years old.
1945–52Factories bombed, the car plant lost to East Germany. BMW survives by making pots, pans and bicycles. S20Resilience.
1955–59BMW sells tiny Isetta bubble cars and large, expensive limousines, and loses money. A BMW historian: "BMW had small cars and big sedans. In between there was nothing." S31A gap in the product range nearly killed the company.
9 Dec 1959Management proposes selling BMW to Daimler-Benz. Small shareholders and dealers revolt and block it. Industrialist Herbert Quandt then invests and keeps BMW independent. S4 S12BMW exists today because the people closest to customers believed in the brand.
1961–62The Neue Klasse ("New Class") BMW 1500: a compact, sporty four-door sedan "designed to fill a gap in the market". Orders far exceed what the factory can build. Within a few years revenue rises sevenfold. S4 S3 S13The original story of finding the right customer requirement. It created the sports-sedan category.
mid-1960sBMW commissions market research from Bernt Spiegel. It finds people still associate BMW with its sporty 1930s cars, not its 1950s luxury cars. BMW commits to sportiness, driving dynamics and technology, and adopts the slogan "Freude am Fahren" (Sheer Driving Pleasure). S24 S12BMW used customer research to define who it is. That is exactly what this challenge asks for.
1966The 02 Series / 2002: the template for the compact sports sedan. S20
1970Eberhard v. Kuenheim becomes CEO at 41 and leads BMW for 23 years, turning it into a global company. S6See his quotes in the next section.
1972The first 5 Series, starting the numbered model names. The board chose numbers that leave "enough space below the 3 Series, above the 7 Series and in between". BMW Motorsport (later "M") is founded. S6The naming system still in use today.
1974–75US agency founder Martin Puris writes "The Ultimate Driving Machine". BMW's sources give both years. S1 S2See section 8.
1975The first 3 Series. US sales grow from 15,007 (1974) to 26,040 (1976), and to nearly 100,000 a decade later. S1
1977–78The first 7 Series flagship. S20One of the cars in our brief.
1998–2003BMW acquires the Rolls-Royce car brand and relaunches MINI, and decides to focus only on premium cars. S4
2004The first 1 Series: "Sheer driving pleasure for the compact class." S4One of the cars in our brief.
2010 → 2019A BMW survey finds 80% of 1 Series owners thought their car was front-wheel drive. It was actually rear-wheel drive, a "sacred" BMW trait. S28 In 2019 BMW switches the 1 Series to front-wheel drive for more interior space. The project lead said: "Most customers can't differentiate between front- and rear-drive anyway." Only 3% had bought the sporty rear-drive versions. S29Key lesson: what enthusiasts say matters and what typical buyers actually notice can differ. Our tool should tell them apart.
2013The i3 and i8 electric cars: visionary, but "prohibitively expensive to build and short on the battery-electric range that customers demanded". S3Right idea, wrong balance of requirements and cost.
2020–23BMW charges a monthly fee to switch on heated seats already built into the car. Customers revolt and BMW drops it. Sales chief Pieter Nota: "People feel that they paid double… perception is reality." S27Key lesson: a requirement can make business sense and still fail because of how customers perceive it.
Sep 2025The new Neue Klasse begins with the electric iX3: up to 805 km range, very fast charging, new central computers (one is called the "Heart of Joy"), and a new dashboard called Panoramic iDrive. BMW says that dashboard was shaped by "individual customer feedback, data from over 10 million connected vehicles and usability studies with more than 3,000 customers". S14 S3BMW's own requirements process in action, and a hint of the scale of data they work with.
2025–26BMW removes the iDrive rotary knob and says "not a single person has requested that we return to the physical dial". Reactions to the new design are mixed. S25 S26Physical buttons versus touchscreens is a live debate, and it appears on the slide ("Physical controls", "Too many menus").
2026The new 3 Series and electric i3: up to 900 km range, production in Munich from August. The M350 from the film launches. A China-only long-wheelbase iX3 is developed with Chinese partners. S15 S16 S37900 km matches the speaker's "going back to 900 km" example.

Where BMW stands now (2025 sales)

  • The BMW brand sold 2,169,739 cars in 2025, down 1.4%. S17 S18
  • China fell 12.5% under pressure from local brands, though it is still BMW's largest single market. Europe grew 7.3% and the Americas 5.6%. S18
  • By model family S19: 3/4 Series 477k (−8%) · 5/6 Series 300k (+19.5%) · 1/2 Series 214k (+8%) · 7/8 Series 53k (−5.6%), small in volume but central to the brand's image.
  • For the first time, one in ten BMWs sold was an M model. S18
Not verified

The current model codes and launch years of the three cars (1 Series ~2024, 5 Series ~2023, 7 Series ~2022) come from general knowledge, not from a source checked in this research. BMW confirms that successors to the 7 Series are in development S18. Check the rest against BMW's data pack. "Three to five years ahead" probably means requirements for cars sold from about 2030 to 2038.

07

Who BMW is: values, DNA and quotes

Purpose and mission

BMW Group states its purpose as "to move body, heart and mind" S8. It says it stands for "first-class individual mobility" and "uncompromising, outstanding products for our customers to enjoy", and that it is committed to "safeguarding the independence of our company" S5. The independence point goes back to 1959.

Its management report describes "a feedback-based planning and control system" in which "underlying assumptions are reviewed" S8. That is BMW's own description of what our tool should support.

The five company values

BMW names five values for how its people work together S7. Each one maps neatly onto a feature of our tool:

ValueBMW's own wordsWhat it means for our tool
Responsibility"We take consistent decisions and commit to them personally."Every decision has a named owner: the product manager.
Appreciation"Clarity, feedback and celebrating each other's success are crucial."Clear, readable output.
Transparency"We do not embellish, but point out contradictions constructively."Show conflicting evidence openly. This is the strongest match to the brief.
Trust"We trust and rely on each other."Every claim links to its source.
Openness"We are excited by change… We learn from our mistakes."A decision log that gets revisited when assumptions turn out wrong.

What makes a car a "true BMW"

BMW's own design statements describe a set of hallmarks S10 S11. A new requirement should not break these without a very good reason:

  • Proportions: long wheelbase, short overhangs, long bonnet, cabin set back. They "evoke the sporty elegance and dynamics of every BMW even before a wheel has turned."
  • The face: the two-part kidney grille (since 1933) and twin headlights "sawn off" at the top for a focused look. The M350's yellow lights in the film are a new take on this.
  • The Hofmeister kink: a small forward curve at the base of the rear side window, used since 1961. It hints at rear-wheel drive.
  • Driver orientation: controls are angled toward the driver and within direct reach.
  • Engineering: the straight-six engine, light construction, and handling.

Markets really are different

BMW's own US marketers explain why "my market is different" is real S2:

"The psychographic of the BMW customer is much different here than in Europe… In Europe, they sell some low-powered BMWs that we would not think of as being the Ultimate Driving Machine."
Jim McDowell, BMW of North America marketing
"The Joy of Driving just doesn't land over here the way it does in Germany."
Carl Flesher, BMW of North America marketing director

The same source reports that research found people rated BMW highly for engineering, "but they equate BMW drivers with aggression and arrogance". For China, BMW calls its new long-wheelbase iX3 its "most China specific" product, with local driving characteristics and digital features S37.

In their own words: BMW's leaders

Each quote below was checked on the source page. Where no verifiable quote exists, we say so.

Franz Josef Popp

First managing director, 1917 · General director until 1942 · no verified direct quote

Popp is usually called BMW's first leader. Germany's national biography says BMW's survival after 1918, and its growth into aircraft engines, motorcycles and cars, "is owed to Popp's commercial skill" S21. He wrote essays such as "Die Automobilisierung Deutschlands" ("The motorisation of Germany", 1924), and bringing cars to ordinary people was a subject he took seriously S34.

A well-known story from 1919, after BMW was banned from making aircraft engines: Popp asks his team "What do we do? How do we go on?" and engineer Martin Stolle answers "We must build motorcycles. People will snatch them out of our hands!" S30

This exchange comes from a dramatised book (Horst Mönnich, BMW – Eine deutsche Geschichte), quoted second-hand. Tell it as a story, not as a verified quote.

Eberhard v. Kuenheim

CEO 1970–1993 · verified on bmwgroup.com S6
"If you want something new, you need the courage to experiment."
"We are often attributed with entrepreneurial instinct, and when it proves to be right and beneficial, we may even speak of a vision in retrospect."

Why it's useful: a decision only looks like vision afterwards. That is the best argument for recording the reasoning when the decision is made.

Herbert Quandt

Major shareholder who saved BMW in 1959–60 · no verified direct quote

BMW's supervisory board chairman, in 2010: "Herbert Quandt's business instinct and his ability to make courageous decisions at that time set a new course for our company and secured BMW's ability to control its own future." S12

His son Stefan Quandt recalled that in 1959 shareholders and dealers "made clear how convinced they were of the strength of the BMW brand" (translated from German) S31.

For balance: Quandt was a Nazi Party member, and his family's factories used forced labour in the Second World War S32. Avoid presenting him as a hero in the pitch.

Martin Puris

Wrote "The Ultimate Driving Machine" · verified on BMW press site S1
"We never said luxury car. The question [to the customer] is, How do you want to spend your money? Is it on leather and burled walnut? Or do you want to spend it on performance? The line itself selects its market."
"If they produce true BMWs, they can use the line forever."

Oliver Zipse

CEO, on the new Neue Klasse · verified S14 S3
"Practically everything about it is new, and yet it is more BMW than ever." (translated from German)
"When else do you get to re-imagine a brand like BMW from the ground up?"

Pieter Nota

Board member for sales, on dropping the heated-seat subscription · verified S27
"People feel that they paid double—which was actually not true, but perception is reality, I always say."
08

What "The Ultimate Driving Machine" means

Where it came from

In the mid-1970s BMW took control of its US sales from an independent importer. Board member Bob Lutz explained why: "You can't define the brand if you have individual distributors and individual companies making up their own minds how to advertise, how to position the car." S1 BMW hired a small new agency, Ammirati & Puris, and Martin Puris wrote the line.

His insight was that BMW's premium status came from performance, not luxury. A BMW was worth the money because of how it drives, not because of leather and wood. The slogan picks its own customers: people who want to drive.

It worked. US sales rose from 15,007 cars in 1974 to 26,040 in 1976 S1. Fifty years later it still closes the M350 film, and BMW's US chief calls the new iX3 "the Next Ultimate Driving Machine" S3.

Two slogans, one idea

  • "Freude am Fahren" / "Sheer Driving Pleasure" (Germany, mid-1960s) describes the emotion. It is used worldwide. S24
  • "The Ultimate Driving Machine" (USA, 1974–75) describes the promise. US marketers defended it for decades, including in 2010 when a global "Joy" campaign seemed to replace it. S2

BMW's own press archive frames the debate as a question: "Is it what the car is, or what the car makes you feel?" S2 The answer is both. So our tool should capture functional requirements (range, charging time) and emotional ones (joy of driving, premium feel).

The slogan as a decision filter

The slogan states what BMW is, and therefore what it is not. Any requirement can be tested against it: does this make the car more of an Ultimate Driving Machine, or does it just add leather and burled walnut?

Why it's harder today

The slide shows customers asking for intuitive software, fast charging and an app that "just works", and comparing BMW with XPeng and Tesla. "Driving" now includes screens, charging and driver assistance. BMW's answer in the new Neue Klasse is to redefine driving pleasure for the software era. One example is Symbiotic Drive: the assistance system keeps working when the driver gently steers or brakes, and the driver's input simply blends in S14.

"Become the Ultimate Driving Machine": three readings

  1. For BMW: stay true to the brand while customers' idea of "driving" changes. The next 5, 7 or 1 Series must be "more BMW than ever" and also compete with software-first Chinese electric cars.
  2. For the product manager: they drive the product. Our tool should feel like a BMW: built around its driver, responsive and precise. Hands on the wheel (the human approves), eyes on the road (evidence always visible), and like Symbiotic Drive (the AI suggests, a nudge from the manager overrides, and it doesn't fight back).
  3. For our pitch: "We built the Ultimate Driving Machine for product managers."
09

What they're looking for

This section is our own analysis, built on everything above.

From their criteria to features

They wantWhat we could build
From a billion findings to a thousand requirements to one carA clear pipeline: collect → clean → group into themes → propose requirements → set measurable targets → rank → log the decision.
Evidence kept apart from assumptionsEach requirement shows its evidence (how many mentions, sample quotes, which markets, source links) separately from its assumptions (forecasts about 2030 and later), each with a confidence level.
Handling conflicting evidenceShow the conflict openly, e.g. "Kidney grille: 34% negative, 41% positive, split by market and age", instead of hiding it in an average. (Illustrative numbers.)
"My market is different"A switch that re-ranks the same list for Europe, China and the US and highlights where they disagree.
Prioritization you can seeA scoring model with weights the manager can see and change (customer value, frequency, severity, gap to competitors, trend momentum, brand fit), plus a plain-language "why is this ranked #3?"
Brand fitA "BMW DNA" check: does this requirement make the car more of an Ultimate Driving Machine?
Turning yes/no into numbersTurn "ventilated seats: yes" into "cools to X °C within Y seconds", and "range" into 600 / 700 / 900 km options compared with competitors.
Human in controlApprove, reject, edit or challenge every proposal. Every override is saved with a reason.
Documentation with contextA snapshot of the evidence at decision time, so in three years anyone can see what was known, what was assumed, and what has changed since.
ScaleThe same engine works for the 1, 5 and 7 Series and for every market.

Signals between the lines

  • The 1,000 km → 900 km story shows they live in trade-offs. A simple "what if" control would resonate.
  • They raised documentation and context twice. Traceability is a top priority.
  • Their named competitors are Chinese tech brands, and China is BMW's weakest market right now. China-specific insight is likely valuable.
  • Write requirements in customer language ("charges while I have a coffee"), not engineering language ("350 kW DC").

Lessons from BMW's own history

  • "Point out contradictions constructively" is an official BMW value S7. Surfacing conflicts fits their culture; it isn't an extra.
  • Say vs notice: 80% of 1 Series owners didn't know which wheels drove their car S28. Separate what customers say, what they actually notice, and what the brand requires.
  • Perception is reality S27: the heated-seat subscription made business sense on paper and still failed. Score requirements on how customers will perceive them.
  • The 1960s story: BMW was saved by customer research that found an unmet gap S13 S24. A pitch line: "We're giving BMW's product managers what market research gave BMW in the 1960s, at the scale of a billion data points."

Ideas for a distinctive angle

  • Decision flight recorder: every requirement has a replayable history (evidence → AI proposal → manager's change → reason). Assumption alarms fire when new data breaks an old assumption, e.g. "A competitor launched 12-minute charging; requirement R-042 assumed 15 minutes was enough."
  • Devil's advocate: for each top requirement, the AI writes the strongest argument against it and lists the evidence that conflicts.
  • Market lens: one list, re-ranked per region, with the differences made visible.
  • Brand DNA gate: a score for whether each requirement strengthens the Ultimate Driving Machine.
  • Proof for the pitch: time saved compared with doing it by hand, share of requirements with traceable evidence, accuracy of the grouping on a hand-labelled sample, number of conflicts found, and agreement between AI ranking and expert ranking.
10

Rules, prizes and the pitch

Mandatory

We must set up the tool Entire in our GitHub repository. The organisers said: "If you do not use it, your submission will be rejected." The speech transcript wrote it as "a tire"; our Notion note links it to entire.io. Confirm in the technical onboarding session.

  • Prizes: overall winner €10,000 cash plus $5,000 in OpenAI credits; second place €3,000; third €2,000; each challenge winner €1,500.
  • Timing: challenge pitches start 30 minutes after the submission deadline, at 12:30, in parallel rooms. Finals for the overall winner are on Sunday at 15:30.
  • Format: 3 minutes for pitch and demo, then 3 minutes of questions. Hard cut-off.
  • Questions go to Discord. The Notion page is the single source of truth.

The pitch structure the organisers asked for

  1. Solution: break down the idea and show its unique angle. Many teams will have similar ideas.
  2. Demo: show that the product solves the problem. Don't overcomplicate it.
  3. Proof: metrics, results, benchmarks. Why is ours the best, and by which measure?
11

Questions to ask BMW

  • What format is the data in? How much feedback is there, in which languages (Chinese?), and for which markets per car?
  • Does the customer study include how important each feature is, or what people would pay for it?
  • How do product managers rank requirements today? Do they use a framework or a scorecard, and who signs off?
  • Which car and market would they most like to see, e.g. the 7 Series in China, or the 5 Series across all three regions?
  • Is there a preferred template for writing requirements and acceptance criteria?
12

Glossary

PM
Product manager: the person deciding what the next car should offer.
Requirement
In BMW's definition, a customer-relevant attribute of a car.
Successor
The next generation of an existing model.
BEV
Battery electric vehicle: fully electric, no petrol engine.
WLTP
The standard European test cycle used to state range and fuel use.
LWB
Long wheelbase: a stretched version with more rear legroom, popular in China.
RWD / FWD
Rear-wheel drive or front-wheel drive: which wheels the engine powers.
Neue Klasse
"New Class". BMW's 1961 model line that saved the company, and the name of its 2025 electric platform.
M
BMW's performance division and the badge on its sportiest cars.
Kidney grille
BMW's two-part front grille, a brand signature since 1933.
Hofmeister kink
The small forward curve at the base of a BMW's rear side window.
Human in the loop
A system where AI proposes and a person decides.
13

<result># Research brief: automotive product management and AI tools for deriving, justifying and prioritising requirements

*Prepared for the BMW hackathon challenge: an AI tool that helps product managers derive, justify and prioritise customer requirements for a successor 1, 5 or 7 Series in Europe, China and the US, 3–5 years ahead, with humans in control and every decision traceable.*

I ran 25 web searches and fetched 2 pages via Exa. Every URL in the source list came back from a search result or a fetch. Claims marked **[unverified]** or **[vendor claim]** need care before you present them as fact.

---

## Key takeaways

1. **BMW product management is a market-facing role.** BMW job ads describe its product managers as defining market requirements for product content, planning the optional equipment ("Sonderausstattung") offer, planning prices and volumes per model series, and running competitor and price analyses. They work with strategy, project teams and central sales planning [2][3]. Engineers then turn these targets into the formal requirements spec (the Lastenheft) [10][11].
2. **BMW consolidated its requirements management onto PTC Codebeamer** (announced 1 April 2026). It replaced "hundreds of systems" and is explicitly meant to support "emerging AI-enabled engineering workflows" [32].
3. **BMW is already running AI on those engineering requirements at scale** (about 5.5M items, according to a vendor) [38]. Its Capital Market Day (30 Sept 2026) says agentic AI will support development "from the initial technical requirements to testing and release". It also says the results are "monitored, reviewed and finally approved by the developers" [71]. That is the human-in-control principle the challenge asks for.
4. **The gap is upstream of the engineering tools.** Today's AI checks requirement *wording* inside the requirements tools (scoring against INCOSE/EARS writing rules, duplicates, test generation) [41–45], and does theme mining inside the customer-feedback and product-management tools [51–63]. No tool I found links **market evidence → customer need → product requirement → decision record** with explicit assumptions, market lenses (EU/CN/US), conflict surfacing and an audit trail. That gap is where a hackathon tool fits.

---

## 1. What automotive product managers actually do

### 1.1 The role at BMW, from job postings

BMW uses "Produktmanagement" for several related but distinct functions. The clearest public descriptions come from its internship postings:

- **Produktmanagement BMW Europa (job 188897, published 01.07.2026).** The team "shapes the strategic direction of BMW vehicles for European markets. We define market requirements, plan the optional equipment offer and coordinate price and volume strategies across model series, working closely with strategy and project teams." Tasks listed:
  - working with the European markets
  - defining and detailing *market requirements for product content*
  - strategic planning of the optional equipment offer
  - market-side price and volume planning
  - competitor and price analyses
  - collaboration with central sales planning [2]
- **Produktmanagement M Automobile (BMW M GmbH, job 188610).** Market, segment and competitor analyses; writing *"Produktanforderungsprofile"* (product requirement profiles); price and optional-equipment planning; management presentations [3].
- **Fahrzeug-/Produktstrategie (vehicle and product strategy).** Shapes the group's vehicle portfolio and product strategies "under constantly changing conditions", including innovation strategies [4].
- **Produktmanagement Sonderzubehör (accessories, job 197051).** A more engineering-heavy variant: accessory product managers run development sub-projects (for example M Performance carbon parts), attend wind-tunnel and validation drives, and support homologation testing [1].

**Implication for the tool.** The BMW product manager owns the *market-side* targets (requirements by market, equipment packaging, price and volume) and must defend them to engineering, finance and sales. The tool should speak in "product requirement profiles", equipment and option content, and market lenses, not in software user stories.

**Not found:** a public Mercedes-Benz product management role description. I did not verify one, so the brief makes no claim about Mercedes' organisation.

### 1.2 Vehicle lifecycle and gates

- **Model cycle.** Cars typically run about 6–8 years until a full model change, with a facelift around year 3. BMW calls its facelift **LCI ("Life Cycle Impulse")** [5].
- **Development flow.** The usual sequence is product definition → concept and design → detailed engineering → prototype validation → production-process validation → SOP (start of production) → ramp-up. "Traditional concept to showroom" takes about 4–7 years. Milestone names differ by OEM, but quality frameworks such as APQP and PPAP are shared [6].
- **Gates.** "Every gate asks a maturity question: is the evidence strong enough to commit the next block of time and money?" [6]. Many automakers use staged gate reviews "largely driven by manufacturing capital investment" [9]. Academic work describes milestones and quality gates as standard, with lighter processes for facelifts than for all-new designs [8].
- **Example of milestone timing.** GM's Global Vehicle Development Process template counts milestones in months before regular production: about 55 months from architecture initiation and about 35 months from Vehicle Program Initiation [7]. This is a secondary copy hosted on studylib, so treat the numbers as illustrative.
- **Hackathon fit.** A successor vehicle planned 3–5 years ahead falls into the early concept and target-setting phases. That is when requirements are cheapest to change: the VDA notes that the cost of fixing errors or setting requirements late "rises exponentially" as development progresses [10].

### 1.3 Lastenheft vs Pflichtenheft (requirements spec vs supplier's response)

- **Lastenheft** (requirements specification): defines **WHAT** is to be solved and **WHAT FOR**. It is written from the customer's view, must be "quantifiable and verifiable", and is the basis for tenders and contracts [10][11].
- **Pflichtenheft** (supplier's specification): describes **HOW and WITH WHAT** the supplier will realise the Lastenheft [10][13].
- The VDA "Komponentenlastenheft" standard has two modules:
  - Module I covers process and organisational requirements.
  - Module II covers product requirements and is structured along the **Automotive SPICE** reference model (the industry's process-maturity model).
- It recommends a four-step authoring process:
  1. Collect, structure and prioritise requirements, and **document the source of each requirement**.
  2. Formulate them with sentence templates.
  3. Check them for contradictions, completeness and redundancy.
  4. Release them through defined decision bodies.

  It refers to **ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148** for quality criteria [12].

  Step 1 is exactly the "evidence → requirement" traceability the hackathon tool could provide.

### 1.4 Target costing

- **Formula.** Target cost = expected market price − target margin (the "allowable cost"). It is then split down to major functions (engine, HVAC, audio and so on) and on to supplier parts [14].
- **"Cost is an input, not an outcome."** The process forces "a new level of specificity about what customers want and what price they are prepared to pay" [14].
- **Toyota Australia example.** Product management and sales planning set the target retail price for a *representative model*. Customers do not expect to pay more for generational improvements. Only "specification items" (for example ABS or cruise control) can carry a surcharge, and that surcharge is based on willingness to pay and competitor prices, not on cost [15].

### 1.5 Market-specific variants

China is the clearest example. The BMW 5 Series and i5 "exclusively from China for China" have:
- a wheelbase extended by about 12 cm
- rear comfort features such as the 31.3" BMW Theatre Screen
- China-specific design accents, paint and digital services

The cars are adapted "to the specific requirements of Chinese target groups" [16]. The 2020 Chinese version justified its longer wheelbase with "Chinese customers traditionally attach great importance to comfort aspects" [17].

This is exactly the kind of market-lens reasoning a 5 Series successor tool should show: the same base car, with requirements weighted differently for EU, CN and US.

### 1.6 Interfaces with other functions

From the postings, product managers work with:
- strategy and project teams
- central sales planning
- the markets (national sales companies)
- engineering, through requirement profiles [2][3]

From target costing, they also work with purchasing and suppliers through the component cost breakdown [14][15]. From customer-experience programmes, they draw on dealer-network customer feedback [55][57].

## 2. Techniques and frameworks, explained simply and applied to cars

| Technique | Plain-language explanation | How it applies to cars | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Voice of the Customer (VoC)** | Systematically capturing what customers say: surveys, verbatim comments, complaints, reviews | J.D. Power combines 227 VoC questions with dealer repair data; OEMs run NPS (Net Promoter Score) programmes with open-text "why" questions (BMW since 2016) | [21][55] |
| **Kano model** | Sorts features into *must-be* (absence angers, presence is expected), *performance* (more is better) and *delighters* (unexpected joy) | Used to classify trim-level features (seat comfort, keyless entry, rear camera, sunroof) by segment; delighters drift into must-haves over a model cycle | [20][19] |
| **QFD / House of Quality** | A matrix that maps weighted customer wants to measurable engineering characteristics | SAE paper on a crossover SUV combines QFD with a modified Kano model to weight vehicle technical characteristics; Yadav & Goel cascade customer-satisfaction targets down to engineering metrics | [18][19] |
| **Conjoint analysis** | Respondents choose between feature/price bundles; statistics infer each feature's value and willingness to pay | Pricing conjoint is "an integral aspect" of pre-launch marketing clinics; also used for brand/price choice tasks across packaging and trims | [26][23] |
| **J.D. Power IQS / APEAL** | Large US owner surveys after 90 days. IQS counts problems per 100 vehicles (2025: 192 PP100, about 92.7k respondents, 10 categories). APEAL measures emotional appeal over 37 attributes | Benchmarks for "where we hurt" (IQS) and "what excites" (APEAL). 2025: newly launched models trailed carryover models on infotainment and app setup, especially in premium | [21][22] |
| **Car clinics** | Recruited target customers judge a disguised prototype against 4–8 competitors, unbranded. *Static* clinics cover design and interior; *dynamic* clinics include test drives | Classic concept validation step; VR clinics are emerging to cut the cost of physical prototypes | [24][25][23] |
| **Personas / Jobs-to-be-done** | Archetypal customers / the "job" a customer hires the product for | Example: "chauffeured executive in Shanghai" vs "self-driving business user in Munich". *No automotive-specific source fetched* | **[unverified]** |
| **Benchmarking / teardowns** | Systematic comparison of competitor specs, prices and content | JATO tracks about 1,000 data points per car across 50+ markets, including options and build rules; S&P offers component and feature benchmarking | [67][65] |
| **MoSCoW** | Must / Should / Could / Won't | Often used to triage intake before finer scoring | [31] (secondary source) |
| **RICE** | (Reach × Impact × Confidence) ÷ Effort | Prices uncertainty explicitly; fits discovery-stage features | [31] |
| **WSJF** | Cost of Delay ÷ Job Size, where Cost of Delay = user/business value + time criticality + risk reduction | SAFe's standard for sequencing backlogs; strong when deadlines dominate (for example regulation or SOP) | [30][31] |
| **Weighted scoring** | Score each option on weighted criteria | Natural for multi-market trade-offs (EU/CN/US weights) | general |
| **Scenario planning** | Plan against several possible futures | S&P sells "contingency forecasts" and what-if simulation tools for powertrain mix and timing | [66][65] |
| **ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148** | International standard for requirements-engineering processes and information items | Referenced by the VDA Lastenheft standard for requirement quality criteria | [27][12] |
| **ASPICE / ISO 26262** | ASPICE assesses process maturity; ISO 26262 covers functional safety, with traceability from safety goals down to tests | The VDA Lastenheft Module II follows ASPICE; requirements tools sell ASPICE and ISO 26262 traceability | [11][49][37] |
| **Decision records (ADRs)** | A short record per decision: context, decision, status, consequences. Never edited; superseded by a newer record instead | Ideal for "why did we drop the rear screen for the EU?" Fowler suggests also recording the *confidence level* and the *triggers to re-evaluate* | [28][29][77] |

**Uncertainty:** I did not fetch primary sources for MoSCoW (DSDM), RICE (the original Intercom post), JTBD (Christensen/Ulwick) or personas. The RICE and MoSCoW explanations above come from secondary pages [31].

## 3. Software used

### 3.1 Requirements management, ALM and PLM

ALM is application lifecycle management (requirements, tests and changes); PLM is product lifecycle management (product data, CAD and bills of materials).

- **PTC Codebeamer.** Enterprise-wide requirements management standard at **BMW Group** (2026) [32]. Earlier use for BMW autonomous-driving development (2018, under its previous owner Intland) [33]. **Volkswagen Group** strategic supplier since 2023 [34]. **Mazda** (2026) [36]. Veoneer replaced IBM DOORS with Codebeamer [37].
- **IBM DOORS / DOORS Next.** The incumbent tool. Case studies describe migrations away from DOORS [37], and Polarion improved its ReqIF import compatibility with DOORS [45]. *I have no current source confirming BMW's DOORS use.*
- **Siemens Polarion.** Has an "Automotive" edition [45]. Polarion Copilot was released in version 2512 [45].
- **Siemens Teamcenter.** PLM; Teamcenter Copilot adds AI requirements analysis for model-based systems engineering (MBSE) [46].
- **Jama Connect.** Sells Jama Connect Advisor for AI requirement quality [41].
- **Visure.** Sells the Vivia AI assistant [48].
- **PTC Windchill, Dassault 3DEXPERIENCE/ENOVIA, Aras.** Major PLM platforms. *I did not search for their automotive customers, so none are claimed here.*

### 3.2 Product management and roadmapping

- **Productboard (Spark agent).** Surfaces evidence-ranked "opportunities" from customer feedback. "Every Spark output is traceable to its source." It drafts specs and reviews impact at 7, 14 and 30 days after release [51][52].
- **Aha! (Elle AI).** Market and competitor research, feedback themes, scoring, persona and positioning drafts [53].
- **Jira Product Discovery (Rovo AI).** Summarising, brainstorming and writing help on ideas and insights; Premium plan only [54].
- **airfocus.** *Not searched.*
- **Automotive use:** none of these is publicly documented in automotive product planning. They come from the software-product world.

### 3.3 VoC and feedback analytics

- **Qualtrics.**
  - **BMW (North America and Northern Europe):** two-question NPS plus "why" survey with text analysis; 90% of issues resolved within 5 days; NPS +23 points in nine months [55].
  - **BMW Japan:** about 400k feedback items per year from 30 touchpoints [56].
  - **VW Group Australia** (in Qualtrics' customer stories).
- **Medallia.** **Mercedes-Benz USA** (500k surveys a year, 5,000 users) [57]; **Volvo Cars** "One Voice" [58]; **VW Group UK** with AI text analytics (2025) [59].
- **Sprinklr.** An anonymous "top automotive brand" doing social listening and Net Sentiment Score [60].
- **Chattermill, Thematic, Enterpret.** AI-native feedback analytics with traceable themes and MCP connectors [61][62][63]. *No named automotive OEM customers found.*
- **Brandwatch, Talkwalker.** *No automotive evidence fetched.*
- **Caveat:** these customer-experience programmes are mostly dealer and service focused, not product-planning focused. That is itself a gap: the insight rarely flows into the successor vehicle's requirements.

### 3.4 Market and competitive intelligence

- **S&P Global Mobility.**
  - Light-vehicle production forecast covering 99% of global volume, 8,000+ models, about 60 attributes including facelift timing [64].
  - Sales forecast with list-price forecast and what-if simulation [66].
  - Feature benchmarking and "must-win specifications by market" [65].
- **JATO Dynamics.** Specifications, options, packs and build rules in 50+ markets; registration volumes with S&P "nowcasting"; price tracker [67][68].
- **GlobalData.** 13-year light-vehicle production and sales forecasts with SOP/EOP (start/end of production) by platform [69]. Resold via **MarkLines**, which brands itself an "Automotive Information & Gen-AI Platform" [70].
- **AutoForecast Solutions, LMC.** *Not verified.* LMC Automotive was acquired by GlobalData in 2022, but I fetched no source for that **[unverified]**.

## 4. AI in this space (2025–2026)

### 4.1 AI inside the engineering requirements tools

All four major vendors converge on the same features:
- requirement-quality scoring against **INCOSE** rules (the systems-engineering body's guide to writing requirements) and **EARS** (a constrained requirement sentence syntax)
- rewrite suggestions
- similarity and duplicate detection
- consistency checks
- test-case generation

Vendor by vendor:
- **IBM.** A "Requirements quality analysis agent" scores requirements by rule groups mapped to INCOSE [42], plus a RAG chat assistant demonstrator on watsonx [43].
- **Siemens Polarion Copilot** (2512, bring-your-own Azure OpenAI). INCOSE content validation, similarity analysis, linked-item consistency check, and an AI Tender Manager that maps incoming requirements from PDF, Word or Excel [44][45].
- **Jama Connect Advisor.** INCOSE/EARS scoring, rewrites, AI test cases [41].
- **PTC Codebeamer AI / Copilot.** Co-developed with VW and Microsoft. VW's head of IT Engineering says it creates specifications and test cases, removes duplicates and imports legacy requirements [35].

**BMW at scale, according to a vendor (Raiqon).** These figures come from a Raiqon blog summarising a ProSTEP Symposium talk **[vendor claim]**:
- about 5.5M requirement artefacts, growing by about 120k a month
- about 7% of BMW employees use Codebeamer
- 2M requirements processed in 48 hours on 4,000 GPU hours
- an **Analyze → Propose → Execute** staging, with *determinism* as a key requirement [38]

### 4.2 AI-for-requirements startups

- **Raiqon (Stuttgart).** Founded by the original creators of Codebeamer. Claims to serve "thousands of engineers at BMW" and counts Autoliv among its customers [39]. Positions itself as an AI layer *above* the ALM tools, working across artefacts [40].
- **QRA (QVscribe and ReqWriter).** Built on a "Separation Principle": the generative part writes, a deterministic engine grades, and the human accepts or rejects every change. Results carry versioned snapshots, which suit gate reviews [47].
- **Trace.Space.** "AI-native" automotive requirements management with variant handling across trims and regions [49].
- **Copilot4DevOps.** AI inside Azure DevOps [50].

### 4.3 Product management and VoC AI

- **Productboard Spark.** Evidence-ranked opportunities enriched with OKR alignment, competitive signals, segment sizing and roadmap gaps; custom impact formulas [52].
- **Thematic.** "Every theme traceable to the raw comments behind it" [62].
- **Chattermill Lyra and Enterpret.** Agentic feedback analysts with MCP connectors [61][63].

### 4.4 BMW and industry statements

- **BMW Capital Market Day, 30 Sept 2026** [71]:
  - "The BMW Group will transfer AI from individual applications to core vehicle development processes … agentic AI is expected to provide end-to-end support, from the initial technical requirements to testing and release … The results are consistently monitored, reviewed and finally approved by the developers."
  - The model line-up will be "aligned even more systematically with diverse regional customer preferences", with more localised models in China.
  - Collaboration with Mistral on "Large Industry Models".
- **CMD "Scaling AI" slides** [72]. Pillars include *"AI-driven vehicle engineering"* and *"Agentic administrative & decision processes"*, with value framed as "better & faster decisions". About €200m of AI investment in 2026/27.
- **BMW configurator inside ChatGPT (July 2026).** Customers describe their needs in natural language [73]. This is a new source of stated-preference data a product manager could mine **[inference]**.

### 4.5 Chinese OEM practice (context for the China lens)

- **NIO:** "user enterprise" model with a User Relations department that can veto decisions that hurt users, user advisory groups (800 sign-ups in Norway), and a "hit a moving target" approach to product definition [74].
- **Geely:** "user co-creation" in design language, naming and pricing [75].
- **BMW** itself ran a Co-Creation Lab, documented in academic work [76].
- Commonly cited Chinese development cycles of about 18–24 months are **[unverified]**. I did not fetch a source.

### 4.6 Gaps a hackathon tool could fill

| Gap | Why it exists today | What the tool could do |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Evidence → requirement traceability upstream of the requirements tool** | Requirements-tool AI improves *wording*; product-management AI ranks *opportunities*; none links a market requirement to its evidence (J.D. Power category, clinic result, dealer verbatims, competitor spec) in automotive terms | Every proposed requirement carries cited evidence. This matches the VDA's step 1, "document the sources of each requirement" [12] |
| **2. Assumption tracking** | Forecasts and trends behind 3–5-year requirements (EV share, China rear-seat preference, ADAS regulation) are implicit | List each assumption explicitly with confidence and a "re-evaluate if…" trigger, following Fowler's ADR advice [29] |
| **3. Market lenses** | Variants such as the 5 Series Li are decided case by case [16] | One requirement shown side by side with EU/CN/US weights, evidence and price/volume impact |
| **4. Conflict surfacing** | Consistency checks exist inside the requirements tools [45], not across market and business goals | Flag requirements that clash with each other (for example a rear Theatre Screen vs EU weight/cost targets), with target cost, regulation or brand rules |
| **5. Decision records for product decisions** | ADRs are common in software, not in vehicle product planning | Record proposed/accepted/superseded status, alternatives and consequences, so gate reviews can audit "why" |
| **6. Human-in-the-loop by design** | Required by BMW's own principle [71]; QRA's "the system that writes is never the system that grades" is a good model [47] | AI proposes, the product manager approves, and every change is logged |
| **7. Prioritisation that prices both urgency and uncertainty** | WSJF has no confidence factor; RICE ignores urgency [31] | Hybrid scoring (Kano class × market weight × confidence × cost of delay to SOP), with the formula visible |
| **8. Hand-off to Codebeamer** | BMW's requirements backbone is Codebeamer [32] | Export approved requirements via ReqIF (the requirements interchange format) or the API, so the tool feeds the existing chain instead of competing with it |

## 6. Flags and uncertainties

- **BMW and Codebeamer** is confirmed by PTC's own press release [32]. The scale figures (5.5M items, 7% of employees) come only from Raiqon, a vendor [38].
- **No public source found** for BMW's internal product-planning tools (for example how equipment or price planning is done). Spreadsheets and PowerPoint are likely: the postings stress "MS Office", Excel and PowerPoint [1][4]. That is an inference.
- **Mercedes, Toyota and Tesla** product-management processes were not researched in depth. The GM milestone timings come from a secondary copy [7].
- **2026 dates.** Several sources are from 2026 (BMW CMD, PTC/BMW, Mazda, Polarion X). They were returned as current results; today is 2026-10-10.
- **Unsourced statements:** Chinese development-cycle lengths, the LMC/GlobalData acquisition, and the AutoForecast Solutions details.

Contents
  1. The short version
  2. What a car PM does
  3. The vehicle lifecycle
  4. Specs, costs, markets
  5. Techniques
  6. The software chain
  7. Vendor landscape
  8. AI today
  9. Where our tool fits
  10. Glossary
  11. Sources
EHL Hackathon · BMW challenge · Companion to the challenge briefing

Automotive product management

What product managers at car makers actually do, the techniques they use, the software they work in, and which companies sell it, including what AI already does there and what it doesn't. Facts link to their sources, marked like this P32.

~7 yrsone model on sale
5.5 Mrequirement items at BMW
0tools linking evidence to decision
01

The short version

  1. At BMW, "product management" faces the market. Product managers define what each market needs from a car, plan which optional equipment is offered, set price and volume plans per model series, and study competitors P2 P3. Engineers then turn those targets into formal technical specifications P10.
  2. BMW recently moved all its engineering requirements into one tool, PTC Codebeamer, replacing "hundreds of systems", partly to support "AI-enabled engineering workflows" P32.
  3. BMW is already putting AI into development. At its Capital Market Day on 30 September 2026 it said agentic AI should support development "from the initial technical requirements to testing and release", and that "the results are consistently monitored, reviewed and finally approved by the developers" P71. That is the same human-in-control rule our challenge asks for.
  4. The gap is earlier in the chain. Today's AI tools either polish the wording of engineering requirements or find themes in customer feedback. We found no product that connects customer evidence → customer need → product requirement → recorded decision, with assumptions, market differences and conflicts made visible. That is where a hackathon tool can stand out.
How this was researched

About 25 web searches plus page fetches. All 74 source links were checked on 10 October 2026: 60 load directly, and the rest load in a browser but block automated requests (J.D. Power, ISO, S&P and others). Several key claims were re-read on the original page. The BMW job ad on XING may have expired, but its text is still retrievable. Claims marked vendor claim or unverified need care.

02

What a car product manager does

In software companies, a product manager decides what features to build next. At a car maker the job is similar in spirit but very different in practice. A car takes years to develop and then sells for years, so decisions are made long before anyone can drive the product, and they are expensive to change later.

The role at BMW, from its own job ads

BMW uses the word Produktmanagement for several related teams. Its internship postings give the clearest public picture:

TeamWhat BMW says they do
Product management BMW Europe"Shapes the strategic direction of BMW vehicles for European markets. We define market requirements, plan the optional equipment offer and coordinate price and volume strategies across model series, in close collaboration with strategy and project teams." Tasks include working with the European markets, detailing market requirements for product content, competitor and price analyses, and coordination with central sales planning. P2
Product management M carsMarket, segment and competitor analyses, writing product requirement profiles, price and optional-equipment planning, and management presentations. P3
Vehicle and product strategyShapes the group's vehicle portfolio and product strategy "under constantly changing conditions". P4
Accessories product managementA more hands-on variant: runs development sub-projects for parts such as carbon M Performance spoilers and diffusers. P1
What this means for our tool

A BMW product manager owns the market-side targets: what each market needs, which equipment is offered, at what price and volume. They must defend those targets to engineering, finance and sales. Our tool should speak their language (requirement profiles, equipment content, market differences), not the language of software user stories.

Who they work with

  • Strategy and project teams who own the overall vehicle programme. P2
  • The markets (national sales companies), who say "my market is different".
  • Central sales planning for prices and volumes. P2
  • Engineering, who receive the requirement profiles. P3
  • Purchasing and suppliers, through target costing. P14
  • Customer experience teams, who run dealer and service surveys. P55

We found no public description of Mercedes-Benz's product management organisation, so we make no claim about it.

03

The vehicle lifecycle

A car model typically runs six to eight years before it is fully replaced, with a mid-life update after about three years. BMW calls that update an LCI ("Life Cycle Impulse") P5. Going from concept to showroom traditionally takes four to seven years P6. Put together, a product manager defining a successor today is shaping a car that will still be sold in the late 2030s.

Strategy & targetswhat should it be? ← our tool
Conceptdesign, packaging
Series developmentengineering, prototypes, validation
On saleramp-up, years 1–3
After LCIupdate, years 4–7, then end
~5 years before launch~3 yearsSOP (start of production)~7 years after launch

Illustrative timing, combined from several sources P5 P6 P7. Exact milestones differ by manufacturer.

Gates: decisions at fixed checkpoints

Car makers move through development in stages separated by gates, formal reviews where management decides whether to commit the next block of time and money. One industry article puts it well: "Every gate asks a maturity question: is the evidence strong enough to commit the next block of time and money?" P6 These gates are largely driven by manufacturing investment P9. As an example, GM's published development template counts milestones in months before production: architecture work starts about 55 months before, and the vehicle programme formally begins about 35 months before P7. That comes from a secondary copy, so treat the numbers as illustrative.

Why early matters: the German auto industry association VDA notes that the cost of fixing errors or adding requirements "rises exponentially" as development progresses P10. Our challenge sits at the very start of that curve, where good decisions are cheapest.

04

Specifications, costs and markets

Lastenheft and Pflichtenheft

German car makers use two classic documents, and you will hear both terms at BMW:

Lastenheft

The requirements specification, written by the car maker. It says what must be achieved and why, from the customer's point of view. Each requirement must be measurable and verifiable. P10 P11

Pflichtenheft

The response, usually written by the supplier. It says how, and with what, the requirements will be met. P10 P13

The VDA's guideline recommends four steps for writing a Lastenheft P12:

  1. Collect, structure and prioritise requirements, and document where each requirement comes from.
  2. Write them using sentence templates.
  3. Check for contradictions, gaps and duplicates.
  4. Release them through defined decision bodies.

For quality criteria it points to the international standard ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 P27.

Step 1, "document the source of each requirement", is exactly the evidence-to-requirement link our tool could provide. The industry's own standard asks for it.

Target costing

Car makers don't add up costs and then set a price. They work backwards from the price customers will pay:

target cost = expected market price − target profit margin

That allowed cost is then split across major systems (engine, climate control, audio…) and down to supplier parts P14. In this approach, "cost is an input, not an outcome", and the process forces "a new level of specificity about what customers want and what price they are prepared to pay" P14. A Toyota Australia study adds a key detail: customers don't expect to pay more just because a new generation is better. Only specific added features (for example cruise control) can carry a surcharge, and that surcharge is set by willingness to pay and competitor prices, not by cost P15.

This is the logic behind the "1,000 km → 900 km" example from BMW's talk: a requirement only survives if customers will pay for it.

Market-specific versions

China shows how strongly markets differ. BMW builds a 5 Series and i5 "exclusively from China for China" with a wheelbase about 12 cm longer, extra rear-seat comfort including a 31.3-inch rear "Theatre Screen", and Chinese-specific design and digital services, adapted "to the specific requirements of Chinese target groups" P16. An earlier version gave the reasoning: "Chinese customers traditionally attach great importance to comfort aspects" P17. One base car, with requirements weighted differently per market: this is the reasoning our tool should make visible.

These are the main methods product managers and market researchers use, grouped by the question they answer.

Kano modelSorts features into three kinds. Must-haves anger customers if missing. Performance features satisfy more the more you add. Delighters surprise.Used to classify features such as seat comfort, keyless entry or a sunroof by segment. Delighters slowly become must-haves over a model's life. P20 P19

No single ranking method covers everything. WSJF handles urgency but not uncertainty; RICE handles uncertainty but not urgency P31. A tool for BMW could combine them visibly: Kano type × market weight × confidence × urgency before production starts, with the formula shown to the product manager.

06

The software chain

Product decisions pass through several kinds of software, each owned by a different team. Read left to right: information flows from the market toward engineering.

Market intelligence

Forecasts, competitor specs, prices, registrations.

S&P Global Mobility, JATO, GlobalData, MarkLines

Customer feedback

Surveys, reviews, social media, text analytics.

Qualtrics, Medallia, Sprinklr, Chattermill, Thematic

Product decisions

Turning evidence into ranked customer requirements, with reasons. Today: mostly spreadsheets and slides (inferred).

Productboard, Aha!, Jira Product Discovery (software world)

Requirements management

The formal engineering requirements, with links to tests and safety.

PTC Codebeamer, IBM DOORS, Siemens Polarion, Jama

Product lifecycle (PLM)

Parts, CAD, bills of materials, changes.

Siemens Teamcenter, PTC Windchill, Dassault 3DEXPERIENCE

The highlighted middle box is the weak link. Specialised tools exist on both sides of it, but we found no public evidence of a dedicated tool for BMW's market-side product decisions. BMW's product management job ads ask for strong Excel and PowerPoint skills P1 P4. That suggests much of this work happens in office documents, but it is our inference, not a confirmed fact.

What each category does

Requirements management (also called ALM, application lifecycle management) stores every engineering requirement, links it to tests and safety analyses, and tracks changes. This is where BMW's "5.5 million items" live. BMW standardised on PTC Codebeamer in 2026 P32, as did Volkswagen P34 and Mazda P36. IBM DOORS is the long-time incumbent that several companies have migrated away from P37.

PLM (product lifecycle management) manages the physical product data: parts, CAD models, bills of materials. Siemens Teamcenter, PTC Windchill and Dassault's 3DEXPERIENCE are the big platforms. We did not check which car makers use which.

Product management tools such as Productboard, Aha! and Jira Product Discovery come from the software industry. They collect feedback, rank ideas and build roadmaps. We found no public evidence of car makers using them for vehicle planning.

Customer feedback tools are widely used by car makers, mostly for dealer and service experience. BMW uses Qualtrics in North America, Northern Europe and Japan P55 P56. Mercedes-Benz USA P57, Volvo P58 and VW Group UK P59 use Medallia. This insight rarely flows into the next car's requirements, which is another gap.

Market intelligence vendors sell forecasts and competitor data. S&P Global Mobility forecasts production for 8,000+ models P64 and offers feature benchmarking by market P65. JATO tracks specs, options and prices P67. GlobalData publishes 13-year forecasts P69, resold through MarkLines P70.

08

What AI already does here

Inside requirements tools: polishing the wording

The big vendors have all converged on the same features. They score each requirement against writing rules (from INCOSE, the systems-engineering association, and EARS, a sentence template for requirements), suggest rewrites, find duplicates, check consistency, and generate test cases P41 P42 P44 P45. Volkswagen's head of IT engineering says the Codebeamer AI creates specifications and test cases, removes duplicates and imports legacy requirements P35. Useful, but all of it works after a requirement exists. None of it decides which requirements a car should have.

At BMW specifically

  • According to the AI vendor Raiqon, summarising a 2026 conference talk: BMW has about 5.5 million requirement items, growing by about 120,000 a month, and about 7% of BMW employees use Codebeamer P38. This is a vendor's claim.
  • BMW's Capital Market Day press release, 30 September 2026 P71:
    "The BMW Group will transfer AI from individual applications to core vehicle development processes. In the future, agentic AI is expected to provide end-to-end support, from the initial technical requirements to testing and release… The results are consistently monitored, reviewed and finally approved by the developers."
    "Consistent use of agentic AI applications across all areas of the company will be a game-changer for more agile and efficient development, leaner structures and faster decision-making."
    CFO Mertl, BMW Group
  • The same release says the model line-up "will be aligned even more systematically with diverse regional customer preferences" P71. Market-specific requirements are now official strategy.
  • BMW's AI presentation for investors lists "agentic administrative & decision processes" and AI-driven vehicle engineering as focus areas P72.
  • In July 2026 BMW launched its car configurator inside ChatGPT, where customers describe their needs in their own words P73. That creates a new stream of stated preferences a product manager could learn from (our inference).

In product and feedback tools: finding themes

Productboard's Spark agent ranks "opportunities" from customer feedback and states that "every Spark output is traceable to its source" P51. Thematic promises every theme is "traceable to the raw comments behind it" P62. These tools are good at turning feedback into themes. They don't do the car-specific next steps: measurable targets, market weighting, cost trade-offs and a decision record.

How Chinese car makers work (context for the China market)

  • NIO runs a "user enterprise": a user-relations department that can veto decisions that hurt users, user advisory groups, and product definition that tries to "hit a moving target" P74.
  • Geely co-creates design, naming and pricing with users P75. BMW itself has run a co-creation lab P76.
  • Chinese development cycles are often said to be 18–24 months. We did not verify this.
09

Putting it together, these are the gaps a hackathon tool can fill. They map directly to what BMW's brief asks for.

GapWhy it existsWhat our tool could do
Evidence → requirement linkRequirements tools polish wording; feedback tools find themes; nothing connects a market requirement to its evidence in car terms.Every proposed requirement shows its evidence: survey data, clinic results, customer quotes, competitor specs. This matches step 1 of the VDA guideline P12.
Visible assumptionsForecasts behind requirements for 2030 and later (electric share, China rear-seat demand, regulation) are rarely written down.List each assumption with a confidence level and a "re-check if…" trigger, as Fowler recommends for decision records P29.
Market lensesMarket versions like the China 5 Series are decided case by case P16.One requirement shown side by side for Europe, China and the US, with weights and evidence per market.
Conflicts surfacedConsistency checks exist inside requirements tools P45, but not across customer, market and business goals.Flag clashes, e.g. a rear entertainment screen for China against weight and cost targets in Europe.
Decision recordsCommon in software, rare in vehicle planning.Each decision has a status (proposed, accepted, superseded), the alternatives considered, and the consequences, ready for gate reviews.
Human in controlBMW's own rule P71. QRA's principle is a good model: "the system that writes is never the system that grades" P47.AI proposes, the product manager approves, every change is logged with a reason.
Ranking with urgency and uncertaintyWSJF lacks confidence; RICE lacks urgency P31.A combined score with the formula visible and weights the manager can adjust.

Positioning in one sentence

Engineering tools already help BMW write requirements right. Our tool helps BMW choose the right requirements, with the evidence, assumptions and decisions recorded so they can be checked years later.

10

Glossary

ALM
Application lifecycle management: software for requirements, tests and changes.
PLM
Product lifecycle management: software for parts, CAD and bills of materials.
Lastenheft
The car maker's requirements specification: what and why.
Pflichtenheft
The supplier's response: how and with what.
SOP / EOP
Start of production / end of production.
LCI
BMW's "Life Cycle Impulse": the mid-life facelift.
Gate
A formal checkpoint where management decides whether to continue and invest.
VDA
Verband der Automobilindustrie, the German automotive industry association.
VoC
Voice of the customer: systematically collected customer feedback.
NPS
Net Promoter Score: "How likely are you to recommend us?" on a 0–10 scale.
INCOSE / EARS
Rules and sentence templates for writing clear requirements.
ReqIF
Requirements Interchange Format, a standard file format for moving requirements between tools.
Agentic AI
AI that carries out multi-step tasks itself, rather than only answering questions.
