I've turned everything into two HTML pages that link to each other. Both are private: only you can open them until you share them from each page's Share menu. Local copies are in the project folder.

**1. BMW Challenge Briefing:** https://claude.ai/artifact/NS6BitrKPZXVND9QPpzyWr (`bmw-challenge-briefing.html`)
- Covers the brief, both slides, what BMW's product manager said, the film with nine stills, BMW's history, values and quotes, the meaning of "The Ultimate Driving Machine", what the judges want, the rules, and a glossary.
- Every fact taken from outside material links to its source.

**2. Automotive Product Management:** https://claude.ai/artifact/9fyNRncZ2gUCNz9vUvfPtG (`automotive-product-management.html`)
- **What the role is at BMW:** product managers face the market. They decide what each market needs, which optional equipment is offered, and the price and volume plans per model series. Engineers then turn that into formal specifications.
- **How the work is done:** the vehicle lifecycle and its decision checkpoints, the two classic German specification documents, how car makers set costs by working back from the price, and how BMW adapts cars for China.
- **Techniques, explained simply:** customer feedback programmes, J.D. Power quality studies, car clinics, the Kano model, ranking methods, and decision records.
- **Software and vendors:** the chain of tools from market data to engineering, and a table of 23 companies with their AI features and car-maker customers we could confirm.

**Three findings matter most for your pitch:**
- **BMW moved all its engineering requirements into one tool, PTC Codebeamer, in April 2026.** PTC's announcement says it is partly meant to support AI.
- **BMW committed to agentic AI in development on 30 September 2026.** It said the AI should support development "from the initial technical requirements to testing and release", and that the results are "finally approved by the developers". That is the human-in-control rule the challenge asks for, in BMW's own words.
- **No tool on the market connects customer evidence to a requirement and then to a recorded decision.** Today's AI tools either polish the wording of engineering requirements or find themes in feedback. Linking the two, with assumptions and market differences visible, is the gap your tool can fill.

**How the sources were checked:**
- I checked the 74 links on the product management page. All load in a browser, though some big sites block automated checks.
- I re-read the three most important claims on the original pages: the Codebeamer adoption, BMW's AI statement, and the vendor's figure of 5.5 million requirement items at BMW.
- The 5.5 million figure comes only from that vendor, and the page marks it as a vendor claim.

**Correction to the first page:** Oliver Zipse is no longer BMW's CEO; the 30 September release names Milan Nedeljković. Zipse's quotes are from 2025, when he was CEO, and both pages and `notes.md` now say so.

**Not found:** I couldn't confirm which internal tools BMW's product managers use for equipment and price planning. Their job ads ask for strong Excel and PowerPoint skills, which suggests office documents. The page marks that as our inference.

Quick Guide

 How to Enable,
Review, and Merge
with Trails​
September 2026
Trails is Entire’s answer to reviewing and deploying code in the era of AI.
Unlike a pull request, a Trail can start before code exists, even at the stage of
brainstorming. You can enter a description covering the problem you want to solve and
an intended solution, and then you kick off the Trail from there. As work progresses,
Entire keeps the commits, agent sessions in the recorded history, then presents review
findings, monitor scores, and decisions together on the same page. Then you can merge
the code without relying on the diff alone.
This guide walks through the steps it takes to onboard and use Trails: from creation, to
building, reviewing the evidence and monitor scores, to merging. By the time you’re done
reading, you should be able to hit the Trail running.

 ​

1.​ Get your repository on Entire
Make sure your repository is activated and mirrored on Entire

2.​Enable Trails
●​ Open your repository and visit Settings -> General
●​ Turn on Runners, Auto build on push and Trails
●​ Optionally: Visit Settings -> Gates to enable and configure Gates to evaluate and
enforce merging.
Note: Each Trails is currently backed by a PR on GitHub for CI

3.​Set Up Runners
Runners evaluate each Trail and publish findings or visually display results to judge the
quality of the changes.
Entire has a default set of Runners to start. From the repository root, add the defaults via
the CLI:

 Shell

entire runner setup -y

As you can see, each runner has a config file inside of the .entire/ directory of your
repository. Customize them or merge the generated defaults right away.

4.​Create a Trail
Thanks to the Entire CLI, your agent knows how to use Trails. Just ask and your agent
can create, update, or switch to a specific Trail.
The full set of Trail commands are available by using the​
entire help trail command.
All you need to do is work normally, commit and push your changes to the Trail branch.
The Trail updates automatically, runners evaluate the latest push, and your team can
review and merge from the Trail.

 Key Terms
First, a few definitions, so you can speak our language.
Checkpoint: a checkpoint is basically an autosave, a point at which your work is saved
without committing.
Finding: an issue with your code that prevents a trail from merging.
Gate: a merge requirement.
Runner: evaluation metrics that inform the gates.
Monitor: a judgment “scorecard” monitoring verification status against the runners. Ours run

If You Don’t Already Have Entire Setup
The steps below assume Entire is installed on your machine and your repository is connected
to entire.io with trails turned on. If your team has already done this, start at step 1.
1. Install the CLI
Shell
brew tap entireio/tap
brew trust entireio/tap
brew install --cask entire
On Linux, run curl -fsSL https://entire.io/install.sh | bash. On Windows, use Scoop: scoop
bucket add entire https://github.com/entireio/scoop-bucket.git, then scoop install
entire/entire.
2. Confirm the Install
Shell
entire version
 3. Sign In to Entire
Shell
entire login
4. Enable Entire in Your Repository
This installs the Git and agent hooks and creates the .entire/ settings your team shares:
Shell
entire enable
Pass --agent to skip the prompt, for example entire enable --agent claude-code.
5. Connect the Repository to entire.io
Open repository setup, select Configure GitHub App, and give Entire access to the repository.
A repository owned by a GitHub organization needs an organization admin to install or update
the app.
6. Turn On Trails
Open the repository in entire.io, select Settings, then turn on:
-​ Runners
-​ Trails under Workflow
-​ Auto build on push.
This requires admin permission on the repository. Once the repository appears in entire.io
with trails turned on, continue with the steps below.
If You Do Already Have Entire Setup
0. Turn on Trails if you haven’t already (see above)
1. Create a Trail
In entire.io
1.​ Open a repository and select Trails.
2.​ Select New Trail.
 3.​ Enter a title and, if you like, a description. A good description covers the
problem, intended outcome, and any important constraints or acceptance
criteria.
4.​ Choose the status, type, assignees, and priority.
5.​ Leave the Trail branchless, enter a new branch name, or link an existing branch.
6.​ Select Create Trail.
In the CLI
1.​ Open a terminal in your Git repository.
2.​ Run the interactive creation flow:
Shell
entire trail create
3.​ To skip the form, create a Trail for the current branch by passing a title:
Shell
entire trail create --title "Add account recovery"
Add --checkout to switch to a new branch after Entire creates it from the title.
2. Build the Change
1.​ Work on the Trail’s branch with your coding agent. Entire adds the resulting
checkpoints and agent sessions to the Trail.
2.​ Commit your changes when they’re ready for evaluation:
a.​ Tell your agent to add and commit
b.​ OR
Shell
git add .
git commit -m "Add account recovery"
3.​ Push the branch:
a.​ ask the agent to push the trail. The agent recognizes the trail connected to the
branch with the help of the CLI and it will take care of committing and pushing.
b.​ OR
 Shell
git push
3. Review the Trail
1.​ Read the description and confirm that the implementation matches the intended
outcome.
2.​ Check the Confidence, Risk, Security, and Drift monitors for anything that needs
attention.
3.​ Select View changes and review the diff.
4.​ If there are code review findings, open each finding and decide whether to fix,
resolve, or dismiss it.
5.​ Use Sessions and the timeline when you need the agent context behind a decision.
After another push, findings tied to older code may become stale. Current findings remain
open until they are resolved or dismissed.
Since your coding agent interfaces with Entire through the CLI, you can also complete the
loop from your agent, for example by telling the agent to review open findings on the trail and
address them.
4. Approve and Merge
Gate
What it Evaluates
Options
Up to date
Whether the Trail branch is current with its
base
Allow a clean merge while behind
Human
review
Approvals submitted on the Trail
Minimum approvals, whether the author
counts, and whether pushes reset approvals
Agent review
Unresolved runner findings on the latest push
Minimum severity that counts as unresolved
Checks
CI checks reported through GitHub
Use GitHub-required checks or provide
specific check names
1.​ Review the gates section for anything blocking the merge. Gates show which
conditions are satisfied, pending, or blocking the merge. ​
A repository can require an up-to-date branch, human approvals, an agent review
without unresolved findings, and passing checks. You can also choose who may
bypass a blocking gate. Every bypass is recorded on the Trail.
2.​ Select Approve when your review is complete.
3.​ Select Merge after every blocking gate passes.
 One-Time Runner Setup For Repo Owners
Repository owners configure runners (the repo evaluators) and gates (the verification checks)
once. Everyone else can start with the workflow above.
Add the Default Runners
1.​ Open a terminal at the repository root.
2.​ Create the default runner configuration:
Shell
entire runner setup -y
3.​ Commit the generated runner files to the default branch:
Shell
git add .entire/runners
git commit -m "Configure trail runners"
4.​ Push and merge the runner configuration.
The defaults add a Trail summary, review focus, code review findings, and Confidence,
Risk, Security, and Drift monitors.
5.​ Optionally, tailor the runner prompts to your repository:
Shell
entire runner setup --run
6.​ Review and commit the updated runner files.
 Configure Merge Gates
1.​ Open the repository in entire.io.
2.​ Select Settings, then Gates.
3.​ Turn on Enable gates.
4.​ Set each gate to Block, Optional, or Off.
5.​ Start with the requirements your team already uses for pull requests.
6.​ Make Agent review blocking after the trail-review runner is in place.

  - The G60 and G70 comments are 90–95% US. They come from four sources; my guess from the writing style is call-centre notes (about 5,500), owner reviews, quality surveys and appeal surveys.

**Strongest candidate requirements**
1. **Physical controls and simpler menus.** 185 comments criticise the touchscreen (119 of them F70), plus 69 on the operating system. US scores for climate controls are 4.80 (G60) and 4.51 (G70) out of 7.
2. **Reliable software and connectivity.** "Connected services" is the lowest or near-lowest score in all five China/EU columns (7.32–7.86). Feedback adds eSIM (48), CarPlay (65) and the BMW app (52).
3. **Value for money and fewer paid extras.** The EU 7 Series scores 6.47 on value, the lowest number in the sheet. US 7 Series owners rate resale value 3.77 out of 7.
4. **Boot space and storage.** Loading luggage is in the bottom three in four of the five China/EU columns, and the EU 1 Series scores 7.07 on luggage capacity.
5. **Smaller items:**

   - Electric range and charging (109 + 64).
   - More cabin space for China (7 Series rear room 7.52 there vs 9.41 in the EU).
   - Auto start-stop that stays off (74).
   - A hands-free tailgate that works (52).

Strengths to keep: powertrain (1,071 positive comments), handling (626), exterior design (92% positive) and comfort.

**Data quality caveats**
- 2,082 rows have no topic label, and some labels are clearly wrong (praise tagged as "performance not OK").
- 13 identical texts repeat across G60 and G70, which looks templated or synthetic.
- The mix of sources differs by model, so comparing models on raw shares is misleading.
- The two survey sheets use different scales, so they need normalising before you combine them.

The report also covers how the files link: there is no shared key, so we'd need to build a mapping between feedback topics, survey attributes and option codes. It also maps the data to the five process stages and lists 16 requirements with evidence counts.

- These are official **German-market price lists ("Katalog Juli 2026", Ausgabe 1)**. They are written in **German**, with prices in **EUR incl. 19% VAT [and excl. VAT in brackets]**. 433	## 6. Data quality issues
434	
435	1. **Long-format duplication:** F70 averages 1.92 rows per ID, with up to 18 rows for one ID in G60. Counting rows instead of unique IDs inflates F70 especially (4,076 rows vs 2,128 IDs).
436	2. **Unclassified records:** `no_class_found` appears in 2,082 rows (F70 1,087 = 26.7% of rows; G60 525; G70 470), always with `Feedback Type` = NaN. Another 400 rows (all of Source D and 126 Source C rows) have no VFC labels at all. F70 rows often pair one real label with one `no_class_found` row.
437	3. **Label noise / misclassification:** praise texts are labelled "Drive power/driving performance not OK". Examples: F70-1736 "the low-speed torque is excellent", F70-0344 "the performance is adequate… a point i would recommend". Touch screen issues are labelled "Size not user friendly" (62 F70 IDs). "Wants" includes "Dislike: price-performance ratio". Treat the VFC labels as hints and re-classify text where it matters.
438	4. **Uninformative topics:** `Body equipment, overall technology` (483 IDs), `General enquiry: customer feedback`, and `Drive, driving dynamics… overall technology` are catch-all buckets.
439	5. **Language and encoding:** all texts are English. Source A is entirely lower-cased and machine-translated (JP bullets "・", full-width spaces, "▶" artefacts, emojis, odd phrasing like "the driving feel is firm and moist"). 31 texts contain non-ASCII artefacts. There are typos ("experiance", "awaye", "Lunid Air").
440	6. **Templated duplicates:** 19 texts appear under 2+ IDs (39 IDs). 13 of them repeat across G60 and G70 (e.g. "Customer stated it is a beautiful car."). This suggests synthetic or templated generation **[inferred]**.
441	7. **Coverage gaps and bias:**
442	   - No China verbatims and no Germany.
443	   - F70 is ICE-only and has a single source (A).
444	   - G60/G70 are around 90–95% US and dominated by Source B (customer-care notes), which are skewed toward "how do I…" usability calls. This explains why DTU is high for G60/G70.
445	   - Channel mix differs by model, so **cross-model comparisons of raw shares are confounded by source**.
446	8. **No dates in feedback:** only incidental text mentions ("4/05/2023", "since february 2025", "2026 model"), so trends cannot be analysed.
447	9. **Odd values:** `Engine Type` = `BEVE` (not BEV). `Brand` and `Sales Description` are stringified lists (`[BMW]`).
448	10. **Customer studies:**
449	    - CN_EU has a multi-row header with merged cells, no scale definition and no n.
450	    - The US sheet has no n, two blank separator rows, a trailing space in "BMW 7 Series G70 " and a typo ("blid spot").
451	    - Some G70 distributions look implausible (e.g. "Delightful" only 1.5–1.6% while "I Love It" is 26–30% on Mobile App and Customization; Customization "I Hate It" is 17.9%). They may be synthetic **[inferred]**.
452	    - The scales differ between sheets (1–10 means vs 7-point distributions), so they need normalising before comparison.
453	    - Some extreme CN_EU values (EU G60 quality of ride 9.95, exterior 9.83 vs EU G70 sportiness 6.97) look synthetic or stylised **[inferred]**.
454	11. **Sales:** round numbers. G60 and G68 are merged. There is no RoW breakdown and no powertrain split. 2030 is unlabelled as forecast.
455	12. **Option lists:** German language and Germany only. Prices are not comparable to US/CN. The section-header parser is approximate (some lines are mis-sectioned; e.g. G70 `2Z2` chassis is tagged under "Entertainment"). Package contents are bullets that need text extraction.

EHL Hackathon · Munich · 10–11 October 2026 · Research briefing

BMW challenge: AI for product decision making

Everything we know about the challenge, the company behind it, and what "The Ultimate Driving Machine" means, explained in plain language. Each fact taken from outside material links to its source, marked like this S1.

1,000,000,000customer findings
1,000requirements
1car, sold for 7–8 years
01

The short version

BMW wants a tool that helps its product managers decide what the next generation of a car should offer customers. Those managers face an ocean of information: complaints, reviews, sales numbers, competitor launches, market trends. They have to turn all of it into a short list of clear requirements for the engineers, and defend every choice.

Today that work is manual, slow, and hard to trace afterwards. BMW wants AI to do the heavy lifting: reading, sorting, grouping and suggesting. The human must stay in charge of every decision, and anyone looking later must be able to see why each one was made.

The idea to hold on to

BMW's slogan is "The Ultimate Driving Machine". In this challenge the product manager is the driver and our tool is the machine: powerful, precise, responsive, but it never takes the wheel. BMW's own design rule for its cars is "Hands on the wheel, eyes on the road" S14. For our tool that means the manager approves everything, and the evidence is always in view.

What the judges will reward, in BMW's own words: trustworthy sources, transparent reasoning, thoughtful prioritization, and a clear understanding of uncertainty and conflicting evidence. They care about what customers value, not about engineering specifications, regulation or detailed business cases.

02

The challenge brief, explained

The official two-page brief is titled "AI for Product Decision Making". It asks one question: What should the next generation of a BMW vehicle offer its customers?

What we have to build

An AI-powered application that helps product managers derive (find), justify (explain) and prioritize (rank) customer requirements for a successor vehicle, meaning the next generation of a car that already exists. Every proposal must be grounded in customer feedback, BMW's product and sales data, and research from the web.

The scope we can choose from

03

The two slides, explained

Slide 1: "From billions of findings to one BMW vehicle"

At the bottom of the slide is BMW's working definition:

Customer Requirement = Customer Relevant Attribute of a Car. A requirement is anything about the car that a customer would notice and care about, written in the customer's language.

The left column shows raw customer quotes. They are messy on purpose, and some contradict each other:

  • "Charging takes too long."
  • "The app should just work."
  • "Too many menus."
  • "Too much plastic."
  • "Ugly kidney grille."
  • "I love the design."
  • "Uncomfortable seats."
  • "More rear space, please."
  • "Very nice exterior colors."
  • "The NEW XPENG."
  • "Tesla and GROK"

Two things stand out. First, the direct contradiction (in red): one customer hates the grille, another loves the design. Our tool must show such conflicts, not average them away. Second, customers name XPeng and Tesla/Grok as reference points. These are software-first electric car brands from China and the US, not the traditional rivals Mercedes and Audi.

The middle of the slide is a word cloud of themes. Some words are bright and bold, others are faded, which seems to signal different importance:

Prominent
Intuitive UXPremium feelRangeFast chargingLong battery lifeIconic designSafetyEasy charging
Medium
Joy of drivingReliable softwareClear displaysComfortable seatsSmooth rideFast app responsePhysical controlsRoom for familyEasy child seat fitData privacyEasy updatesGreat soundHome chargingPersonalized…
Faded
AffordableEfficiencyEveryday spaceSeat ventilationReal-world rangeDynamicSustainableElectricLow running costs

What this tells us: feedback arrives unstructured, duplicated, emotional, contradictory and market-specific. The job is to turn it into a clean list of customer-relevant attributes, then weigh them. Software, user experience and charging seem to be where BMW feels the pressure.

Slide 2: "The Process"

ChoiceOptionsWhat it means
VehicleBMW 1 Series, 5 Series, 7 Series, or a mixThe 1 Series is the small entry car, the 5 Series the mid-size business sedan, the 7 Series the luxury flagship.
MarketsEurope, China, USA, or any subsetCustomers differ strongly between these regions, so a market view matters.
Time horizon3 to 5 years aheadWe must guess what customers will want when the new car launches, not only what they want today.
They wantWhat we could build
From a billion findings to a thousand requirements to one carA clear pipeline: collect → clean → group into themes → propose requirements → set measurable targets → rank → log the decision.
Evidence kept apart from assumptionsEach requirement shows its evidence (how many mentions, sample quotes, which markets, source links) separately from its assumptions (forecasts about 2030 and later), each with a confidence level.
Handling conflicting evidenceShow the conflict openly, e.g. "Kidney grille: 34% negative, 41% positive, split by market and age", instead of hiding it in an average. (Illustrative numbers.)
"My market is different"A switch that re-ranks the same list for Europe, China and the US and highlights where they disagree.
Prioritization you can seeA scoring model with weights the manager can see and change (customer value, frequency, severity, gap to competitors, trend momentum, brand fit), plus a plain-language "why is this ranked #3?"
Brand fitA "BMW DNA" check: does this requirement make the car more of an Ultimate Driving Machine?
Turning yes/no into numbersTurn "ventilated seats: yes" into "cools to X °C within Y seconds", and "range" into 600 / 700 / 900 km options compared with competitors.
Human in controlApprove, reject, edit or challenge every proposal. Every override is saved with a reason.
Documentation with contextA snapshot of the evidence at decision time, so in three years anyone can see what was known, what was assumed, and what has changed since.
ScaleThe same engine works for the 1, 5 and 7 Series and for every market.

Signals between the lines

  • The 1,000 km → 900 km story shows they live in trade-offs. A simple "what if" control would resonate.
  • They raised documentation and context twice. Traceability is a top priority.
  • Their named competitors are Chinese tech brands, and China is BMW's weakest market right now. China-specific insight is likely valuable.
  • Write requirements in customer language ("charges while I have a coffee"), not engineering language ("350 kW DC").

Lessons from BMW's own history

  • "Point out contradictions constructively" is an official BMW value S7. Surfacing conflicts fits their culture; it isn't an extra.
  • Say vs notice: 80% of 1 Series owners didn't know which wheels drove their car S28. Separate what customers say, what they actually notice, and what the brand requires.
  • Perception is reality S27: the heated-seat subscription made business sense on paper and still failed. Score requirements on how customers will perceive them.
  • The 1960s story: BMW was saved by customer research that found an unmet gap S13 S24. A pitch line: "We're giving BMW's product managers what market research gave BMW in the 1960s, at the scale of a billion data points."

Ideas for a distinctive angle

  • Decision flight recorder: every requirement has a replayable history (evidence → AI proposal → manager's change → reason). Assumption alarms fire when new data breaks an old assumption, e.g. "A competitor launched 12-minute charging; requirement R-042 assumed 15 minutes was enough."
  • Devil's advocate: for each top requirement, the AI writes the strongest argument against it and lists the evidence that conflicts.
  • Market lens: one list, re-ranked per region, with the differences made visible.
  • Brand DNA gate: a score for whether each requirement strengthens the Ultimate Driving Machine.
  • Proof for the pitch: time saved compared with doing it by hand, share of requirements with traceable evidence, accuracy of the grouping on a hand-labelled sample, number of conflicts found, and agreement between AI ranking and expert ranking.
  • S32PressWikipedia, "Herbert Quandt". en.wikipedia.org
  • S34BMWBMW Group Mobile Tradition live, portrait of Franz Josef Popp (PDF, hosted by 7-forum.com). 7-forum.com
  • S35BMWBMW M, "The new BMW M350 xDrive Sedan" (YouTube, 5 Oct 2026). youtube.com
  • S37BMWBMW Group China press, FY2025 and the Neue Klasse in China (PDF). press.bmwgroup.com
    • What is our own interpretation

    Not backed by a checked source: the current model codes and launch years of the 1, 5 and 7 Series; successor timing; our reading of the film's symbolism; and the analysis in section 9.

    Compiled 10 October 2026 for the EHL hackathon team. Companion page: Automotive Product Management, covering what car product managers do, their tools and the vendor landscape.

EHL Hackathon · Munich · 10 October 2026 · Data analysis

What BMW's data actually says

An analysis of the hackathon dataset (customer feedback, satisfaction studies, sales volumes and price lists for the 1, 5 and 7 Series), plus the labelled photos from the opening talks. Counts are unique feedback records unless stated. Anything marked inferred is our interpretation, not something the data states.

10,128customer comments

01

The short version

Customers love how these BMWs drive and look, but they are frustrated by the screens, the software and the value for money. The same pattern shows up in the free-text feedback, the satisfaction surveys and the price lists.

  • Keep: driving dynamics (1,071 positive comments on the drivetrain alone), exterior design (92% positive), comfort (97% positive).
  • Fix: touchscreen-only controls and deep menus, infotainment and connectivity glitches, value perception and paid extras, boot and storage space, 7 Series air conditioning, EV range and charging.
  • Blind spot: there is no customer feedback from China and none from Germany. China is covered only by survey scores and sales numbers.
Why it matters for the pitch

The data is deliberately uneven: different sources per model, missing markets, noisy labels, two survey scales. A tool that shows those gaps and conflicts instead of hiding them is exactly what BMW asked for ("a clear understanding of uncertainty and conflicting evidence").

02

What BMW gave us

Eight files, now stored in data/bmw/ and kept out of git. The model codes are BMW's internal names: F70 = 1 Series, G60 = 5 Series sedan, G68 = 5 Series long-wheelbase for China, G70 = 7 Series.

FileWhat it isSizeMarkets

feedback/G70_feedback_hackathon.xlsxLabelled customer comments, 7 Series (ICE, EV, plug-in hybrid)4,000 comments95% US, plus KR, JP, GB, CA
customer-studies/F70_G60_G68_G70_customer_studies.xlsx2025 satisfaction surveys: 37 attributes (China + EU, mean scores) and 103 attributes (US, 7-point distributions)2 sheetsCN, EU, US

Each feedback row has an ID, a source (A–D), country, model code, powertrain, a feedback type (Likes, Wants, Defect, Difficult to Use), the verbatim comment, and BMW's two-level topic labels (e.g. Touch screen, operation → Not user-friendly). One comment can carry several labels, so it appears on several rows: 13,771 rows, but only 10,128 comments. BMW showed exactly this sheet live on stage (see the photos).

The four feedback sources inferred from writing style

A3,677Owner reviews, often translated, all lower-case. The only source for the 1 Series."i really miss the old bmw control wheel…"
B5,479US customer-care call notes. They skew towards "how do I…" questions."Customer stated… Writer advised…"
C698US quality survey, with self-rated severity"I had a very serious problem with…"
D274US appeal survey: "love most / improve most""need extra storage"
03

Coverage & gaps

The challenge scope is 1/5/7 Series × Europe/China/US. This is what evidence actually exists for each cell:

7 Series (G70)EU survey, sales, price list, 19 commentsChina survey + sales only. No comments.3,792 comments, US survey, sales
Consequence

China, about 85,000 cars in 2025 and BMW's most contested market, can only be argued from survey scores, sales and outside research. Our tool should label China requirements as lower-confidence and say why.

  • Connected services is the weakest or near-weakest attribute everywhere. It is BMW's most consistent gap.
  • 7 Series, China vs Europe: Chinese owners are happier overall (+1.65) and on value (+1.82), but rate space much lower (front −2.00, rear −1.89) and braking (−1.79). This supports long-wheelbase variants for China inferred.
  • European 7 Series: value for money at 6.47 is the lowest number in the whole sheet.

USA: 7-point "I hate it … I love it" scale (G60, G70)

We turned each distribution into a mean (1–7) and a "bottom-3 box" (share who answered hate / failure / unsatisfactory). These are the weakest items:

Strongest US items: 5 Series prestige 6.07, handling 6.06, performance 6.04; 7 Series rear-seat comfort 6.24, front roominess 6.20, ride comfort 6.20. The 7 Series scores below the 5 Series on almost every controls, connectivity and cost item, despite costing about twice as much.

The 5 Series is two thirds of volume, so its requirements carry the most weight. Its market split is balanced: EU 39%, US 26%, China 25%. The 7 Series is small but grows fastest. These volumes can serve directly as market weights in prioritisation.

07

Option lists (German price lists, July 2026)

These are the official catalogues: variants and base prices, standard equipment, and every option with its option code (e.g. 5AU) and price. They are German-market only and written in German.

ModelBase price rangeOption codesOption prices
1 Series€34,250 (116) – €57,150 (M135 xDrive)56€200 – €3,950
5 Series€60,000 (520i) – €100,200 (i5 M60)58€300 – €5,900
7 Series€117,900 (740 xDrive) – €182,400 (i7 M70)84€290 – €25,840

Where the price lists meet the complaints:

  • "Paid extras" complaint: the 1 Series sells BMW Digital Premium as a time-limited option (€480), and good assistance systems cost €700–2,280 extra.
  • "Missing dual-zone climate" (GB owners): it is standard in Germany. Equipment differs by market, and that drives value perception inferred.
  • "Want an opening sunroof": the 5 Series panorama roof (€1,630) is fixed glass.
  • 7 Series signature features such as automatic doors (€1,600) are among the most-liked items in the feedback.
08

Data quality: what to watch out for

  1. Count comments, not rows. One comment spans up to 18 rows.
  2. 2,082 rows are unlabelled (no_class_found), a quarter of all 1 Series rows. Re-classifying them with AI is an easy, demonstrable win.
  3. Some labels are wrong. For example, "the low-speed torque is excellent" is tagged as "driving performance not OK". Treat BMW's labels as hints.
  4. Catch-all topics such as "Body equipment, overall" (483 comments) say little.
  5. Source mix differs by model. The 5 and 7 Series are dominated by customer-care calls, the 1 Series by reviews. Raw shares across models are not comparable.
  6. No dates in the feedback, so no trends over time.
  7. Templated duplicates: 13 identical texts appear in both 5 and 7 Series files. Parts of the data look synthetic inferred.
  8. Two survey scales (1–10 means vs 7-point distributions), with no sample sizes. Normalise before combining.
  9. Small oddities: BEVE instead of BEV, list-as-text fields ([BMW]), and typos. The option lists are Germany-only.
  10. No shared key between files. Linking a complaint topic to a survey attribute and an option code needs a mapping (manual or AI-built).
09

Candidate requirements already visible

A first ranking: how often it comes up, how bad the survey gap is, and how much volume it touches. This is our starting hypothesis; the tool should let the product manager re-weight it.

Strengths to protect: "must not lose"

Driving dynamics and powertrain; exterior design; comfort and luxury; brand prestige; reliability (except China 7 Series at 8.22, a watch item); 7 Series signature features such as automatic doors and ambient light. These are the "Ultimate Driving Machine" core, and requirements must not trade them away.

Conflicts our tool should surface
  • 1 Series ride: GB comments call it too firm, yet the EU survey rates ride quality highly.
  • Design: 92% positive overall, yet the illuminated kidney grille is a specific dislike (55 mentions).
  • China: high overall satisfaction (9.64) next to low space and braking scores.
10

How the data feeds our tool

Mapped onto BMW's five-stage process (slide 5):

01

Situation analysis

Sales as market weights; survey heat map by attribute × market; complaint share by topic.

sales · studies
02

Structure & context

One shared taxonomy linking BMW topic labels ↔ survey attributes ↔ option codes. Tag evidence by model, market, powertrain and source.

all files
03

Requirements definition

AI clusters comments into "The successor shall…" statements with quotes and counts. Re-label the 2,082 unclassified rows.

feedback
04

Prioritization

Score = frequency × severity × survey gap × market volume. The PM can see and change the weights. Strengths are listed separately.

feedback · studies · sales
05

Documentation

One card per requirement: statement, evidence, quotes, survey metric, markets, linked option, confidence, and the PM's decision with a reason.

everything + Entire trail
11

Event photos, labelled

The photos shared on WhatsApp, checked one by one and renamed by content. Exact duplicates are in images/_duplicates/. The full table is in images/README.md.

BMW product management talk

Entire keynote (mandatory tool)

Organisation

Read across the two talks

BMW wants every requirement traceable to evidence and a human decision. Entire sells "a traceable unit richer than a commit" for code. Our pitch can connect the two: each requirement is a traceable unit made of evidence, AI reasoning, the PM's decision and its context. BMW's own ontology prototype (bmw-06) shows they already think in REQUIRES / CONFLICTS_WITH / DERIVED_FROM graphs.

content.text:
I've organised the folder, labelled every photo by what it shows, analysed the BMW data, and added a `.gitignore` that keeps all the data out of git. I tested the `.gitignore` in a throwaway repo: data, PDFs, the video and the duplicates are ignored, and the notes and labelled slides are still tracked. This folder isn't a git repo yet.

**What the data says**
- Customers love how these BMWs drive and look: 1,071 positive comments on the powertrain, 92% positive on exterior design and 97% on comfort.
- They're frustrated with screens, software and value for money:
  - **Touchscreen-only controls and deep menus:** 185 complaints. US owners score the climate controls 4.5–4.8 out of 7.
  - **Connectivity:** "connected services" is the weakest or near-weakest survey score in every China and Europe column.
  - **Value for money:** the European 7 Series scores 6.47, the lowest number in the survey sheet. US 7 Series owners rate resale value 3.77 out of 7.
  - **Also recurring:** boot and storage space, 7 Series air conditioning, EV range and charging, start-stop that won't stay off, and the hands-free tailgate.
- **There is no customer feedback from China, and none from Germany.** China (about 85k cars in 2025) can only be argued from survey scores and sales, so our tool should mark those requirements as lower confidence.
- **The 5 Series is two-thirds of sales**, so its requirements carry the most weight. The 7 Series grows fastest.
- **The data is deliberately messy:**
  - 13,771 rows but only 10,128 comments, because one comment gets one row per label.
  - 2,082 rows have no label, and some labels are clearly wrong.
  - The 5 and 7 Series comments are mostly customer-care calls, so comparing models on raw shares is misleading.
  - The China/EU and US surveys use different scales.
  - Some texts look templated or synthetic.

  Showing these gaps and conflicts openly is exactly what BMW asked for.

**What the photos added**
- BMW showed a prototype on stage: a knowledge graph comparing BMW with Xiaomi, with links like REQUIRES, CONFLICTS_WITH and DERIVED_FROM. That's a strong hint at what they're exploring.
- The guide in the folder confirms that "Entire" is entire.io, with the setup steps. I've removed that from the "unverified" lists.
- I renamed all 23 distinct photos by content into `images/bmw-talk/`, `images/entire-talk/` and `images/ehl/`. `images/README.md` says what each one shows and why it matters.
- 14 files were exact copies, including the two `image*.webp`. I moved them to `images/_duplicates/` rather than deleting them; that folder is safe to delete.

**How the folder is organised now**
- `data/bmw/`: the original BMW files, sorted into feedback, customer studies, sales and option lists. Nothing in them was changed.
- `data/DATA-REPORT.md`: the full analysis with every number, plus derived tables in `data/analysis/`.
- `docs/`: the BMW briefing PDF and the Entire guide.
- `README.md`: an index of everything.

**Changes to your existing files**
- **`notes.md`:** new §11 on the photos and data, plus the new file paths.
- **Both earlier HTML pages:** the Entire confirmation, and links to the new data page.

The `.gitignore` also excludes the two photos that show BMW's spreadsheet and prototype on screen. The new data page is ignored too, because it quotes customer comments from the dataset.

Files are in `/Volumes/PJ/peresjav/hackathons/ehl-final-minuch-2026/`:
- `bmw-data-analysis.html` (new): the readable data write-up with charts, 12 candidate requirements, and a gallery of the labelled photos
- `data/DATA-REPORT.md`
- `images/README.md`
- `README.md`
- `.gitignore`

import json, sys, os, re, urllib.parse, urllib.request, html

    line=line.strip()
    if not line: continue
    slug,title=line.split('|',1)
    url='https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/api.php?'+urllib.parse.urlencode({'action':'query','format':'json','titles':title,'prop':'imageinfo','iiprop':'url|extmetadata','iiurlwidth':1600})

    src=ii.get('thumburl') or ii['url']
    fn=f"{out}/{slug}.jpg"

"""Render the 30-second BMW history story from images/bmw-history/.

Usage (from the project root):
  uv run --with pillow python -I story/make_story.py landscape   # 1920x1080
  uv run --with pillow python -I story/make_story.py vertical    # 1080x1920
Requires ffmpeg on PATH. Frames are piped straight into ffmpeg.
"""
import json, subprocess, sys
from pathlib import Path
from PIL import Image, ImageDraw, ImageFont, ImageFilter

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
IMG = ROOT / "images" / "bmw-history"
MODE = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "landscape"
W, H = (1920, 1080) if MODE == "landscape" else (1080, 1920)
FPS = 30
SHOT = 2.6      # seconds per photo
FADE = 0.4      # cross-fade
END = 4.0       # end card

# (file, year, headline, subline) — facts follow the "ENTIRE History of BMW Ep.1" video, cross-checked in notes.md
SHOTS = [
    ("01-1918-bmw-iiia-aircraft-engine.jpg", "1916", "It started in the sky.", "Aircraft engines from Munich's Oberwiesenfeld airfield."),
    ("02-1923-r32-first-motorcycle.jpg", "1923", "Grounded, BMW took to the road.", "R32: boxer engine and shaft drive, still the template."),
    ("03-1928-dixi-3-15-first-car.jpg", "1928", "The first BMW car.", "Dixi 3/15, a licensed Austin 7."),
    ("04-1933-303-first-kidney-grille.jpg", "1933", "The kidney grille is born.", "303: the first six-cylinder BMW."),
    ("05-1936-328-roadster-racing-legend.jpg", "1936", "Light. Fast. A winner.", "328 Roadster: Nürburgring and Mille Miglia."),
    ("06-1955-isetta-bubble-car-saved-bmw.jpg", "1955", "A bubble car kept the lights on.", "Isetta: cheap to buy, cheap to run."),
    ("07-1962-1500-neue-klasse.jpg", "1961", "The Neue Klasse.", "1959: shareholders refused a takeover. 1961: the sports sedan was born."),
    ("08-1968-2002-rally-giant-killer.jpg", "1968", "2002: the driver's car.", "Small, light, eager: a giant killer on track."),
    ("09-1973-2002-turbo.jpg", "1973", "Turbo.", "One of Europe's first turbocharged production cars."),
    ("10-2025-ix3-neue-klasse-today.jpg", "2025", "Neue Klasse, again.", "Every comeback began with what drivers wanted next."),
]
CREDITS = {c["file"]: c for c in json.loads((IMG / "credits.json").read_text())}

F = "/System/Library/Fonts/Supplemental/DIN Condensed Bold.ttf"
A = "/System/Library/Fonts/Avenir Next.ttc"
s = W / 1920 if MODE == "landscape" else W / 1080
year_f = ImageFont.truetype(F, int(220 * s))
head_f = ImageFont.truetype(A, int(64 * s), index=5)   # Avenir Next Demi Bold
sub_f = ImageFont.truetype(A, int(34 * s), index=7)    # Avenir Next Regular
small_f = ImageFont.truetype(A, int(20 * s), index=7)
tag_f = ImageFont.truetype(A, int(26 * s), index=5)

def cover(im, w, h):
    r = max(w / im.width, h / im.height)
    im = im.resize((int(im.width * r) + 1, int(im.height * r) + 1), Image.LANCZOS)
    x, y = (im.width - w) // 2, (im.height - h) // 2
    return im.crop((x, y, x + w, y + h))

def gradient(w, h):
    g = Image.new("L", (1, h))
    for y in range(h):
        t = max(0, (y - h * 0.45) / (h * 0.55))
        g.putpixel((0, y), int(235 * t ** 1.3))
    return g.resize((w, h))

GRAD = gradient(W, H)

def wrap(draw, text, font, maxw):
    words, lines, cur = text.split(), [], ""
    for wd in words:
        t = (cur + " " + wd).strip()
        if draw.textlength(t, font=font) <= maxw: cur = t
        else: lines.append(cur); cur = wd
    lines.append(cur)
    return lines

def overlay(year, head, sub, credit):
    ov = Image.new("RGBA", (W, H), (0, 0, 0, 0))
    black = Image.new("RGBA", (W, H), (0, 0, 0, 255)); black.putalpha(GRAD)
    ov = Image.alpha_composite(ov, black)
    d = ImageDraw.Draw(ov)
    m = int(80 * s)
    d.text((m, m * 0.8), "BMW  ·  FROM THE SKY TO THE NEUE KLASSE", font=tag_f, fill=(255, 255, 255, 210))
    d.rectangle((m, m * 0.8 + 40 * s, m + 90 * s, m * 0.8 + 46 * s), fill=(28, 105, 212, 255))
    maxw = W - 2 * m
    sub_lines = wrap(d, sub, sub_f, maxw)
    y = H - m - len(sub_lines) * 46 * s
    for ln in reversed(sub_lines):
        pass
    yy = y
    for ln in sub_lines:
        d.text((m, yy), ln, font=sub_f, fill=(230, 233, 238, 255)); yy += 46 * s
    head_lines = wrap(d, head, head_f, maxw)
    y -= len(head_lines) * 78 * s + 10 * s
    yy = y
    for ln in head_lines:
        d.text((m, yy), ln, font=head_f, fill=(255, 255, 255, 255)); yy += 78 * s
    d.text((m - 6 * s, y - 210 * s), year, font=year_f, fill=(28, 105, 212, 255))
    cw = d.textlength(credit, font=small_f)
    d.text((W - m - cw, H - 34 * s), credit, font=small_f, fill=(255, 255, 255, 150))
    return ov

def endcard():
    im = Image.new("RGB", (W, H), (10, 14, 20)); d = ImageDraw.Draw(im)
    m = int(110 * s); maxw = W - 2 * m
    big = ImageFont.truetype(A, int(76 * s), index=5)
    lines = wrap(d, "From raw findings to the ultimate driving machine.", big, maxw)
    y = H / 2 - len(lines) * 96 * s / 2 - 40 * s
    for ln in lines:
        d.text((m, y), ln, font=big, fill=(255, 255, 255)); y += 96 * s
    d.rectangle((m, y + 24 * s, m + 120 * s, y + 31 * s), fill=(28, 105, 212))
    d.text((m, y + 60 * s), "110 years of listening to drivers. Our turn: AI for product decisions.", font=sub_f, fill=(200, 206, 214))
    d.text((m, H - 70 * s), "EHL Hackathon · Munich · Oct 2026   |   Photos: Wikimedia Commons, CC BY / CC BY-SA (see credits.json)", font=small_f, fill=(140, 148, 160))
    return im

# pre-render shots (oversized base for Ken Burns zoom)
shots = []
for i, (fn, yr, hd, sb) in enumerate(SHOTS):
    c = CREDITS[fn]
    base = cover(Image.open(IMG / fn).convert("RGB"), int(W * 1.12), int(H * 1.12))
    credit = f"Photo: {c['author'][:48]} · {c['license']}"
    shots.append((base, overlay(yr, hd, sb, credit).convert("RGBA")))
end = endcard()

def shot_frame(i, t):
    base, ov = shots[i]
    z = 1.12 - 0.10 * (t / SHOT)                    # slow push-in
    cw, ch = int(W * z / 1.12 * base.width / W * (1.12 / 1.12)), 0
    cw, ch = int(base.width * (z / 1.12)), int(base.height * (z / 1.12))
    dx = (base.width - cw) * (0.5 + (0.25 if i % 2 else -0.25) * (t / SHOT))
    dy = (base.height - ch) / 2
    fr = base.crop((int(dx), int(dy), int(dx) + cw, int(dy) + ch)).resize((W, H), Image.BILINEAR).convert("RGBA")
    a = min(1.0, t / 0.35)                          # text fades in
    o = ov.copy(); o.putalpha(o.getchannel("A").point(lambda v: int(v * a)))
    return Image.alpha_composite(fr, o).convert("RGB")

out = ROOT / "story" / f"bmw-30s-story-{MODE}.mp4"
ff = subprocess.Popen(["ffmpeg", "-loglevel", "error", "-y", "-f", "rawvideo", "-pix_fmt", "rgb24", "-s", f"{W}x{H}", "-r", str(FPS), "-i", "-",
                       "-c:v", "libx264", "-pix_fmt", "yuv420p", "-crf", "20", "-preset", "medium", "-movflags", "+faststart", str(out)], stdin=subprocess.PIPE)
step = SHOT - FADE
total = len(SHOTS) * step + FADE + END - FADE
n = int(round(total * FPS))
for f in range(n):
    t = f / FPS
    i = min(int(t // step), len(SHOTS) - 1)
    lt = t - i * step
    if i == len(SHOTS) - 1 and lt > SHOT - FADE:      # into the end card
        k = min(1.0, (lt - (SHOT - FADE)) / FADE)
        fr = Image.blend(shot_frame(i, min(lt, SHOT)), end, k) if k < 1 else end
    else:
        fr = shot_frame(i, lt)
        if lt > step and i + 1 < len(SHOTS):          # cross-fade to next
            fr = Image.blend(fr, shot_frame(i + 1, lt - step), (lt - step) / FADE)
    ff.stdin.write(fr.tobytes())
ff.stdin.close(); ff.wait()
print(out, f"{total:.1f}s")

"""Core data contracts for MarketPulse (Pydantic v2).

Every agent returns one of these models as structured output, so each step is
typed, validated and traceable. IDs link everything back to raw evidence.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

from datetime import datetime
from enum import Enum
from typing import Literal
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field


class Market(str, Enum):
    EU = "EU"
    CN = "CN"
    US = "US"
    # extensible: LATAM, AFRICA, MENA, ... (out of BMW's challenge scope, same pipeline)


class SourceKind(str, Enum):
    bmw_feedback = "bmw_feedback"      # data/bmw/feedback/*.xlsx
    bmw_survey = "bmw_survey"          # customer studies
    social = "social"                  # Reddit, YouTube comments, Autohome, ...
    search_trend = "search_trend"      # Google Trends / Baidu Index
    concept_test = "concept_test"      # reactions to our own generated concepts (flagged!)


# ---------- ① evidence -------------------------------------------------------

class LabelledEvidence(BaseModel):
    """Output of the labelling agent for one raw text."""
    evidence_id: str
    market: Market
    model: Literal["F70", "G60", "G68", "G70", "competitor", "unknown"]
    competitor: str | None = Field(None, description="e.g. 'XPeng P7+', 'Mercedes E-Class'")
    customer_attribute: str = Field(..., description="Customer-relevant attribute, customer language, e.g. 'climate controls easy to reach'")
    polarity: Literal["like", "dislike", "want", "defect", "neutral"]
    severity: int = Field(..., ge=0, le=3, description="0 none … 3 safety/strong anger")
    quote: str = Field(..., description="Shortest verbatim span that supports the label")
    source_kind: SourceKind
    confidence: float = Field(..., ge=0, le=1)


# ---------- ② requirements ---------------------------------------------------

class Assumption(BaseModel):
    text: str                      # e.g. "Fast-charging expectations in CN keep rising until 2030"
    basis: str                     # trend source or reasoning
    confidence: Literal["low", "medium", "high"]


class Conflict(BaseModel):
    description: str               # e.g. "GB comments: ride too firm, EU survey: ride quality 9.2/10"
    evidence_for: list[str]
    evidence_against: list[str]


class Requirement(BaseModel):
    id: str = Field(..., pattern=r"^R-\d{3}$")
    market: Market
    statement: str = Field(..., description="'The successor shall …' in customer language")
    metric: str | None = Field(None, description="Measurable target, e.g. 'cabin from 35 °C to 24 °C in < 6 min'")
    acceptance: str | None = None
    evidence_ids: list[str]
    evidence_count: int
    survey_signal: str | None = None   # e.g. "US AC controls 4.51/7, 20 % bottom-3"
    assumptions: list[Assumption] = []
    conflicts: list[Conflict] = []
    is_strength_to_keep: bool = False
    confidence: Literal["low", "medium", "high"]


class ScoreBreakdown(BaseModel):
    """Transparent prioritisation: each factor 0–1, weights set by the PM."""
    frequency: float
    severity: float
    satisfaction_gap: float
    market_volume: float
    trend_momentum: float
    brand_fit: float              # does it make the car more of an Ultimate Driving Machine?
    total: float
    explanation: str              # plain-language "why is this ranked #3?"


class Decision(BaseModel):
    requirement_id: str
    action: Literal["approve", "edit", "reject", "defer"]
    reason: str
    pm: str
    at: datetime
    evidence_snapshot_hash: str   # what was known at decision time


# ---------- ③ car profiles ---------------------------------------------------

class MarketContext(BaseModel):
    market: Market
    road_quality: str             # e.g. "potholes common" (the Venezuela insight)
    climate: str
    charging_infrastructure: str
    energy_prices: str
    typical_use: str              # e.g. "chauffeur-driven, rear seat matters (CN 7 Series)"


class MaterialChoice(BaseModel):
    part: str                     # "body-in-white", "battery", "interior trim"
    material: str                 # "aluminium", "LFP cells", "recycled PET textile"
    why: str
    requirement_ids: list[str]


class CarProfile(BaseModel):
    id: str                       # "CN-5-B"
    market: Market
    base_model: Literal["F70", "G60", "G68", "G70"]
    name: str                     # working title, e.g. "The Quiet Executive"
    persona: str
    story_hook: str               # emotional one-liner for the video
    powertrain: Literal["BEV", "PHEV", "ICE", "MHEV"]
    requirement_ids: list[str]
    strengths_kept: list[str]
    materials: list[MaterialChoice]
    visual_brief: dict[str, str]  # {"wheels": "...", "interior": "...", "exterior": "..."}


class Feasibility(BaseModel):
    profile_id: str
    cost_index: float = Field(..., description="Relative to current model = 100")
    main_cost_drivers: list[str]
    commodity_exposure: dict[str, float]   # {"lithium": 0.18, "aluminium": 0.11, ...}
    risk: Literal["low", "medium", "high"]
    note: str


# ---------- ④ concept test ---------------------------------------------------

class PanelReaction(BaseModel):
    profile_id: str
    respondent: str               # persona id or anonymous panel id
    market: Market
    preferred: bool
    score: int = Field(..., ge=1, le=7)
    reasons: list[str]
    mode: Literal["synthetic", "panel", "landing_page"]

# MarketPulse: data contracts (plan, not code)

These are the objects that move through the pipeline. Each agent returns exactly one of these as structured output, so every step is typed and every object links back to raw evidence. Implementation comes later, with Pydantic models and Supabase tables.

## 1. Evidence: one labelled piece of customer voice
| Field | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| evidence_id | Stable ID, links back to the raw row or post | `G70-1910`, `reddit:t3_abc` |
| market | EU · CN · US (extensible: LATAM, AFRICA, …) | `US` |
| model | F70 · G60 · G68 · G70 · competitor · unknown | `G70` |
| competitor | If about a rival | `XPeng P7+` |
| customer_attribute | What the customer cares about, in their language | "climate controls easy to reach" |
| polarity | like · dislike · want · defect · neutral | `defect` |
| severity | 0–3 | `2` |
| quote | Shortest verbatim span that proves the label | "still cant use the esim…" |
| source_kind | bmw_feedback · bmw_survey · social · search_trend · **concept_test** | `bmw_feedback` |
| confidence | 0–1, from the labelling agent | `0.86` |

## 2. Requirement: what the successor shall offer
| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| id | `R-042` |
| market | Which market lens it belongs to |
| statement | "The successor shall…", in customer language |
| metric + acceptance | Measurable target, e.g. "cabin from 35 °C to 24 °C in < 6 min" |
| evidence_ids / count | Traceable proof |
| survey_signal | e.g. "US AC controls 4.51/7, 20 % unhappy" |
| assumptions[] | Forward-looking guesses, each with a basis and confidence. **Kept separate from evidence.** |
| conflicts[] | Evidence for vs against, shown side by side |
| is_strength_to_keep | Must-not-lose items (driving dynamics, design…) |
| confidence | low / medium / high |

## 3. Score: transparent prioritisation
Each factor is scored 0–1, and the PM can see and move the weights: **frequency · severity · satisfaction gap · market volume · trend momentum · brand fit** (does it make the car more of an Ultimate Driving Machine?). Total score + a plain-language "why is this #3?".

## 4. Decision: the PM stays in control
requirement_id · action (approve / edit / reject / defer) · reason · who · when · **hash of the evidence snapshot** (what was known at the time). Every decision is also an Entire trail entry.

## 5. Market context: why one car does not fit all
road quality (the Venezuela insight: potholes → ground clearance, robust tyres, reliability) · climate · charging infrastructure · energy prices · typical use (e.g. chauffeur-driven 7 Series in China).

## 6. Car profile: one concept per market
id (`CN-5-B`) · market · base model · working name ("The Quiet Executive") · persona · story hook · powertrain · requirement IDs · strengths kept · materials [part, material, why, requirement IDs] · visual brief {wheels, interior, exterior}.

## 7. Feasibility: can BMW build it at a sensible price?
cost index (current model = 100) · main cost drivers · commodity exposure {lithium, aluminium, copper, …} · risk · note.

## 8. Asset: generated visual
kind (wheel / interior / exterior / hero / video) · file · **requirement IDs it visualises** · model used · "AI concept" label.

## 9. Panel reaction: concept-test feedback
profile_id · respondent (persona or anonymous panel ID) · market · preferred? · score 1–7 · reasons[] · mode (synthetic / panel / landing page). It goes back into Evidence with `source_kind = concept_test`, so it is never mixed up with real owner feedback.

This is the official deck behind the challenge. It defines the vocabulary we should use in the pitch: *customer requirement = customer-relevant attribute*, the 5 process stages, and where BMW expects **AI alone** versus **AI + human**. ## Slide by slide

### Slide 1: "Emotions, engineered into a product." / "Sheer Driving Pleasure"
- A large white heart-shaped symbol on a dark blue-teal gradient. Below it: **SHEER DRIVING PLEASURE**, the English form of "Freude am Fahren".
- **Reading:** product management turns emotion into specification. Requirements are not only functional ("range 600 mi"). They have to keep the feeling of driving a BMW.
- **For us:** every car profile carries an emotional *story hook*, and the prioritiser has a **brand-fit / joy-of-driving** factor. Strengths to keep (driving dynamics, design) stay protected.

### Slide 2: "The Product Management Universe."
- PRODUCT MANAGEMENT sits in the centre of five forces: **Brand · Markets/Sales · Competition · Customer · Engineering**.
- **For us:** the dashboard should show each requirement through these five lenses. Customer evidence alone is not enough: add brand fit, market volume, competitor gap and engineering feasibility.

### Slide 3: "From billions of findings to one BMW vehicle."
- The funnel: 1 billion findings → 1,000 requirements → one car. **"Customer Requirement = Customer Relevant Attribute of a Car."**
- **11 sample verbatims.** Contradictions are deliberate ("Ugly kidney grille" vs "I love the design"), and competitors are named (XPeng, Tesla + Grok).

- The car image is labelled "Future BMW sedan, AI concept visual". **BMW itself uses an AI-generated concept car**, so our AI concept visuals are on-brand, provided they are labelled.

### Slide 4: "The Process." Robot icon = AI, person icon = human
| Stage | Box | Who | What it asks for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Situation analysis | Baseline: previous BMW model, BMW portfolio, sales volume | 🤖 + 👤 | Start from the current car and its numbers |
| | Competition | 🤖 | AI scans competitors |
| | Customer / public feedback | 🤖 | AI reads feedback |
| | Product and global trends | 🤖 | AI tracks trends |

**Key reading:** the human appears exactly where **judgement** is needed: the baseline, the quantification and the prioritisation. AI alone does collection, clustering and tracking. Our PM review gates should sit exactly there.

## Organiser guidance received in chat (10 Oct): "measurable targets are always SMART"
Shared together with the requirements-definition box. Each metric our tool proposes should be:
| | Meaning | Example for "Seat ventilation: fast enough?" |
|---|---|---|

EHL Hackathon · BMW track · Product plan v0.1 · 10 Oct 2026 · planning only, no code yet

MarketPulse: listen per market, imagine the car, test before you build

A product manager's co-pilot. It turns BMW's customer data and live market signals into traceable, SMART requirements for each market, then makes them tangible as AI concept cars and short stories, and tests them with people before a single part is ordered.

3 marketsEU · China · US lens
5 stagesBMW's process, 1:1
3 profilesper market, tested
100%traceable decisions
01

The idea in one minute

Startups don't build first. They put up a landing page, collect a waitlist, and build what people actually want. MarketPulse brings that loop to car product management, per market:

  1. Listen. Collect what people say about BMW and its competitors, separately for each market: BMW's own feedback and surveys, plus Reddit, YouTube, search trends and Chinese platforms.
  2. Understand. AI agents label, de-duplicate and cluster it into customer requirements, keeping evidence separate from assumptions.
  3. Decide. The product manager reviews the ranked, SMART requirements and approves, edits or rejects each one, with a reason.
  4. Imagine. For each market the system composes 2–3 car profiles (persona, requirements, materials, powertrain), then generates component images (wheels, interior, exterior), a composite hero image and a 10–30 s story video tuned to local culture.
  5. Check feasibility. A cost agent prices the material and powertrain choices against live commodity data.
  6. Test. The profiles are shown to a panel. Reactions flow back in as a separate evidence class, and the loop repeats every few months.
Why per market, not global

One car does not fit all. On roads full of potholes (the founder's experience in Venezuela), a low-profile luxury setup is a liability; people want ground clearance, robust tyres and reliability. BMW's own data shows the same pattern. Chinese 7 Series owners rate rear space 7.52 while European owners rate it 9.41, and competitors talked about in Germany are not the ones that matter in China. So every signal, requirement and profile carries a market tag, plus a market context (roads, climate, charging, energy prices, typical use).

02

Does it fit what BMW asked for?

We checked the idea against the brief, the keynote deck, the organisers' chat and the dataset. Mostly yes, with five adjustments that make it stronger.

BMW asks forSourceHow MarketPulse answersFit
Derive, justify, prioritise customer requirements for a successor (1/5/7 Series; EU/CN/US; 3–5 yrs)Brief p.1Core pipeline (stages 1–4). Market lens = EU/CN/US. Demo on the 5 Series (66% of volume; data for all three markets incl. G68 for China)strong
PM stays in control; transparent reasoning; traceabilityBrief, keynote slide 4Human gates exactly where the keynote shows the person icon: baseline, quantification, prioritisation. Each decision stores a reason and an evidence snapshot (Entire trail)strong
Evidence vs assumptions; conflicting evidenceBriefSeparate fields. Conflicts shown side by side (e.g. 1 Series ride: "too firm" in GB comments vs 9.20 in the EU survey). Concept-test reactions are their own evidence classstrong
Measurable targets are always SMARTOrganiser chatA requirement can't be approved until all five SMART fields are filled. AI drafts them, the PM confirmsadded
"Emotions, engineered into a product." / Sheer Driving PleasureKeynote slide 1Story hook per profile, a brand-fit factor in scoring, and "strengths to keep" protectedstrong
Customer view, not engineering specs, regulation or detailed business casesBrief p.2The cost agent gives a feasibility signal (cost index, commodity exposure), not a business case. Keep it lightadjust
Scope EU / China / USBriefContinents (Africa, LatAm…) become an extension that shows scalability. The demo stays on BMW's three marketsadjust
Use the BMW Group Report 2025 for market and R&D dataOrganiser chatIt feeds the situation analysis (regional deliveries, EV share) and a Neue Klasse alignment check for each profileadded
The five adjustments
  1. Don't publish fake BMWs on public social media. Unreleased "BMW" concepts posted publicly are a brand and confidentiality risk. Since 2 Aug 2026 the EU AI Act (Art. 50) also requires clear labelling of realistic AI images and video. Production version: closed panels, car clinics, or clearly labelled tests on owned channels. Demo: a synthetic persona panel grounded in real market evidence, clearly labelled as simulated (see section 08).
  2. No fine-tuning. 10k comments and a 2-day build don't justify it. LLM labelling with structured outputs and a fixed taxonomy, checked against ~100 hand-labelled rows, is faster, cheaper and explainable.
  3. Visuals must trace back to requirements. Every generated wheel, seat or screen is tagged with the requirement IDs it visualises, so the image itself is a piece of documentation.
  4. Cost is a signal, not a verdict. Brief p.2 rules out detailed business cases. Show a cost index and risk flags, and let the PM decide.
  5. China needs honesty. BMW's data has zero Chinese comments, so China requirements lean on survey scores, sales and external signals and are labelled lower-confidence. That is a strength in the pitch: "our tool tells you what it doesn't know."
03

The loop

06

From evidence to a SMART requirement

One worked example, built from real numbers in BMW's data:

R-014 · 5 Series successor · USA · draft by AI, awaiting PM

Statement: "The climate is controlled with one direct, physical-feeling action, without opening a menu."

  • Specific: temperature, fan and defrost for driver and passenger.
  • Measurable: ≤ 1 action and ≤ 2 s glance time per change; US "operation of heater/AC controls" score ≥ 5.5/7 (today 4.80).
  • Attainable: physical controls already exist in the BMW portfolio; Neue Klasse keeps haptic controls check vs annual report.
  • Relevant: 185 touchscreen + 82 climate complaints; 61 mentions of "climate in the screen".
  • Timely: frozen at the concept gate; validated in prototype clinics.

Evidence: 267 comments · 3 sources · survey 4.80/7. Assumption: the screen-fatigue trend continues through 2030 (medium). Conflict: 8% of comments praise the minimal cockpit. Score: 0.81 (#3), mainly frequency × satisfaction gap × volume.

Prioritisation shows its weights: frequency · severity · satisfaction gap · market volume · trend momentum · brand fit. The PM drags a weight and the list re-ranks live, which turns the keynote's "Customer · Business · …" lenses into something you can operate.

07

Car profiles, visuals and story

A profile is a bundle of approved requirements

For each market, the composer builds 2–3 contrasting profiles from the approved requirements plus the strengths to keep. Example for 5 Series successor · China (illustrative):

  • A · "The Quiet Executive": long wheelbase, rear-seat lounge, quietness, smooth braking; BEV. Persona: a chauffeured manager in Shanghai.
  • B · "Connected Family": phone-first infotainment, local apps, flexible storage, fast charging; BEV. Persona: a young family in Shenzhen.
  • C · "Driver's Sedan": shorter wheelbase, sport tuning, the "joy of driving" kept front and centre; PHEV. Persona: an enthusiast in Chengdu.

Visuals: parts first, then the whole car

  1. The visual brief (from requirements) describes wheels, interior, exterior details and colours. Each line references its requirement ID.
  2. The component images (wheel, seat row, cockpit, front light signature) are generated separately with transparent backgrounds.
  3. The composite hero is a multi-image edit that combines the components into one car view. OpenAI image edits accept up to 16 reference images; FLUX.2 on fal accepts up to 8.
  4. Optional render or turntable.

Every image carries an "AI concept" label, as BMW's own slide does ("Future BMW Sedan · AI concept visual").

Story video: 10–30 s, tuned to the culture

The storyteller writes a script from the profile's story hook and the market's culture. For China, A is about arriving rested and B is about the family weekend. The script is cut into 3–4 shots, and each shot is an image-to-video clip from the hero image (Kling 3.0 Pro or Veo 3.1 Fast on fal, 4–15 s each), stitched with ffmpeg. OpenAI's Sora video API was shut down on 24 Sep 2026, so video comes from fal. For the demo, pre-render the videos and keep a slideshow fallback, like the 30 s history story already in story/.

08

Concept test: three ways to get feedback

The "landing page and waitlist" idea is right. The question is who sees the concepts.

A · Synthetic panel

recommended for demo

LLM personas built from each market's real evidence (e.g. 50 US 5 Series personas drawn from the data's segments) react to profiles A/B/C with a score and reasons.

  • + instant, free, repeatable, no brand risk
  • − not real people: label as simulated and use only to rank hypotheses

B · Closed panel / clinic

production

BMW already runs car clinics. Show the concepts to recruited owners and prospects per market (survey tool or a private landing page), collecting choice, score and reasons.

  • + real signal, confidential, GDPR-clean
  • − costs time and money per wave

C · Public social / ads test

risky

Post labelled concepts to social media or run Meta ad split tests, then read engagement and comments.

  • + huge reach, cheap
  • − brand and leak risk, AI Act Art. 50 labels, engagement ≠ purchase intent, bots

Whatever the mode, reactions re-enter the evidence store as source_kind = concept_test and are never mixed with real owner feedback. The dashboard shows them in a different colour.

09

Feasibility agent: can BMW build it at a sensible price?

  • Inputs: profile materials and powertrain; commodity prices; battery pack cost; option-list prices as a proxy for "what customers already pay for".
    • Commodity prices come from the World Bank Pink Sheet and FRED (aluminium, copper, nickel; monthly, free).
    • Lithium and cobalt come from a paid API or a static value.
    • Battery pack cost is from BNEF (Dec 2025): average $108/kWh, BEV packs $99/kWh, LFP $81/kWh, NMC $128/kWh.
  • Output: cost index vs today's model (=100), main cost drivers, commodity exposure, risk flag. Example: "B uses LFP 85 kWh: battery −14% vs NMC, but range −8%, which conflicts with R-021 (real-world range)."
  • Trend check: if the market's signals favour EVs, the agent flags ICE-heavy profiles, and the reverse where charging is scarce. The agent gives a signal, not a business case, as the brief asks.

The 3-minute demo

  1. 0:00 Hook (20 s). The 30 s history story ends on "From raw findings to the ultimate driving machine." Line: "BMW survived three times by listening to what drivers wanted next. We built the tool that listens at the scale of a billion findings."
  2. 0:20 Markets (25 s). Screen 1. Same car, three markets, three different pains. China flagged "low confidence: no comments".
  3. 0:45 Evidence → requirement (45 s). Screens 2–3. Click a theme, see the real quotes, watch AI draft R-014 with a SMART card, then the PM edits the target and approves with a reason.
  4. 1:30 Imagine (35 s). Screen 4. Three China profiles, component images → hero, cost index, and a 10 s clip of profile B.
  5. 2:05 Test & learn (30 s). Screen 5. The synthetic panel prefers B; range doubt becomes a new conflict.
  6. 2:35 Trace (25 s). Screen 6. The decision trail plus an assumption alarm. Close: "Emotions, engineered into a product, with every decision traceable."
16

Risks and open decisions

Risks

  • Scope creep. Images and video are impressive but not the core of the judging. Protect stages 1–5 first; visuals are pre-generated.
  • Synthetic panel credibility. Judges may challenge it. Answer: it ranks hypotheses; real panels decide. It is labelled everywhere.
  • Hallucinated evidence. Every requirement must cite evidence IDs that exist (validator check). No ID, no requirement.
  • Data confidentiality. The BMW dataset is only sent to the agreed model API, and nothing goes into the public repo or Entire transcripts.
  • API access. Reddit and Chinese platforms may not be reachable in time, so prepare cached samples on Saturday night.

Decisions for you

  1. Demo market: China (most interesting, weakest data) or USA (richest data)? Suggestion: show US for the evidence depth and China for the profiles and test.
  2. Product name: "MarketPulse" is a working title.
  3. Concept-test mode in the pitch: synthetic only, or also a tiny real test (e.g. 20 people at the venue scanning a QR code)?
  4. Video provider: Kling 3.0 Pro (cheaper, longer clips) or Veo 3.1 Fast (native audio)?
  5. Qdrant: drop it (recommended) or keep it as a visible tech choice?

Contents

  2. The video
  3. Story arc & frames

EHL Hackathon · Research report · 10 October 2026

BMW 1916–1973: a company that kept reinventing itself

An analysis of the YouTube documentary "ENTIRE History of BMW Ep.1: From Airplanes to the Iconic 2002", checked against our verified sources, plus the 30-second story we built from freely licensed photos of the real cars.

01

The short version

  • The story: BMW was close to collapse at least three times (after WWI, after WWII, in 1959). Each time it survived by building what people needed next: motorcycles, a bubble car, then the "Neue Klasse" sports sedan, a segment nobody else was serving.
  • The facts hold up. We checked 14 claims against our verified sources: 13 are correct and one date is off by a day (the 1959 shareholders' meeting was on 9 December, not the 10th).
  • The pictures don't. Almost all visuals are AI-generated: gibberish gauges, "MÜNCHEN 123" number plates, invented documents. They are nice for mood and useless as evidence. That is a lesson for our own product: label AI visuals, never present them as real.
  • For the pitch: "BMW has always survived by listening for the next requirement. We built the tool that does that at the scale of a billion findings." Our 30-second story opens the pitch with real car photos.
02

The video

TitleENTIRE History of BMW Ep.1: From Airplanes to the Iconic 2002 (1916–1970)
ChannelKnow with Joe (small channel; 709 views, 16 likes at download)
Published28 Sep 2025 · 13 min 27 s
URLyoutube.com/watch?v=wYr8k6hixGE
Local copyresearch/video2/bmw-history-ep1.mp4 (480p, for analysis), with metadata, description, 24 frames and a Whisper transcript (.srt / .txt)
ReliabilityNarration: good, popular-history level. Visuals: AI-generated illustrations, not archival footage. Not a primary source; cite BMW Group Classic instead (sources in notes.md).
03

Story arc & frames

The video's 12 chapters follow a clear rise–fall–rise rhythm. Timestamps are from the video description.

TimeChapterWhat happensMood
0:00Intro"Before BMW was about luxury and performance, it was about flight."hook
0:22Airplanes & aero enginesRapp and Otto, BFW founded 1916 (official birthday 7 March 1916), roundel 1917origin
2:22The R32 motorcycle1923, Max Friz: boxer engine and shaft drive, still the templatereinvention ①
3:20Dixi, 303, 315, 328First car (licensed Austin 7), first kidney grille, 328 wins racesrise
4:17WWII & bombed factoriesAero engines for the war economy; plants dismantled afterwardsfall
5:07Postwar: R241948 single-cylinder bike, >9,000 sold in 1949reinvention ②
6:12BMW 501Elegant luxury saloon, but too expensive to sell wellmisread market
6:40Sales slumpNear bankruptcyfall
6:46IsettaLicensed bubble car, cheap to buy and run, "kept the lights on"survival
7:42Quandt rescue1959: shareholders vote down the Daimler-Benz takeover; Quandt investsturning point
8:20Neue Klasse1961 BMW 1500: Hofmeister kink, M10 engine, demand exceeds supplyreinvention ③
9:52BMW 2002Compact driver's car, racing "giant killer", 2002 Turbo 1973triumph

04

Fact check

Claims from the narration, checked against the verified sources in notes.md (S-numbers refer to its source list).

Claim in the videoVerdictNote
BFW founded 1916 at Oberwiesenfeld; BMW counts 7 March 1916 as its birthdaycorrectS1, S2
Rapp's firm renamed BMW GmbH in 1917; became an AG in 1918; name and engine business moved into BFW in 1922correctS1, S2
Roundel from 1917; propeller reading came later through advertisingcorrectTrademark registered 10 Dec 1917; propeller ad late 1920s (S9)
R32 (1923, Max Friz): boxer engine and shaft drivecorrectS1
1928: bought Fahrzeugfabrik Eisenach; Dixi = licensed Austin 7correctS1
303 (1933): first six-cylinder BMW and first kidney grillecorrectS1, S14
328 (1936) won at the Nürburgring and the Mille MigliacorrectThe Mille Miglia overall win was in 1940
WWII aero-engine production; plants dismantled after the warcorrectThe video does not mention forced labour, which BMW itself documents (S1)
R24 (1948): more than 9,000 sold in 1949correctRoughly 9,100 per BMW Classic figures
501 (1952) never sold wellcorrectThe "Baroque Angel"; high cost, low volume
Isetta licensed from Iso (1955), kept BMW alivecorrectS4
Shareholders' meeting on "10th December" 1959wrong date9 December 1959 (S4, S12, S31)
Neue Klasse 1500 shown in Frankfurt 1961; Hofmeister and Michelotti; M10 engine; orders exceeded capacitycorrectS11, S13
