05

The visuals are AI-generated, and that matters

Tell-tale signs: the speedometer reads "SPELEKT" with "120" repeated, number plates read "MÜNCHEN 123", documents carry unreadable stamps, and car details are generic (the Isetta grille, the 1950s street scene with Mercedes look-alikes). The narration is fine; the pictures are illustrations.

Lesson for MarketPulse
  • AI visuals create emotion, not evidence. Our concept images must always carry an "AI concept" label and link back to the requirement IDs they illustrate, as BMW's own slide does ("Future BMW Sedan · AI concept visual").
  • Check the details. AI gets brand details wrong (grilles, lights, badges). Add a human review step and a brand-detail checklist before anything is shown to a panel.
  • EU AI Act Art. 50 (since 2 Aug 2026) requires disclosure of realistic AI-generated images and video.

For our own story we therefore used real photographs of the real cars from Wikimedia Commons, with credits, and kept AI generation for the future concepts.

06

Lessons for our pitch

  1. BMW's survival pattern is our pitch. Each comeback (R32, R24, Isetta, Neue Klasse) came from reading what customers needed at that moment. The 501 failed because it didn't: a beautiful car for a market that couldn't afford it. That is exactly the decision our tool supports.
  2. The Neue Klasse name is back. BMW chose the 1961 name for its 2025 platform. Linking 1961 to 2025 in our story signals that we understand the brand.
  3. Structure that works: hook question → origin → crisis → reinvention → triumph → teaser. Our 3-minute pitch can use the same arc: problem (a billion findings) → crisis (wrong decisions cost a generation) → our tool → demo → what's next.
  4. Emotion + engineering: the video sells "a machine that made everyday roads feel like racetracks". The keynote's slide 1 says "Emotions, engineered into a product". Our requirements must protect that feeling: the strengths-to-keep list.
07

Our 30-second story

Ten real cars, 1916 → 2025, each with a year, a headline and a one-line fact, ending on BMW's own closing line from the keynote. Rendered from story/make_story.py.

End card (4 s): "From raw findings to the ultimate driving machine. 110 years of listening to drivers. Our turn: AI for product decisions."

12 alternates (BMW 501, R24, Isetta in red, the BMW tower, iX3 rear, …) are in images/bmw-history/alternates/. Swap a file and re-run the script to change the story.

08

Transcript

Timestamped Whisper transcript: research/video2/bmw-history-ep1.transcript.srt (and .txt). The text below is YouTube's caption text; names were misheard by the captioner (e.g. "Herb Kwand" = Herbert Quandt, "Neua Classer" = Neue Klasse).

Show full narration (≈1,900 words)

Before BMW was about luxury and performance, it was about flight. This episode traces a century of reinvention. From airplane engines, and stripped down motorcycles to daring small cars that saved a company, expect engines, war, near collapse, and the little machines that made BMW what it is today. BMW's roots start with two names you might not expect. Karl Rapp and Gustav Otto. In the 1910s, Europe needed aircraft engines and both men were building advanced power plants. Gustav Otto ran Flugmaschinenfabrik Gustav Otto; Karl Rapp headed Rapp Motorenwerke. Consolidation during World War I reshaped those companies. In 1916, Bayerische Flugzeugwerke or BFW was founded at Munich's Oberwiesenfeld airfield. One year later, Rapp's business was renamed Bayerische Motoren Werke GmbH. And by 1918, it became a public company. In 1922, BMW AG transferred its engine construction, its name, and its emblem into BFW. That's why BMW counts March 7th, 1916, the founding of BFW, as its official birthday. The roundel with Bavaria's blue and white appeared in 1917. Advertising soon re-imagined it as a spinning propeller, a symbol that connected BMW to aviation and stuck in the brand's DNA. But after World War I, Germany's restrictions on aircraft manufacture forced BMW to pivot. The company turned to railway brakes, industrial engines, and other mechanical products. Through reshuffles and acquisitions, the workforce, tooling, and brand elements all landed in Munich's Oberwiesenfeld, the same site that remains BMW's global headquarters today.

In 1923, BMW reinvented itself on two wheels. At the Berlin Motor Show, the company unveiled the R32, a motorcycle that completely redefined expectations. Designed by Max Friz, it introduced a boxer engine with cylinders mounted sideways, plus a shaft drive instead of a chain. Riders immediately noticed how durable and easy to service it was. The shaft drive meant less maintenance, and the flat twin delivered smooth, reliable power. Everything about the R32 felt engineered to last. This bike set the template for BMW motorcycles for decades to come. Boxer engines and shaft drives became the brand's signature, a DNA you can still see today. The R32 wasn't just a product. It was a milestone in motorcycle history that proved BMW could do more than airplanes. They could master the road.

By the late 1920s, BMW was ready to build cars. In 1928 they purchased Fahrzeugfabrik Eisenach and with it the license to produce the tiny Austin 7. BMW rebadged it as the Dixi, their very first automobile. Soon after BMW started creating their own designs, the 303 sedan arrived in 1933. The first BMW with a six-cylinder engine and the first to wear the now famous kidney grille. It was a symbol that the company had real ambitions in the car world. Sporty models followed quickly. The nimble 315 Roadster and then the 328 in 1936. Light, fast, and beautifully engineered. The 328 became a racing legend, winning at the Nürburgring and the Mille Miglia and proving BMW could compete with the very best.

As the 1930s wore on, BMW's story took a darker turn. Germany's rearmament shifted the company away from road cars and motorcycles and deep into aircraft engines. Massive factories were built like the one at Allach to meet the demands of the war economy. During World War II, BMW became a major supplier of engines for the Luftwaffe. Cars and motorcycles still existed, but they were a small part of the business. When the war ended, the consequences were severe. Allied forces occupied BMW's plants, stripped out machinery as reparations, and dismantled equipment. What had been vast industrial sites were left gutted. The company's future looked uncertain, and survival would take an entirely new beginning.

After the devastation of the war, BMW needed something simple to rebuild. The answer came in 1948 with the R24, their first new motorcycle of the postwar era. It was based on the pre-war R23, but refined. A single cylinder engine, shaft drive, and rugged frame made it cheap to run and easy to maintain. At a time when Germany desperately needed affordable transport, production was delayed by shortages and missing machinery. But once it got going, the R24 became a hit. In 1949 alone, BMW sold more than 9,000 units. That success proved the company still had its engineering magic. The R24 didn't just bring in money. It restored confidence that BMW could survive and eventually thrive in a world no longer defined by war.

In 1952, BMW returned to automobiles with the 501, a large, elegant luxury saloon. Powered by an improved version of their pre-war 6-cylinder engine, the 501 could seat six in comfort. It was a car meant to reestablish BMW's place in the premium market, but high costs and limited demand meant the 501 never became a big seller. Still, it signaled that BMW was back in the car business. By the late 1950s, BMW faced collapsing sales and mounting financial trouble. Salvation came in the unlikeliest form, the tiny BMW Isetta. In 1955, BMW licensed the bubble car design from Italy's Iso, then re-engineered it with their own 250 cc motorcycle engine. The result was cheap to buy, cheap to run, and perfect for a country still rebuilding. Its front opening door and egg-shaped body made it instantly recognizable. Families squeezed in, students zipped through city streets, and suddenly BMW had a best seller. The Isetta wasn't glamorous, but it sold in huge numbers and kept the lights on. More importantly, it rebuilt goodwill with buyers and proved BMW could adapt. Without this quirky little micro car, the company might not have survived the 1950s.

By 1959, BMW was on the brink. Sales were weak, debts were rising, and Daimler-Benz offered to take over. At the 10th December shareholders meeting, collapse seemed certain. But small investors and workers refused to give in, voting the deal down. That stand gave industrialist Herbert Quandt the confidence to increase his stake. With his money, government support, and a leaner strategy, BMW pulled back from disaster. Quandt's gamble kept the company independent, a turning point that set the stage for everything to come.

The real comeback arrived in 1961 with the Neue Klasse, the new class of sporty sedans that redefined BMW. It began with the BMW 1500 shown at the Frankfurt Motor Show. Designed by Wilhelm Hofmeister with styling input from Giovanni Michelotti. The car introduced clean lines, a modern cabin, and the Hofmeister kink at the rear window. A design cue that still defines BMW today. Under the skin sat the brand new M10 4-cylinder engine. Oversquare and incredibly robust, it delivered smooth power and became the backbone of BMW's lineup for decades. Independent suspension and disc brakes gave the 1500 handling far sharper than rivals in its class. Demand was immediate. Orders poured in faster than BMW could build them. The lineup expanded quickly. 1600s, 1800s, and hotter twin carb versions. Each reinforcing the formula, practical size, modern engineering, and a sporty edge. The Neue Klasse didn't just save BMW financially. It created the template for the modern sport sedan. Its DNA carried straight into the next generation, including the 02 series, and cemented BMW's reputation worldwide.

By the late 1960s, BMW had distilled the Neue Klasse formula into something even more focused, the BMW 2002. Compact, light, and powered by a 2-litre version of the M10, the 2002 had sharp steering, a short wheelbase, and an engine that loved to rev on twisting mountain roads. It felt alive, eager in the corners, quick to respond, and genuinely fun to drive. The 2002 became the blueprint for the modern sports sedan. It wasn't just transportation. It was a driver's car. A machine that made everyday roads feel like racetracks. In the city, the BMW 2002 was just as special. Its compact size made parking easy. Its lively engine kept traffic entertaining, and the cabin had real space for everyday use. It turned commuting into something more. Proof that even a practical car could feel exciting. The BMW 2002 wasn't just a fun street car. It proved itself on the track. Thanks to its light weight, sharp handling, and tunable M10 engine, the 2002 became a favorite among privateers and club racers. It was affordable to modify, durable under stress, and competitive against much larger rivals. Twin carb and tii versions added more power, and soon the 2002 was taking podiums in touring car events across Europe. In 1973, BMW even launched the 2002 Turbo, one of the very first turbocharged production cars in Europe and a sign of the company's bold engineering spirit. On circuits from the Nürburgring to smaller national series, the 2002 earned a reputation as a giant killer. It blended agility, strength, and personality, proving that the compact sedan could win races and capture hearts. This motorsport legacy set the stage for BMW's future dominance, laying the groundwork for the M division and the performance culture that would define the brand in the decades ahead.

The BMW 2002 drove off into history, a symbol of survival and reinvention. Next time, the story shifts into high gear. We'll explore the birth of the 3 Series, the car that defined BMW for generations. From the E21 to the legendary E30 M3, discover how BMW built an icon and how the brand's performance DNA went from racetrack to everyday roads.

I've finished everything you asked this round. The main new piece is the product plan at `product/pipeline.html`. Per your "plan first" instruction it is planning only, with no product code. The `story/make_story.py` script was written before that instruction, and it only renders the story video.

**The plan (MarketPulse)**
- **Your idea fits the brief well.** Market-specific listening, AI-written requirements, the product manager approving each one, then car profiles, visuals and a test loop.
- **Mermaid workflow:** four diagrams (system overview, one loop step by step, data model, 30-hour build plan). All four render correctly in Chrome.
- **Six dashboard mock-ups:** Markets, Evidence, Requirements, Profiles, Test and Log. They use BMW's real numbers where marked; the rest is illustrative.
- **Grounding:** the plan uses the organisers' SMART rule, keynote slide 1 ("Emotions, engineered into a product") and the 2025 annual report. Two annual report facts matter most: China deliveries fell 12.5% while the 5 Series grew 19.5%, and BMW says it already uses "AI agents and agentic workflows" internally.

**Five changes I'd make to your idea, all explained in the plan:**
1. **Don't post AI-generated BMWs on public social media.** It's a brand and leak risk, and since 2 Aug 2026 the EU AI Act requires labelling realistic AI images and video. For the demo, use a simulated panel of AI personas built from each market's real data, labelled as simulated. A real version would use closed panels or car clinics.
2. **No fine-tuning.** Labelling with an LLM and checking against about 100 hand-labelled rows is faster and easier to explain.
3. **Every generated image is tagged** with the requirement IDs it shows, so the image itself documents the decision.
4. **The cost agent gives a signal, not a business case.** The brief rules out detailed business cases.
5. **China is labelled low-confidence**, because BMW's data has no Chinese customer comments.

**Tech stack corrections from the research:**

**Pair typefaces.** Typography determines how the page reads even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the only font host the Artifact CSP allows; link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=...&display=swap">`). A face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI, or the browser silently uses a fallback. In both cases, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide. Set a type scale and keep to it. Give headings `text-wrap: balance`, give body text comfortable spacing, and give uppercase labels a little letter-spacing.

**Load libraries instead of inlining them.** When the page really needs a library (React, a charting or highlighting package), load its UMD build from cdnjs with one `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/...">`, pinned to an exact version at least two weeks old and placed before the inline script that uses its global; don't inline the library's source or hand-write a substitute. Only the script loads this way; a library's stylesheet still has to be inlined, and the page contract above lists the few other script hosts the CSP admits. The page's own CSS and JS, its images, and its data ship with the page. Most pages don't need any library; use one only when it does substantial work for the page.

**Choose neutrals deliberately.** A pure mid-grey looks unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent looks intentional. Pure white and near-black are fine backgrounds when they suit the subject, as long as you chose the neutral deliberately instead of inheriting a default.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states: an explicit choice sets `data-theme="dark"` or `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting sets *nothing*. Most viewers see the document with no `data-theme` attribute, where only `prefers-color-scheme` distinguishes light from dark. Structure the CSS at the token level for all three. The bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice overrides a dark OS setting; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also overrides in the other direction; wherever the dark palette applies - both dark blocks, or bare `:root` in a dark-first or single-dark design - also set `color-scheme: dark` (the skeleton pins `light` on `:root`), so native form controls and scrollbars follow the palette. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block: a color defined only inside `[data-theme]` never applies when no `data-theme` attribute is set, and the page then shows one theme's text on the other theme's background. Two more rules keep each theme consistent. First, the artifact is composited over a background the viewer paints in *its own* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token; a transparent body shows the host's background with no warning. Second, every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never from a literal that works in only one theme. Declare every token in the bare `:root` block before any media or `[data-theme]` block redefines it; a color that exists only inside one of those blocks is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first: don't simply invert it; keep contrast legible and keep the accent working on both backgrounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme: then omit the media query and `[data-theme]` blocks entirely but still set the background and every color explicitly, so the page looks right on either host background; do this by choice, never by omission.

**Use layout for spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap` instead of per-element margins, which collapse or double without warning. Keep a side gutter of at least 16px at every width: set it once as side padding on `body` or one outer wrapper, whose vertical padding uses `padding-block` and never a `padding` shorthand that zeroes the sides. Let rows wrap or stack to one column at phone width (about 400px). Give images and any `aspect-ratio` box `max-width: 100%`, and don't give anything a `min-width` wider than the screen. Only wide tables, code, and diagrams may exceed it; give each `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. The publish skeleton pads `:root` top and bottom by the phone's safe-area insets (zero everywhere except a phone app) so the page runs edge to edge while its content stays clear of the system bars; keep that padding. A bar fixed to the top or bottom stays at `0` and adds `env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)` or `env(safe-area-inset-bottom, 0px)` to its own padding. A sticky page header uses `top: env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)` and never `0`. Size a one-screen app with `height: 100%` on `html` and `body` instead of `100vh`, so it fits inside that padding. A page that includes its own viewport meta gets this padding only when that meta declares `viewport-fit=cover`. Use `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Make repeated elements consistent.** For cards in a row, label/value pairs down a list, or badges on sibling items, use the same edges, baselines, and inner padding on each, and put any recurring element in the same place on each. Let content set a container's height and pick a column count the items fill, so nothing stretches over empty space or sits alone in a row. Make text that can outgrow its track wrap or scroll in its own container; clipped text is a bug.

**Use card styling selectively.** Border, fill, radius, and shadow each mark an element as a separate object. Apply them by role, to set off the one element that needs it; applying the same radius and shadow to every block flattens the hierarchy. Open with big-number tiles only when those figures are the point of the page.

**Draw charts to scale.** Place marks, ticks, and labels with one scale, and make every label name a value the chart actually reaches. Color chart text from the theme tokens so it is readable in both themes. Keep marks, labels, and edges clear of one another and inside the drawing's bounds; in SVG, leave room in the viewBox for the outermost labels and give every drawn shape an explicit fill.

**Make the page complete at rest.** Everything meant to be read is visible once the page has loaded, with no scrolling to trigger it; that first still frame is what a thumbnail, a shared link, and a skimming reader all see. A section may animate in, but from a visible resting state, never left at `opacity: 0` waiting for an observer. Size a hero to its content instead of to the viewport; a `100vh` opener pushes the rest of the page out of that first frame. A tool or app opens in a realistic working state: the user's real data where it exists, otherwise example rows, a loaded sample, or a plausibly filled form, clearly marked as examples and never presented as the user's own figures. The first view shows what the tool does; an empty shell waiting for input shows nothing. When those records live in the `db` capability, keep them out of the page source. Its first frame renders before the store answers, so make that frame a designed empty state that names what will appear and how to add the first entry, then fill it from the store. Seed the store through the `ArtifactData` tool (what type instructions call `write_db`) after the first publish: the user's real data, or marked examples for a tool only the user will use. For a store other people will fill with their own entries, seed only what the user gave you or asked for, never invented people or records.

**Avoid AI-generated design.** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. When the user specifies a visual direction, follow it exactly; their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. When nothing is specified, don't use that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly.** Watch for overlapping elements, cascade collisions, and silent font fallbacks. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, and respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. Give every form control a stable `id` (the platform preserves form values, focus, and scroll position across a republish). For generative or decorative graphics, use Canvas or WebGL instead of hand-writing long SVG path data.

**CSS rules.** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificity. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out, e.g. a type-based selector like `.section` and an element-based one like `.cta` both setting padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't undo your spacing unnoticed.

**Writing the copy.** Treat words as design material and never as decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen: name things by what people recognize instead of how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*; they don't manage *webhook config*). Use active voice; a control states exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it, without apologies or vagueness. Prefer specific to clever. Write plainly, the way a knowledgeable person would talk. Avoid mannered devices: asides set off by em-dashes, "not X, but Y" framing, colon-then-reveal sentences, scare quotes around invented labels, and stock phrases such as "worth noting" or "honest caveat". Prefer short, direct sentences over compressed or clever phrasing.

**Name the page like a product; don't caption it.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it gives the reader a first impression of the care taken. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject; or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which then is the page's name. When the user already has a specific name for the thing, use that name for the title rather than coining a new one. Stop at the name; a title that adds its own explanation after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it appears beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could apply to any of them fails as a name just as an appended explanation does. When a candidate title combines the name with a generic word (a greeting, a category, a page-type label), keep the name; a trim that drops the identifying part and keeps the generic word produces a title that could apply to any page. This rule removes explanations and doesn't require brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. Put the explanation in the one-sentence publish `description`; the gallery shows it directly under the title.

**Structure is information.** Structural devices (numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels) should encode something true about the content instead of decorating it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but those fit only if the content actually is a sequence, such as a real process or a typed timeline where the order is information the reader needs. Before adding numbered markers or similar devices, check that they actually make sense.

**When the page is a UI (dashboard, tool).** It is scanned and operated instead of read top to bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Put the summary before the detail. Encode state in form as well as in numbers (a pill, a chip, a severity stripe) so that whatever needs attention is visible at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. Interactive elements should look interactive.



## Process

Start from what the viewer should be able to do on the page, in addition to what they will read. If the page should take input, keep what people change for whoever opens it next, show live data, or ask Claude something, load the `artifact-capabilities` skill now and design around what it makes available to this user. A page that is only read doesn't need that.

Before writing the page, settle a short design plan (a compact token system) and write it into the file itself, as the `:root` block at the top of the page's `<style>`, rather than into your reply:
- **Color**: the palette as 4-6 named color tokens.
- **Type**: font tokens for 2+ roles: a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: the layout concept as a one-line comment above the tokens.

Then build the rest of the page from those tokens, deriving every color and type decision from them. The plan is working material, not part of the answer: unless the user asks about the design, one plain sentence on the direction is the most to say about it, with no hex values or font names.

**Write, check once, publish.** Before publishing you may look at the rendered page once, where this session offers a way: one `ArtifactCheck` preview (or the Artifact tool's own `action: "preview"` where there is no separate `ArtifactCheck` tool), or else one screenshot of the local file; if the session offers none of these, skip the look. The preview renders desktop and phone widths in light and dark and lists overflow, colors that ignore the theme, blocked loads and console errors, including a script that fails to parse, so nothing it covers needs a check of your own. The look is optional: if you take it, make one pass of edits for what it shows, without a second look; then publish. For a page that charts real numbers, take the look rather than skip it, and spend it on the chart. A page whose point is logic (dates, money, scoring, parsing) may get one more check before publishing: one run of a pure function on a sample input, or, where no preview ran, one syntax check of its script; nothing more. A page that declares `capabilities` takes the look rather than skipping it, then one functional pass after the first publish, because the preview cannot run that code: read back once what the page stores or serves (one read of its stored data or one read-only route call; where that read alone would prove nothing, as on an empty store, you may first write one probe document yourself and delete it after the read, passing the `version` the write returned as `if_version`; no other test writes unless the user wants one), tell the user in one line what you exercised and what you could not, and stop. None of this becomes a loop, because the user is waiting for a link: no second screenshot, no scripts that probe the DOM, no re-running a check that passed. Review happens on the live page, and further polish is for the user to request; if the user reports something visibly broken (a clipped column, unreadable text, a control that does nothing), fix that, take at most one more look if the session offers a way, and republish once. These checks are for code you wrote into this page, not for content you fill into an Artifact made from an Artifact type (a Slides deck, a Design canvas): there the type's own instructions say whether to check, and if they say nothing, don't.

**Open viewers.** You don't need to do anything for viewers who already have the page open: published changes are delivered to them automatically at their next quiet moment, with state preserved where possible. If your page has state a viewer would miss (a game, a long form), register `window.claude?.hot?.snapshot(...)` and boot through `window.claude?.hot?.ready ? window.claude.hot.ready(start) : start(window.claude?.hot?.data ?? {})`; `hot` is the viewer's own update hook, not a capability behind `claude.use()`, and is absent outside a viewer, hence the `?.`.

## When the request is editorial

The stance changes here: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated decisions, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part in the plan itself, without narrating the revision to the user. Write the code only after the plan is specific to this subject, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero states the thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world (headline, image, live demo, interactive moment). 
- Typography sets the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, avoiding the families you would use on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design instead of a neutral container for the content. 
- Use motion deliberately. Think about whether and where animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. One orchestrated moment is usually more effective than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation adds to the impression that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Put your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent clashes with the background, shift it toward an analogous hue or desaturate it instead of replacing it.

MarketPulse ProblemHow it worksMarketsA requirementCar profilesTestingWhy BMWBuild planDemoTechDecisions
EHL Hackathon · BMW track · Munich, 10–11 Oct 2026

MarketPulse

A co-pilot for BMW product managers. It listens to customers in each market, turns what they say into clear requirements, shows them as concept cars, and tests them with people before anything is built.

1Listen→ 2Understand→ 3Decide→ 4Imagine→ 5Check cost→ 6Test↺

Startups build a landing page and a waitlist before they build the product. MarketPulse brings that loop to car development, separately for Europe, China and the US, and the product manager signs off every decision.

The problem

Too much feedback, too many markets, too little trace

1 billion

findings for one car

Reviews, complaints, surveys and social posts. BMW's own slide: 1 billion findings → 1,000 requirements → one car.

−12.5%

BMW deliveries in China, 2025

What drivers want differs by market. A requirement that wins in Germany can lose in China (BMW Group Report 2025).

3 years

later, nobody knows why

BMW's product manager: "you need to document your decisions and the context at the time you took them."

How it works

Six steps, one loop

Each step has its own colour. AI marks what the system does, and PM marks where the product manager decides.

1 · Listen situation analysis

Collect what people say about BMW and its competitors, tagged by market.

InputBMW feedback, surveys and sales · Reddit, YouTube, Google Trends · Autohome and Weibo for China
OutputRaw comments, each tagged with market, model and source
WhoAI

2 · Understand structure & context

Label every comment, merge duplicates and group them into themes, like "climate controls are hard to reach".

InputRaw comments
OutputThemes with counts, real quotes and source mix
WhoAI

3 · Decide requirements + prioritization

AI drafts each requirement with SMART targets, ranks the list with visible weights, and explains each rank. The PM approves, edits or rejects each one and gives a reason.

InputThemes, sales volume per market, trends
OutputRanked, approved requirements with evidence, assumptions and conflicts
WhoAI draftsPM decides

4 · Imagine car profiles

Bundle the approved requirements into 2–3 car profiles per market. Generate the parts first (wheels, interior, lights), then the whole car, then a 10–30 s story video tuned to local culture.

InputApproved requirements + market context (roads, climate, charging)
OutputProfiles with images and a short video, every visual tagged "AI concept"
WhoAIPM picks

5 · Check cost feasibility

Price each profile's materials and battery against live commodity data, and check whether it fits the EV trend in that market. This is a signal for the PM, not a business case.

InputMaterials, battery type, metal prices, BMW option prices
OutputCost index (today's car = 100) and risk flags
WhoAI

6 · Test concept test

# Overview: BMW evaluation criteria (judging rubric)

| | |
|---|---|
| **File** | `data/sources/bmw-evaluation-criteria.png` (screenshot shared by the user, 10 Oct 2026) |
| **What** | The five criteria the BMW jury uses, plus an explicit "we reward honesty" note |
| **Why it matters** | This is the scoring sheet. Every demo minute and every feature must earn points on one of these rows |

## The rubric (verbatim summary)
| # | Criterion | What the jury looks for |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Decision and Scoring Logic** | Quality, consistency and explainability of how requirements are derived, evaluated, scored and prioritised. Which factors influence decisions, **how evidence and sources are weighted and combined**, how **trade-offs, uncertainties and conflicting signals are resolved** |
| 2 | **Workflow and Human Decision-Making** | End-to-end workflow from heterogeneous findings to prioritised requirements, with **clearly defined roles, decision gates, review steps**, and **boundaries between AI-supported, autonomous and human decisions** |
| 3 | **Traceability and Auditability** | Trace every requirement, score, modification and decision back to its evidence and sources, with a **complete, reconstructable history of approvals, modifications, postponements and rejections** |
| 4 | **Solution Quality, Usability and Feasibility** | Quality of the prototype, usefulness of the generated requirements, ease of use for **PMs and engineering teams**, realistic fit in a **complex enterprise** environment |
| 5 | **Innovation, Scalability and Business Impact** | Originality, scaling across **products, markets and data volumes**, less manual effort and rework, **shorter decision cycles**, better requirement and decision quality |
| + | **We reward honesty** | Show where the app **lacks evidence, meets conflicting signals or reaches uncertain conclusions**, and how this is surfaced to the PM. "Honest limitations are a strength, not a weakness." |

## How MarketPulse scores today, and what to add
| Criterion | Already in the plan | Gap → add |
|---|---|---|
| 1 Scoring logic | Visible weights (frequency, severity, satisfaction gap, volume, trend, brand fit); "why #3?"; conflicts shown | **Evidence weighting rules**: weight per source type and bias, sample size, recency and cross-source agreement → a confidence score. **Conflict-resolution policy**: never average; split by segment or market, flag it, and the PM decides. **Trade-off view**: e.g. range vs cost index. **Sensitivity check**: does the top 10 change if weights move ±20%? |
| 2 Workflow & roles | Human gates at baseline, targets and priorities (matches the keynote icons) | **Explicit autonomy levels**: autonomous (collect, label, cluster), AI-proposes (drafts, ranks, profiles), human-only (approve, reject, postpone, change weights). **Named gates G1–G4. Roles**: PM (owner), market lead (per-market review), engineering (feasibility review), with sign-off rules |
| 3 Traceability | Decision log, reason, evidence snapshot, Entire trail | **Postpone** as a first-class action (the rubric names it). **Version history of every score and edit** (diff view). Every requirement has a click path back to the raw comments. **Replay**: "show the list as it was on date X" |
| 4 Usability & feasibility | Dashboard mock-ups; SMART cards | **Hand-off to engineering**: export to **PTC Codebeamer**, which BMW adopted for all engineering requirements (see `reports/automotive-product-management.html`), e.g. via ReqIF/CSV. **Role-based views** (PM vs engineer). Fits next to existing tools instead of replacing them |
| 5 Innovation & impact | Market lens, concept-test loop, AI visuals | **Measured impact**: minutes per requirement (manual vs tool), % requirements with ≥3 evidence sources, labelling accuracy vs a hand-labelled sample, decision cycle time. **Scale**: the same pipeline for the 1/5/7 Series × 3 markets without new code |
| Honesty | China flagged low-confidence; simulated panel labelled | A dedicated **"What we don't know" panel**: missing markets (no CN or DE comments), weak samples, unresolved conflicts, label noise, synthetic-looking rows. **Confidence on every requirement**, with the reason |

## Consequence for the demo
Criteria 1–3 are three of the five rows and all about **logic, workflow and trace**. Images and video only touch criterion 5. → **Build priority:** scoring + gates + audit trail + honesty panel first. Car visuals and video are pre-generated garnish.

| Criterion | What we had | What I added |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Decision and scoring logic** | Six visible weights and a "why is this #3?" explanation | How evidence is weighted (by source type and bias, sample size, agreement across sources). A rule that conflicts are split by market or segment and never averaged. A trade-off view (e.g. range vs cost) and a check that the top 10 holds if the weights move ±20% |
| **2. Workflow and human decisions** | The PM decides where BMW's process slide shows a person | Three autonomy levels: AI alone (collect, label, cluster), AI proposes (drafts, ranking), human only (approve, reject, postpone, weights). | **3. Traceability** | Decision log with reasons | **Postpone** as its own action (the rubric names postponements explicitly). A history of every score and edit, and a way to see the list exactly as it was on any past date |
| **4. Usability and feasibility** | SMART requirement cards | Export to **PTC Codebeamer**, the tool BMW already uses for engineering requirements, plus a separate view for engineers |
| **5. Innovation and impact** | Market lens and concept testing | Measured results in the demo: minutes per requirement by hand vs with the tool, share of requirements backed by 3+ sources, labelling accuracy on a hand-checked sample |

# Conversation 03: team debrief after the BMW conversations
_10 Oct 2026, EHL hackathon, Munich. Three members of our team summarise what they heard. Edited from `../raw/03-team-debrief.raw.md`._

**Speakers.** **A**, **B**, **C** = team members (the transcript's Speakers 1, 2, 3).
**Editing marks.** `[cut]` = the recording broke ("sometimes it doesn't record", 03:05). `[fix: X]` = corrected. `[unclear]` = cannot be recovered.

---

**[00:01] A:** What can you remember about it?

**B:** The thing you mentioned, but also what he said at the end?

**[00:10] A:** My understanding: he wants **every input and output to be validated, with a reason for why that output comes out of the pipeline.** For example, if the AI says "let's build a red car", we should be able to **trace back whatever input we have that shows it should be a red car.**

**[00:46] B:** **Data traceability is really important.** We could always check exactly where an output comes from.

**[00:51] B:** The other thing discussed was the framework, or the visualisation, of **the layers**:
- **Layer 1, the hard layer:** the strongest principles and patterns we have for different continents and markets. That is really what makes the final decision, **[?about 60% of it]**.
- **Layer 2:** assumptions and estimates.
- **Layer 3:** maybe social stuff, customer comments and so on.

**[01:40] A:** So basically we're building an algorithm:
- **Layer 1 = fundamentals per country.**
- **Layer 2 = what we get from all the data and trends, everything generated by AI.**
- **Layer 3 = the feedback we get from social media on the profiles.**

**[02:02] B:** That last one isn't really accurate, and it's very sensitive.

**[02:08] A:** So **the third layer gets a really low weight** in the final output.

**[02:21] B:** The other important realisation: **where in the pipeline (input, transformation, output) is the best place to put the human in the loop?** That's a really important decision. We have to be creative and put a lot of effort into finding exactly the right places.

**[02:52] A:** To recap: the third layer is the social posts… [cut, 03:01–03:13]

**[03:13] A:** …so the third layer is **validating the profile ideas with customers on social media** and feeding that back into the loop, but with a lower weight in the equation. **Fundamentals (layer 1) get a high score, AI analysis (layer 2) a middle score, and social (layer 3) the lowest**, because on social media people can comment random things that aren't really relevant to the product.

**[04:07] B:** So we have the foundation layer… [cut]

**[04:17] A:** In short, what they're looking for:
1. **Every output must be traceable through the pipeline**: why the decision was taken and the reasoning behind everything. Every step well documented.
2. **Every decision a product manager takes is recorded in a memory the AI can access**, and **the product manager can edit that memory.** That's a good place for the human in the loop: product managers see and edit what the system remembers about past decisions.

**[05:25] C:** I think the specific data isn't that important, because they can swap it. We can use what we have and set the principles. **The main thing is to show "you can easily replace this with your real data and it still works."**

**[05:50] C:** Even if it's not accurate for the current market, that's fine, **as long as we can explain how it happens and what the agents went through.**

**[06:09] A:** [unclear: "So, Ferro Nomo"] [end of recording]

# Overview and product analysis: conversations with BMW experts (10 Oct 2026)

| | |
|---|---|
| **Files** | `data/sources/conversations/2026-10-10-bmw-experts/`: `raw/` (verbatim transcripts) and `edited/` (cleaned, with gaps and guesses marked) |
| **Who** | 01 + 02: a BMW expert (former owner of his department's AI strategy; responsible for automated driving on the current 3 Series) talking with our team. 03: our team's debrief |
| **Quality** | Automatic transcripts with breaks. Quotes below come from the edited versions; anything marked `[?]` in the edited files is our guess |
| **Why it matters** | This is the closest we have to the jury's own voice. It tells us **what to build and what to drop** |

---

## 1. The eight things BMW told us

| # | What they said | Where | What it means for MarketPulse |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **"If you just give us a car, even a very good car, we don't care if we can't understand the reasoning or the lineage."** "We don't actually need a car." "No, the logic." | 01 · 06:10–07:12 | **The core product is the reasoning chain, not visuals.** AI car images and video drop from core to optional. |
| 2 | **"Focus on one or two [of the 3–5 buckets]… explain why… the rest can just pass through."** "Even if you only solve where it's best to have a human in the loop, you can win the challenge." | 02 · 01:03–03:02 | Pick two buckets and go deep: **(a) weight logic / prioritisation** and **(b) human-in-the-loop design.** The other steps run as a simple pass-through. |
| 3 | **"Which sources should be prioritised and which deprioritised, a weight logic. This is what we need to solve."** "How should we prioritise customer studies versus professional outlets? Guess, but tell us why and how we could change it." | 02 · 01:03–01:33 | A **visible, editable source-weight model** with a written rationale for every default weight. |
| 4 | **Weights differ per car:** "For a 1 Series social media resonance matters more… for a 7 Series, what social media says is not relevant." "If I can tweak which source has priority for which car… amazing." | 02 · 02:03–03:02 | **Weight profiles per model (and per market).** The same pipeline, different weights for the 1 Series vs the 7 Series. |
| 5 | **"Your layer idea is awesome."** Take 5–10 principles from a Google search as the **hardest layer**; that's "totally fair". Principles come from management decisions ("a manager at BMW decides 'we do it this way', and that becomes a basic principle") and must be able to change. | 01 · 00:00, 03:43–04:19 | A **three-layer model** with a **principles layer** on top (see §2). Principles are documented, owned and versioned, with a change process. |
| 6 | **Lineage example:** Japan wants a smaller 7 Series (parking garages); the US and China want it bigger. "We deprioritise Japan… because of larger markets. Next data point: sales. That's why we propose bigger." | 01 · 07:12–09:05 | Our **flagship demo story**: a market conflict resolved by a rule (volume-weighted), shown step by step. Our own data supports it (see §4). |
| 7 | **Tacit knowledge is the real problem.** "We didn't write down the reasoning… everybody in the project knew why." Amazon-style written decisions; "it's in the heads of the product managers." | 01 · 00:47–03:03 | A **decision memory**: every PM decision and its reason is stored, the AI uses it, and **the PM can read and edit it** (team debrief 03 · 04:17). |
| 8 | **"We want 90% of requirements derived by AI"**, then humans adjust for complexity, law and restrictions: "you should simply be able to edit or keep… no black box." | 01 · 05:33 | Target split: AI drafts about 90%; humans gate the rest. Every AI output has **Keep / Edit** controls. |

**Also mentioned:**
- **Missing data is a decision.** The smart-opener usage was never logged, so "do we need it?" couldn't be answered (02 · 00:00–00:30). MarketPulse should flag **evidence gaps** and suggest what to measure.
- **Regulation and ESG are not raw inputs.** "In many cases this is interpretation" (01 · 03:43). Legal positions enter as **principles set by people**, not as scraped news.
- **Carry-over parts.** A part already used in other series costs almost nothing to offer. "You get it from the engineer", via a bill-of-materials check (SAP) (01 · 04:19–05:22). This belongs at the **engineering review gate**.
- **"Trustworthy AI and sustainability"** [as in: lasting, consistent] is what they look for; "we are in a volatile market… we need some consistency" (01 · 06:10).
- **The data is swappable.** Show that BMW can plug in its real data and the pipeline still works (03 · 05:25).

---

## 2. The three-layer model: our recommendation

The team's debrief (03) defined three layers. One adjustment is needed. The debrief put "customer comments" in the lowest layer, but **BMW's own customer feedback and surveys are strong evidence**, not noise. Only *social media and concept-test reactions* are weak. Recommended version:

| Layer | Contains | Role in the decision | Default weight | Who owns it |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **L1 · Principles** (hard layer) | 5–10 rules per market and brand: brand DNA ("joy of driving"), legal interpretations, data-privacy stance, market rules ("Japan: smaller; US/China: larger"), carry-over policy | **Gate + strong prior.** A requirement that breaks a principle is blocked or flagged; one that matches gets a boost | Highest (the team suggested about 60% of the final decision; to be tuned) | Named managers. Changes only through a proposal + approval (an employee vote can be an input) |
| **L2 · Evidence** | BMW customer feedback, customer studies, sales volumes, quality data, expert/press reviews, competitor specs | **The main scoring engine**, weighted by source quality | Medium | PM, with the source-weight table |
| **L3 · Signals** | Social media, search trends, concept-test reactions (simulated or real) | **Tie-breaker and early warning.** Never decides alone | Lowest by default, **adjustable per model** (high for the 1 Series, near zero for the 7 Series) | PM per model |

**Default source-weight table (a first guess, editable; BMW asked us to explain our ranking):**

| Source | Default | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Sales volume / market size | 1.0 (used as a market multiplier) | Hard business fact; resolves market conflicts (the 7 Series example) |
| BMW customer studies (surveys) | 0.9 | Structured, representative, comparable across markets |
| Quality / defect reports | 0.85 | Real problems, often with a stated severity |
| Customer-care and owner feedback | 0.7 | Real owners, but biased toward problems and "how do I" questions |
| Professional outlets / expert reviews | 0.6 | Informed, but a reviewer's view is not a buyer's view |
| Search trends | 0.4 | Shows interest, not need |
| Social media | 0.2 (1 Series: 0.5 · 7 Series: 0.05) | Noisy and unverified; matters more for young entry-level buyers |
| Concept-test reactions (simulated) | 0.1 | Hypothesis ranking only, always labelled |

---

## 3. Where the human sits: a placement rule we can explain

BMW said this alone could win the challenge. A rule that justifies each placement: **put a human where a step is hard to reverse, needs knowledge that isn't written down, or carries legal or brand risk; let AI run where steps are cheap to redo and easy to check.**

| Step | Mode | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Collect and clean sources | 🤖 autonomous | Cheap to redo; mechanical |
| Label and cluster feedback | 🤖 autonomous + spot check | Errors are visible and fixable; a weekly 5% sample is checked by an analyst |
| Set principles (L1) | 👤 human only | Interpretation, law, brand: "a manager decides" |
| Set source weights per model | 👤 human, AI suggests | Business judgement ("social matters for the 1 Series") |
| Draft requirements + SMART targets | 🤖 proposes (~90%) | BMW's own target |
| Resolve conflicts between markets | 🤖 proposes the rule-based answer → 👤 confirms | High impact (e.g. 7 Series size); needs the lineage view |
| Engineering check (carry-over parts, BOM, complexity) | 👤 engineer | Knowledge sits with engineers and in SAP |
| Approve / edit / postpone / reject | 👤 PM only | Accountability |
| Decision memory | 🤖 records → 👤 PM can edit | Captures tacit knowledge; the PM corrects what the AI remembers |
| Evidence gap → "measure this" | 🤖 flags → 👤 decides whether to collect | Smart-opener lesson |

---

## 4. Demo story built from what they said
**"Should the next 7 Series be bigger?"** This uses the expert's own example, and our data can show it:
1. **L1 principle:** "The 7 Series must look clearly above the 5 Series" (from 01 · 07:38, "if it looks like a 5 Series, nobody cares").
2. **L2 evidence:** our China survey rates the 7 Series' rear space lower than Europe does (see `data/DATA-REPORT.md`); US owners praise rear comfort. Japan feedback is a small sample in our data [check counts before the demo].
3. **Market weights:** 2025 sales of 7 Series: US 12k, China 10k, Europe 13k; Japan is inside "rest of world" (7k). [verify in `data/bmw/sales/`]
4. **Conflict rule:** volume-weighted preference → "bigger", with Japan's objection shown, not hidden.
5. **Human gate:** the PM approves "bigger" and writes the reason. The decision memory stores it. An evidence-gap card says "Japan size data is thin: collect parking-garage fit data".
6. **Lineage view:** click "bigger" → see each layer, each source, each weight and each decision step. That is exactly the "why did it land here?" they asked for.

---

## 5. What changes in our plan

| Area | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Core message | Signals → requirements → concept cars → test loop | **A principled, weighted, traceable requirement engine.** The PM can always see why |
| Focus buckets | All five stages | **Prioritisation (weight logic)** + **human-in-the-loop design**. Documentation/lineage is the spine; other steps pass through |
| AI car images and video | Step 4, with a 10–30 s video | **Optional garnish** at most (one illustrative card). "We don't need a car" |
| Social media publishing loop | Step 6 | Becomes the **L3 signal layer**: low weight, adjustable per model, simulated in the demo |
| New features | | **Principles layer (L1)** with owners and a change process · **per-model source-weight profiles** · **decision memory** the PM can edit · **evidence-gap cards** · **carry-over/BOM check at the engineering gate** · **Keep/Edit on every AI output** |
| Proof for the jury | | Show the data is swappable: same pipeline, BMW's real data plugs in |

## 6. Open questions to settle as a team
1. **Layer weights:** is "about 60% for L1" a target or just an impression? Proposal: L1 acts as a gate plus a boost instead of a fixed percentage, so it stays explainable.
2. **Who changes principles?** The team proposed an employee vote; the expert said "a manager decides". Proposal: the manager decides, and a vote is one input, logged.
3. **Which customer comments go where?** Recommendation above: BMW's own feedback = L2 (strong), social = L3 (weak).
4. **Do we keep the concept-test loop at all in the demo?** Proposal: keep it as one slide showing the L3 layer, not as a built feature.

I saved the three conversations in `data/sources/conversations/2026-10-10-bmw-experts/`, inside `data/`, so they never go to git. Each has an untouched raw copy and a cleaned version, plus an analysis of what they mean for the product.

**How I edited them:** in the cleaned versions I merged lines the transcriber split, and marked every change so you can check it:
- `[fix: …]` for corrected words, such as "VMware" → BMW, "friction in car" → fridge, "bit of materials" → bill of materials, "human in the youth" → loop.
- `[cut]` where the recording breaks.
- `[unclear]` where a word can't be recovered, such as "The Forbidden", "Portland" or "Ferro Nomo". I didn't guess those.

**What changes the product.** The analysis is in `data/sources/overviews/bmw-expert-conversations-overview.md`.

1. **They don't need the car.** The expert said: "If you just give us a car, even a very good car, we don't care if we can't understand the reasoning or the lineage." So the AI car images and video drop from core to optional.
2. **Go deep on one or two steps, not all five.** He named the two that matter most: how sources are weighted, and where the human sits in the loop ("you can win the challenge for this"). The other steps can run as a simple pass-through.
3. **The weights depend on the car.** Social media matters for the 1 Series (young buyers) and is "not relevant" for the 7 Series. So I propose a weight profile per model, with a default source-weight table and a reason for each weight. He explicitly asked us to explain our ranking and how BMW could change it.
4. **Your layer idea was praised.** I recommend one change to the team's version, though. The debrief put customer comments in the weakest layer, but BMW's own feedback and surveys are strong evidence. Only social media and concept-test reactions should be weak. My proposed layers:
   - **Principles:** a few hard rules per market, owned by managers.
   - **Evidence:** BMW feedback, surveys and sales; this does most of the scoring.
   - **Signals:** social media, search trends and concept tests, weighted low.
5. **A demo story from his own example: "Should the next 7 Series be bigger?"** Japan wants it smaller, the US and China bigger, and sales volume settles it. I checked our data and it supports this:
   - Chinese owners rate the 7 Series' rear space 7.52 out of 10, versus 9.41 in Europe.
   - US plus China bought 22,000 7 Series in 2025. Japan sits inside a 7,000 "rest of world" figure.
   - Japan has only 40 comments in our data, which we flag honestly as a thin sample.
6. **New features to add:**
   - A decision memory the product manager can read and edit, so the reasoning that today stays in people's heads gets written down.
   - Cards that flag missing evidence, like his smart-opener example where usage was never measured.
   - A parts-reuse check at the engineering review.
   - Keep or Edit on every AI output, since BMW wants about 90% of requirements drafted by AI.

There's also a table of where the human should sit at each step, with the reason for each placement.

Four questions for the team are at the end of the analysis. The first is whether the principles layer should carry a fixed ~60% weight or act as a gate.

/* Memtrack sample data: ILLUSTRATIVE ONLY, not BMW figures.
 * Shaped like the real pipeline output so the UI can be tested end to end.
 * To use real data locally, create data/prototype/memtrack-data.js (git-ignored) that sets window.MT_DATA
 * with the same shape. The views load it after this file, so it overrides the sample automatically.
 */
window.MT_DATA = {
  meta: {
    label: "Sample data: illustrative, not BMW figures",
    version: "sample-0.1",
    asOf: "2026-10-11",
    isSample: true
  },

  models: [
    { id: "F70", name: "1 Series", segment: "Entry, younger buyers" },
    { id: "G60", name: "5 Series", segment: "Business sedan, volume driver" },
    { id: "G70", name: "7 Series", segment: "Luxury flagship" }

  markets: [
    { id: "EU", name: "Europe" },
    { id: "CN", name: "China" },
    { id: "US", name: "USA" },
    { id: "JP", name: "Japan" }
  ],

  /* Three-layer model agreed after the BMW expert conversations (10 Oct). */
  layers: [
    { id: "L1", name: "Principles", short: "Hard layer", desc: "5–10 rules per market and brand, owned by named managers. Gate + strong prior. Changes only through a proposal and approval." },
    { id: "L2", name: "Evidence", short: "Main engine", desc: "BMW customer feedback, customer studies, sales, quality data, expert reviews. Weighted by source quality." },
    { id: "L3", name: "Signals", short: "Tie-breaker", desc: "Social media, search trends, concept-test reactions. Low weight by default, adjustable per model." }
  ],

  /* Share of the final score per layer, per model profile. PM-editable in the Weights view. */
  layerWeights: {
    F70: { L1: 0.45, L2: 0.35, L3: 0.20 },
    G60: { L1: 0.50, L2: 0.42, L3: 0.08 },
    G70: { L1: 0.55, L2: 0.43, L3: 0.02 }
  },

  /* Default source weights (0–1) with the reason BMW asked us to give. */
  sources: [
    { id: "sales",   name: "Sales volume",               layer: "L2", weight: 1.00, why: "Hard business fact. Used to resolve conflicts between markets." },
    { id: "survey",  name: "Customer studies",           layer: "L2", weight: 0.90, why: "Structured, representative and comparable across markets." },
    { id: "quality", name: "Quality / defect reports",   layer: "L2", weight: 0.85, why: "Real problems with a stated severity." },
    { id: "care",    name: "Owner feedback / care calls",layer: "L2", weight: 0.70, why: "Real owners, but biased toward problems and 'how do I' questions." },
    { id: "press",   name: "Expert reviews / press",     layer: "L2", weight: 0.60, why: "Informed, but a reviewer is not a buyer." },
    { id: "trends",  name: "Search trends",              layer: "L3", weight: 0.40, why: "Shows interest, not need." },
    { id: "social",  name: "Social media",               layer: "L3", weight: 0.20, why: "Noisy and unverified. Matters more for young entry-level buyers." },
    { id: "concept", name: "Concept-test reactions",     layer: "L3", weight: 0.10, why: "Simulated panel: ranks hypotheses only, always labelled." }
  ],
  /* Per-model overrides of source weights (BMW: "social matters for the 1 Series, not for the 7 Series"). */
  sourceOverrides: {
    F70: { social: 0.50, concept: 0.20 },
    G60: {},
    G70: { social: 0.05, press: 0.70 }

    { id: "P-02", market: "ALL", model: "G70", text: "The 7 Series must look and feel clearly above the 5 Series.", owner: "Product Line Manager 7 Series", since: "2024-01", version: 2, status: "active", basis: "BMW expert, 10 Oct: 'if it looks like a 5 Series, nobody cares'" },
    { id: "P-03", market: "JP", model: "G70", text: "Japan: the car must fit standard multi-storey garages.", owner: "Market Lead Japan", since: "2022-09", version: 1, status: "active", basis: "Long-standing Japan market requirement" },
    { id: "P-04", market: "ALL", model: "ALL", text: "Customer data only with opt-in. We collect less than competitors, by choice.", owner: "Data Protection Officer", since: "2021-02", version: 3, status: "active", basis: "Legal interpretation, set by management" },
    { id: "P-05", market: "ALL", model: "ALL", text: "Carry-over first: reuse shared parts where customers cannot tell the difference.", owner: "Head of Vehicle Concepts", since: "2023-11", version: 1, status: "active", basis: "Cost and complexity" },
    { id: "P-06", market: "EU", model: "ALL", text: "Follow Legal's interpretation of EU rules before customer wishes.", owner: "Legal, Product Compliance", since: "2024-06", version: 2, status: "active", basis: "Regulation is interpretation, not a raw input" },

# Memtrack brand guide (v0.1, 10 Oct 2026)

**Memtrack** = *memory* + *track*. It remembers every decision and tracks the path from a raw finding to a requirement. Working name for the BMW hackathon.

> The colours are **inspired by** BMW's public brand and BMW M colours. They are not official BMW design tokens, and we do not use the BMW logo or roundel.

## Files
| File | Use |
|---|---|
| `tokens.css` | **Single source of colour, type and spacing.** Import it first; style components only with `--mt-*` tokens. Light and dark themes included |
| `logo.svg` | Mark + wordmark (wordmark uses `currentColor`, so it works on light and dark) |
| `logo-mark.svg` | Square mark: app icon, favicon |
| `brand-sheet.html` | Visual reference: logo, colours, layers, modes, type, components |

## The idea in the mark
An **M** drawn as a decision track with five nodes: a light-blue signal enters, passes through BMW-blue evidence, reaches the white decision point in the middle, and ends at an **M red** node, the human sign-off.

## Colour system: the depth of blue shows the strength of a signal
| Role | Token | Light | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| Primary action | `--mt-primary` | `#1c69d4` (BMW blue) | Buttons, links, active nav |
| **L1 Principles** | `--mt-l1` | `#16588e` (M dark blue) | Hard rules, the strongest layer |
| **L2 Evidence** | `--mt-l2` | `#1c69d4` (BMW blue) | Feedback, studies, sales |
| **L3 Signals** | `--mt-l3` | `#2f95e6` (M light blue, tuned for contrast) | Social, trends, concept tests |
| **Human decision** | `--mt-human` | `#e22718` (M red) | Gates, sign-offs, "you decide". **Use sparingly**: red means a person is accountable |
| AI on its own | `--mt-auto` | slate `#5b6676` | Autonomous steps |
| AI proposes | `--mt-propose` | BMW blue | Drafts awaiting review |
| Approved / Postponed / Rejected / Draft | `--mt-ok` / `--mt-wait` / `--mt-bad` / `--mt-draft` | green / amber / red / slate | Status only, never decoration |
| Markets | `--mt-eu` `--mt-cn` `--mt-us` `--mt-jp` | blue / red / dark blue / violet | Charts and market chips |
| Navigation | `--steel-900` | `#0b1626` | Sidebar (dark in both themes, like a BMW cockpit) |

Every token has a dark-theme value; never hard-code a colour.

## Type
- **Barlow Semi Condensed** (headings) and **Barlow** (UI text): a free stand-in for BMW's proprietary *BMW Type Next*, with a similar technical, slightly condensed feel.
- **IBM Plex Mono**: IDs (`R-701`, `P-03`, `G2`), hashes and numbers in tables.
- Scale: 12 · 14 · 16 · 20 · 28 · 36 px. Tabular numerals in all tables.

## Voice
- Plain and short. Name things the way a product manager would ("Postpone", "Why this rank").
- Always show **why**: every number has a source, every decision a reason.
- Be honest: label sample data, simulated panels and low confidence openly.

## Do / don't
- ✅ Use red only where a human must act. ✅ Show the layer colour on anything that carries weight.
- ❌ No BMW logo, roundel or model photography in the product UI. ❌ No gradients on data. ❌ Never show AI concept images without the "AI concept" label.

# Memtrack dashboard prototype

Static, clickable views for UI/UX testing. There is no build step: open `dashboard-demo/index.html` in a browser.

## Views
| # | File | What the PM does there | Answers BMW's… |
|---|---|---|---|
| 01 | `views/cockpit.html` | See where the model stands per market; what needs a decision today | situation analysis |
| 02 | `views/requirements.html` | Ranked list, SMART card, "why this rank", Keep / Edit / Postpone / Reject | scoring logic, human decision |
| 03 | `views/lineage.html` | "Should the next 7 Series be bigger?": every principle, source, weight and decision | traceability (flagship demo) |
| 04 | `views/weights.html` | Layer and source weights per model; live re-rank; stability check | weight logic |
| 05 | `views/principles.html` | Hard rules per market, owners, versions, change proposals | L1 principles |
| 06 | `views/hitl.html` | Where the human sits, why, gates G1–G4, what is waiting | human-in-the-loop placement |
| 07 | `views/memory.html` | Decision history, replay, what the AI remembers (PM-editable) | auditability, tacit knowledge |
| 08 | `views/gaps.html` | Missing evidence, conflicts, uncertainty | "we reward honesty" |

## How it fits together
- `../branding/tokens.css`: colours, type and spacing (light + dark).
- `assets/app.css`: shared layout and components.
- `assets/app.js`: the shell (navigation, model/market scope, theme), the **scoring engine** (`MT.score`), and decisions/weights saved in the browser (localStorage).
- `assets/sample-data.js`: **illustrative sample data, not BMW figures.**
- `views/_template.html`: start here for a new view.

## Swapping in real data (stays out of git)
Create `data/prototype/memtrack-data.js` (inside the git-ignored `data/` folder) that sets `window.MT_DATA` with the same shape as `sample-data.js`, and set `meta.isSample = false`. Every view loads it after the sample and uses it automatically. This shows BMW's point that "you can easily replace this with your actual data".

## Reset
Decisions and weight edits live in your browser. To reset, clear this site's local storage, or run `localStorage.clear()` in the console.

content.text:
Memtrack now has a brand folder and a clickable dashboard demo with 8 views, and both plan pages plus the architecture diagrams are updated to the new direction. All 8 views load with no errors.

**Branding (`branding/`)**
- **Colours:** BMW-inspired. The darker the blue, the stronger the layer: deep M blue for principles, BMW blue for evidence, light M blue for signals. BMW M red is used only where a human has to decide.
- **Logo:** an "M" drawn as a decision track, ending in a red node for the human sign-off. There's a version for light and one for dark backgrounds.
- **Fonts:** Barlow, a free stand-in for BMW's own typeface.
- **No BMW logo or roundel** is used anywhere.
- **Files:** `brand-sheet.html` shows everything visually, `tokens.css` holds all colours for light and dark mode, and `README.md` is the brand guide.

**Dashboard demo (`dashboard-demo/`, start at `index.html`)**
I built the shared shell and scoring logic first so all views behave the same, then four subagents built two views each.

| View | What you can do there |
|---|---|
| Cockpit | See where the model stands per market, what's waiting for you, and the top unknowns |
| Requirements | Ranked list, SMART card, "why this rank" broken down so you can check it, and Keep / Edit / Postpone / Reject (postpone and reject require a reason) |
| Lineage | "Should the next 7 Series be bigger?", step by step, ending with your decision. This is the centre of the pitch |
| Weights | Move a slider and the ranking updates. Compare the 1 Series and 7 Series at a glance, and run a ±20% stability check |
| Principles | The hard rules, their owners and versions; change proposals where votes are input and the owner decides |
| Human in the loop | Where the human sits and why, the four decision gates, a "what if" mode, and what's waiting for a decision |
| Decision memory | Every decision with its reason, a replay of how the list looked on any date, lessons the AI uses that you can edit, and an exportable audit log |
| What we don't know | Missing evidence, conflicting signals and uncertainty, which the jury explicitly rewards |

- **Sample data only.** The demo runs on illustrative data, labelled as such on every page. Real data can be dropped into `data/prototype/memtrack-data.js`, which stays out of git, and every view picks it up. That demonstrates the expert's point that the data is swappable.
- **Data check.** I checked the committed folders for anything copied from BMW's dataset. I replaced one real figure (the count of Japanese comments) with "a few dozen".
- **Subagent fixes.** The subagents flagged shared issues, and I applied them: one thing pushed the page sideways, dates sorted in the wrong order, and an "edit" didn't keep its status.

**Architecture and plan pages**
- **Diagrams:** the five Mermaid diagrams in `product/diagrams/` are rewritten for Memtrack: system overview, the 7 Series decision sequence, data model, re-prioritised build plan, and a new map of where the human sits. All five render without errors.
- **Pages:** both are republished at the same links and renamed. They now include quotes from the BMW experts, and treat car images and video as optional because BMW said they don't need a car.
  - Memtrack Explained: https://claude.ai/artifact/8YuDYUjQbAho3r7QC9bbrP
  - Memtrack Technical Spec: https://claude.ai/artifact/V2iFJ52ryHgmMbNMkSBWUP
- **Sharing:** both links are still shared as "Anyone with the link", and the Technical Spec now quotes the BMW expert conversations.

**Limits of the testing**
- I only checked the views visually in dark mode. Light mode uses the colour tokens but wasn't looked at.
- Headless Chrome can't render narrower than 500px, so the 400px phone layout was checked with a script, not seen on a real phone.

input.description: Build the 3D market globe
input.prompt:
Build the real 3D globe component for "Memtrack", a Next.js 16 app (BMW hackathon product). Light mode, polished, performant.

APP: /Volumes/PJ/peresjav/hackathons/ehl-final-minuch-2026/web (Next.js 16.4 App Router, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind v4, pnpm). FIRST read web/AGENTS.md: this Next version has breaking changes; consult node_modules/next/dist/docs/ (e.g. 01-app/02-guides/lazy-loading.md: `dynamic(..., { ssr: false })` must be used inside a Client Component). Also read the project rules in ../AGENTS.md (never commit data; plain copy).

YOU OWN ONLY: web/src/components/globe/** . Do not edit any other file (globals.css, markets.ts, pages are owned by others). If you need a change elsewhere, say so in your final report.

ALREADY THERE (read them):
- web/src/components/globe/MarketGlobe.tsx: the stable entry point with the props CONTRACT (variant "hero" | "picker", selected, onSelect, showComments, autoRotate, size, className) and currently a placeholder stub. Replace the stub with a real implementation, keeping the exported default component name, file path and props exactly (other agents are building the landing page and dashboard against it right now).
- web/src/lib/markets.ts: MARKETS (id EU/CN/US/JP, name, lat/lng, ISO numeric country codes matching world-atlas ids, colorVar, focus) and SAMPLE_COMMENTS (lat/lng, market, brand BMW or competitor, model, sentiment good/bad, text, source).
- web/src/app/globals.css: colour tokens as CSS variables (--brand #1c69d4, --brand-deep, --brand-soft, --brand-sky, --good, --bad, --eu/--cn/--us/--jp, --line, --ink, --muted, --surface, --bg-soft). Read CSS variables at runtime (getComputedStyle) for WebGL colours instead of hard-coding where practical.
- Installed: react-globe.gl 2.38, three 0.186, world-atlas 2 (countries-110m.json), topojson-client, lucide-react.

DESIGN:
- Light, clean, premium (think Stripe/Vercel globe but light): a white/very light-blue sphere (no satellite texture), subtle graticule or none, soft atmosphere in light brand blue, countries as flat polygons in a very light grey-blue; the market countries (MARKETS[].countries) highlighted in their market colour (EU countries share --eu) with slight altitude; transparent canvas background so it sits on the page.
- variant "hero": slow auto-rotation (respect prefers-reduced-motion: no rotation), no user zoom (allow drag rotate is fine), market labels optional. Comment bubbles: HTML elements anchored at SAMPLE_COMMENTS lat/lng (react-globe.gl htmlElementsData), appearing a few at a time on a timer (e.g. 3–4 visible, cycling every ~2.5 s, fade/scale in), each a small card: brand + model, short text, a good (green) / bad (red) marker, source tag. Bubbles on the far side of the globe must be hidden (check visibility vs camera or use react-globe.gl's built-in occlusion if available). Keep them readable and not overlapping too much.
- variant "picker": no comments, gentle idle rotation off by default; hover a market's countries → highlight + tooltip with market name and focus; click → onSelect(id); the selected market is strongest highlighted and the camera flies to it (pointOfView with transition). Also render accessible fallback controls (visually subtle list of market buttons under or beside the globe, or an sr-only list) so keyboard users can select.
- Client-only: implement the WebGL part in web/src/components/globe/GlobeCanvas.tsx and load it from MarketGlobe via next/dynamic with ssr:false (MarketGlobe is "use client"). Show a light skeleton circle while loading. Size: fill the parent width with a square aspect by default (ResizeObserver to set width/height on the globe); respect the `size` prop.
- Performance: load world-atlas once (module-level memo), convert with topojson-client `feature`, keep polygon count reasonable (110m), cap devicePixelRatio at 2, pause animation when the tab is hidden or the globe is off-screen (IntersectionObserver).
- Types: no `any` leaks in the public API; TypeScript must pass (`pnpm exec tsc --noEmit`), and `pnpm lint` should pass for your files.

VERIFY:
- A shared dev server is already running at http://localhost:3100 (do NOT start another `next dev`; it would conflict on .next). Create a temporary test route web/src/app/_globe-test/page.tsx? No: routes starting with _ are private. Instead create web/src/app/globe-test/page.tsx (you may own this file temporarily) rendering both variants side by side, check it, and DELETE it before you finish.
- Screenshot with headless Chrome (WebGL needs software GL): "/Applications/Google Chrome.app/Contents/MacOS/Google Chrome" --headless=new --use-angle=swiftshader --enable-unsafe-swiftshader --ignore-gpu-blocklist --user-data-dir=/Volumes/PJ/DevCache/claude-tmp/claude-501/-Volumes-PJ-peresjav-hackathons-ehl-final-minuch-2026/7fd52f13-5d0c-4e7f-8ec6-8a947b2499a1/scratchpad/chrome-agent-globe --virtual-time-budget=12000 --window-size=1400,900 --screenshot=<scratchpad>/globe.png http://localhost:3100/globe-test (wrap with `timeout 60`).
