input.description: Build the landing page
input.prompt:
Build the landing page for "Memtrack", a Next.js 16 app for the BMW hackathon challenge "AI for Product Decision Making". Light mode, real product quality (think Linear/Stripe/Vercel marketing pages, but light and calm, BMW-inspired blues).

APP: /Volumes/PJ/peresjav/hackathons/ehl-final-minuch-2026/web (Next.js 16.4 App Router, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind v4, pnpm). FIRST read web/AGENTS.md: this Next version has breaking changes; consult node_modules/next/dist/docs/ before using APIs (e.g. next/image, next/link, metadata, Server vs Client Components). Read ../AGENTS.md for project rules (data/ never committed; no BMW dataset quotes in this repo; plain, short, active copy).

YOU OWN: web/src/app/page.tsx, web/src/components/landing/**, web/src/components/site/** (Navbar, Footer). Do not edit other files (globals.css, globe, markets.ts, dashboard are owned by others). Need a shared change? Put it in your final report.

USE (read them):
- web/src/app/globals.css: tokens exposed as Tailwind colours: bg, bg-soft, surface, ink, ink-soft, muted, line, brand, brand-deep, brand-soft, brand-sky, l1/l1-soft (principles), l2/l2-soft (evidence), l3/l3-soft (signals), human/human-soft, good/good-soft, bad/bad-soft, wait, eu/cn/us/jp; radius-card, shadow-card, shadow-float. Use these classes (e.g. `bg-brand-soft text-brand-deep`), no raw hex.
- web/src/components/brand/Logo.tsx: <Logo /> and <LogoMark />.
- web/src/components/globe/MarketGlobe.tsx: default export <MarketGlobe variant="hero" /> (a 3D globe with highlighted markets and pop-up good/bad comments about BMW and competitors; currently a placeholder stub while another agent builds the real one; same props). It's a Client Component; render it inside your hero.
- web/src/lib/markets.ts: MARKETS and SAMPLE_COMMENTS (illustrative).
- Product image: another agent is generating web/public/images/product-dashboard.png (16:9-ish, light UI on a laptop/monitor). Until it exists, your section must still look good: render an HTML/CSS product preview card (a mini dashboard mock built with divs) as the main visual, and if /images/product-dashboard.png exists use next/image for it (you may check with fs at build/render time in a Server Component, or simply build the coded mock as the hero visual of that section and place the photo as a secondary framed image that you add only if the file exists; keep it simple and never ship a broken image).

PRODUCT STORY (use for copy; keep it short):
- Memtrack listens to customers market by market (Europe, China, USA, Japan), weighs every signal, and turns it into requirements for the next BMW, with a traceable reason for every decision.
- Three layers: L1 Principles (hard rules per market, owned by managers, e.g. "Japan: must fit multi-storey car parks"), L2 Evidence (customer studies, owner feedback, sales, quality reports; the main engine), L3 Signals (social media, search trends, concept tests; low weight, tuned per model: more for the 1 Series' young buyers, almost none for the 7 Series).
- Process (simple steps): 1 Listen (collect per market) → 2 Weigh (three layers, per-model weights) → 3 Decide (AI drafts ~90% of requirements as SMART targets; the product manager keeps, edits, postpones or rejects, with a reason) → 4 Remember (every decision, its reason and evidence snapshot stored; the AI reads it, the PM can edit it; full lineage from comment to requirement).
- Honesty: Memtrack shows what it doesn't know (missing markets, thin samples, conflicting signals).
- Headline quotes for the product section: write 3 short product headlines/pull quotes in our own voice (e.g. "Every requirement, traceable to its source." / "The PM decides. The AI shows its work." / "Know what you don't know."). Do NOT quote BMW people or customers by name; do not use BMW's logo, model photos or trademarks beyond plain text mentions.

PAGE STRUCTURE:
1. Navbar (sticky, white with subtle blur/border on scroll): Logo; links Process, Product, Contact (anchor links); primary button "Open dashboard" → /dashboard (next/link).
2. Hero: big headline + one-line subhead + CTA buttons ("Open dashboard" primary, "See how it works" secondary → #process); the globe as the dominant visual (large, right side on desktop, below on mobile), with a small legend: market colours and good/bad comment markers, plus a tiny note "Sample comments, illustrative". Light background with a very subtle radial brand-soft glow.
3. Process section (#process): 4 steps as clean cards or a horizontal stepper with icons (lucide-react installed), and a compact visual of the three layers (stacked bands L1/L2/L3 in deep→light blue showing default weight shares, e.g. 7 Series: 55/43/2 vs 1 Series: 45/35/20), with one line each.
4. Product section (#product): the product visual (coded mock + optional image) with the 3 headline quotes arranged editorially (large type), plus 3 small feature points (Lineage, Human in the loop, What we don't know).
5. Contact footer (#contact): short "Built for the BMW challenge at the EHL Hackathon, Munich 2026" line, a simple contact block (team email placeholder text like team@memtrack.dev shown as selectable text, not a mailto that pretends to send), a minimal contact form UI that handles submit client-side with a "Thanks, we'll get back to you" state (no backend), small links, © Memtrack 2026, and the "Open dashboard" button again.
- Responsive down to 375px, no horizontal scroll. Accessible: semantic landmarks, alt text, focus states, colour contrast. Subtle motion only (CSS transitions; respect prefers-reduced-motion).
- Server Components by default; Client Components only where needed (form, navbar scroll state). Update metadata in page/layout only within your files (page.tsx can export metadata).

VERIFY: TypeScript (`pnpm exec tsc --noEmit`) and `pnpm lint` pass for your files. A shared dev server is ALREADY running at http://localhost:3100. Do NOT start another `next dev`. Screenshot with headless Chrome: timeout 60 "/Applications/Google Chrome.app/Contents/MacOS/Google Chrome" --headless=new --use-angle=swiftshader --enable-unsafe-swiftshader --user-data-dir=/Volumes/PJ/DevCache/claude-tmp/claude-501/-Volumes-PJ-peresjav-hackathons-ehl-final-minuch-2026/7fd52f13-5d0c-4e7f-8ec6-8a947b2499a1/scratchpad/chrome-agent-landing --virtual-time-budget=10000 --window-size=1440,4200 --screenshot=<scratchpad>/landing.png http://localhost:3100/ ; look at it with the Read tool (crop with ffmpeg if tall), also once at --window-size=500,5200 (Chrome's headless minimum width ~500). Iterate at most twice. Check the dev log /Volumes/PJ/DevCache/claude-tmp/claude-501/-Volumes-PJ-peresjav-hackathons-ehl-final-minuch-2026/7fd52f13-5d0c-4e7f-8ec6-8a947b2499a1/scratchpad/next-dev.log for errors.
Report: files, section summary, anything needed from other owners.

APP: /Volumes/PJ/peresjav/hackathons/ehl-final-minuch-2026/web (Next.js 16.4 App Router, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind v4, pnpm; next.config has cacheComponents: true). FIRST read web/AGENTS.md: this Next version has breaking changes; consult node_modules/next/dist/docs/ before using APIs (params are Promises; dynamic routes; generateStaticParams; Client vs Server Components; with cacheComponents, uncached data access may need <Suspense>; read the relevant docs). Read ../AGENTS.md for project rules (data/ is never committed; no real BMW dataset values or quotes in this repo: use the illustrative sample data only).

YOU OWN: web/src/app/dashboard/**, web/src/components/dashboard/**, web/src/lib/dashboard-data.ts. Do not edit other files (globals.css, globe, markets.ts, landing are owned by others). Need a shared change? Put it in your final report.

USE (read them):
- web/src/app/globals.css: tokens as Tailwind colours: bg, bg-soft, surface, ink, ink-soft, muted, line, brand, brand-deep, brand-soft, brand-sky, l1/l1-soft, l2/l2-soft, l3/l3-soft, human/human-soft, good/good-soft, bad/bad-soft, wait/wait-soft, eu/cn/us/jp; radius-card, shadow-card, shadow-float. No raw hex.
- web/src/components/brand/Logo.tsx: <Logo />, <LogoMark />.
- web/src/components/globe/MarketGlobe.tsx: default export, Client Component. Use <MarketGlobe variant="picker" selected={id|null} onSelect={(id)=>…} />. It is currently a placeholder stub (renders market buttons) while another agent builds the real 3D globe with the same props; build against the props.
- web/src/lib/markets.ts: MARKETS (EU, CN, US, JP with name, focus, sampleShare) and types.
- Reference data model to port from: /Volumes/PJ/peresjav/hackathons/ehl-final-minuch-2026/dashboard-demo/assets/sample-data.js (an earlier prototype: models 1/5/7 Series, layers, sources & weights, principles, requirements with smart/signals/markets/principleFit/conflicts/gaps/status, gaps). Port what you need into typed web/src/lib/dashboard-data.ts (illustrative sample only; add a `SAMPLE_LABEL = "Sample data: illustrative, not BMW figures"`). Also port the scoring idea in a small pure function (layer weights × source weights × market support) or simplify, documented.

FLOW:
1. /dashboard: "Choose a market" screen. Minimal top bar (Logo → "/", "Dashboard" label, small sample-data badge). Centre: the picker globe large, a heading ("Which market are you deciding for?"), and a row of market cards (name, focus line, sample share) synced with the globe selection. Selecting a market (globe click or card) highlights it and shows a "Continue to Europe →" primary button; continue navigates to /dashboard/[market] (lowercase id, e.g. /dashboard/eu). Also allow "All markets" as a secondary option → /dashboard/all.
2. /dashboard/[market]: a CLEAN dashboard for that market. Layout: slim left sidebar or top tabs (only a few items: Overview active; others greyed as "coming soon": Requirements, Lineage, Weights, Memory), a header with market name + model switcher (1 Series / 5 Series / 7 Series, client state or searchParams) + "Change market" link back to /dashboard + sample-data badge. Content (keep it to these):
   - 4 KPI cards: requirements, approved, waiting for your decision, open evidence gaps.
   - "Top requirements" list (5): title, short statement, score bar split by layer (L1/L2/L3 colours), status pill, this market's stance (+ supports / – opposes / 0 neutral).
   - "What customers here care about" short list (the market's focus/themes, sample).
   - "What we don't know" card (2–3 gaps relevant to this market).
   - Small three-layer legend explaining L1/L2/L3 in one line each.
   Use generateStaticParams for eu/cn/us/jp/all and notFound() for unknown markets. Keep components small and typed.
- Responsive down to 375px; accessible (landmarks, labels, focus states, keyboard selection of markets); calm motion only.

VERIFY: `pnpm exec tsc --noEmit` and `pnpm lint` pass for your files. A shared dev server is ALREADY running at http://localhost:3100. Do NOT start another `next dev` (conflicts). input.description: Image generation scripts + product image
input.prompt:
Create an image-generation scripts folder for the "Memtrack" project (BMW hackathon) and generate the product image for the landing page, using the OpenAI Images API.

PROJECT: /Volumes/PJ/peresjav/hackathons/ehl-final-minuch-2026. Read AGENTS.md first (rules: data/ never committed; secrets never committed or printed). The OpenAI key is in /Volumes/PJ/peresjav/hackathons/ehl-final-minuch-2026/.env as OPENAI_API_KEY. NEVER print, echo, log or copy the key anywhere (no `cat .env`, no printing env). Load it inside the script only.

YOU OWN: /Volumes/PJ/peresjav/hackathons/ehl-final-minuch-2026/scripts/** and web/public/images/** . Don't touch other files.

1. scripts/generate-image.mjs (Node 26, zero dependencies; use global fetch, FormData, Blob):
   - Reads OPENAI_API_KEY from process.env or parses ../.env (relative to the script's location; handle quotes and comments).
   - CLI: `node scripts/generate-image.mjs --prompt "..." --out web/public/images/name.png [--size 1536x1024|1024x1024|1024x1536|auto] [--quality low|medium|high|auto] [--model <id>] [--background transparent|opaque|auto] [--ref path.png ...] [--n 1]`. Also `--prompt-file prompts.json` for batch: an array of {name, prompt, size, quality, background}.
   - Without --ref: POST https://api.openai.com/v1/images/generations. With one or more --ref: POST /v1/images/edits (multipart, image[] fields) for compositing (e.g. components → hero).
   - Model: default from env OPENAI_IMAGE_MODEL, else try "gpt-image-2.5-flare", and if the API returns a model-not-found / invalid model error, automatically fall back to "gpt-image-2", then "gpt-image-1". Print which model was used. (Recent docs list gpt-image-2.5-sunburst for precise edits and gpt-image-2.5-flare for fast generation; verify with one call.)
   - Decode b64_json and write PNG(s); create directories; print output paths, size and model. Clear error messages (status code + API error message, never the key).
   - Writes a sidecar JSON next to each image (same name + .json) with prompt, model, size, quality, created time, and "ai_generated": true, so every AI visual is traceable and can be labelled "AI concept" in the UI.
2. scripts/README.md: what it does, usage examples, how the key is loaded (.env, git-ignored), cost note, the rule "label every AI image as AI-generated in the UI (EU AI Act Art. 50)", and "never generate BMW logos/badges or real people".
3. scripts/prompts/landing.json with prompts for the landing page, then GENERATE them (quality "high" for the main one, "medium" for others; keep it to ≤ 3 images to control cost):
   - product-dashboard: a photorealistic, bright, minimal studio scene: a modern laptop on a light desk showing a clean light-mode analytics dashboard with a world map/globe, a ranked list and small blue charts; soft daylight, white and light grey palette with BMW-style blue (#1c69d4) accents; shallow depth of field; no logos, no brand names, no readable text, no people. 1536x1024.
   - optionally layers-abstract: an abstract, elegant illustration of three translucent stacked layers in deep navy, BMW blue and light sky blue on white, isometric, soft shadows, no text. 1536x1024.
   Save to web/public/images/product-dashboard.png (and layers-abstract.png), each with its .json sidecar. Check the result visually with the Read tool; if it has visible fake text that looks bad, logos, or brand marks, regenerate once with a stricter prompt.
4. Make sure secrets stay out of git: confirm .env is ignored by the root .gitignore (`.env`) and that no script writes the key. Do not modify .gitignore unless something is missing (then report it).

Report: files created, the model actually used, image paths + dimensions, approximate cost, and any issues.

## 4. Rules
- **Data stays private.**
  - Never commit `data/`, `memory.md` or `prompts/`. New BMW or third-party material, and any page that quotes BMW data, goes **inside `data/`**. `.gitignore` also blocks data file types anywhere as a safety net.

- **Facts:**

- **Images:** only use images with a clear license (e.g. Wikimedia Commons CC BY / BY-SA), and record the author and license in a `credits.json` next to them. Label AI-generated concept images as "AI concept".
- **Stack (default):**

  - OpenAI for text, structured outputs and images; fal.ai for video.
  - Qdrant is optional; use it only if pgvector is not enough.
- **Python:** run with `uv run --with <pkgs> python -I …`. Don't install packages globally.
- **Research:** prefer the exa MCP (larger quota), with tavily as a second opinion. Keep query counts modest.

# Dixi brand guide

**Dixi** is named after the Dixi 3/15, BMW's first car (1928). The product listens to customers in every market and turns what they say into traceable requirements for the next BMW.

> The colours are inspired by BMW's public brand and BMW M colours. They are not official BMW design tokens, and Dixi never uses the BMW logo or roundel.

## Files
| File | Use |
|---|---|
| `logo.svg` | Mark + wordmark, for light backgrounds (default) |
| `logo-on-dark.svg` | Mark + wordmark, for dark backgrounds |
| `logo-mark.svg` | Square mark: app icon, favicon (same as `web/src/app/icon.svg`) |
| `tokens.css` | Colour tokens, mirrored from `web/src/app/globals.css` (the app is the source of truth) |
| `brand-sheet.html` | Visual reference: open it in a browser |

In the app, use the React logo `web/src/components/brand/Logo.tsx` (`<Logo />`, `<LogoMark />`).

## The mark
A **globe** (the markets we listen to) crossed by a **decision track**. The track starts at a light-blue node (a signal), passes a BMW-blue node (evidence), and ends at an **M-red node**: the human sign-off. Every requirement in Dixi follows that path.

## Wordmark
Lowercase **dixi**, semibold, tight tracking: "di" in ink, "xi" in BMW blue.

## Colour
Light mode first. The depth of blue shows how strongly a signal counts.

| Role | Token | Hex | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| Primary | `--brand` | `#1c69d4` | Buttons, links, active states (BMW-style blue) |
| Deep | `--brand-deep` | `#0f3d75` | Headings accents, the track in the logo |
| Sky | `--brand-sky` | `#8ec5ff` | Soft highlights, signal node |
| **L1 Principles** | `--l1` | `#0f3d75` | Hard rules: the strongest layer |
| **L2 Evidence** | `--l2` | `#1c69d4` | Customer studies, feedback, sales |
| **L3 Signals** | `--l3` | `#5aa9f0` | Social, trends, concept tests |
| **Human decision** | `--human` | `#e22718` | Only where a person decides. Use sparingly |
| Good / Bad | `--good` / `--bad` | `#1e8e3e` / `#d93025` | Comment sentiment, approved / rejected |
| Markets | `--eu` `--cn` `--us` `--jp` | `#1c69d4` `#e0483a` `#0f3d75` `#7c5cd6` | Globe and market chips |
| Ink / Muted / Line | `--ink` `--muted` `--line` | `#0d1b2a` `#6b7a8f` `#e3e8ef` | Text, secondary text, borders |
| Background | `--bg` `--bg-soft` | `#ffffff` `#f5f7fb` | Page, alternate sections |

## Type
- **Geist Sans** for everything (headings semibold, tight tracking), **Geist Mono** for IDs and numbers (`R-701`, `G3`).
- Big, calm headlines; short sentences; no jargon.

## Voice
- Plain and short. Name things the way a product manager would ("Postpone", "Why this rank").
- Every number has a source; every decision has a reason.

## Do / don't
- ✅ Red only where a human must act. ✅ Layer colours on anything that carries weight. ✅ Label AI-generated images.
- ❌ No BMW logo, roundel or badges. ❌ No dark-mode-only designs for now. ❌ No gradients on data.

# Dixi docs

Architecture and design of the Dixi app. Diagrams are [Mermaid](https://mermaid.js.org); GitHub renders `.mmd` content when it is pasted in a ```` ```mermaid ```` block, and VS Code / mermaid.live preview the files directly.

## `architecture/`
| File | What it shows |
|---|---|
| `01-system-overview.mmd` | The whole pipeline: sources → three layers (principles, evidence, signals) → scoring → SMART requirements → human gates G1–G4 → decision memory and lineage → hand-off to engineering |
| `02-feedback-loop.mmd` | One decision end to end, as a sequence: "Should the next 7 Series be bigger?" including postpone and a memory edit |
| `03-data-model.mmd` | Entities and relations: markets, models, layers, sources and per-model weights, principles, evidence, requirements, scores, lineage, decisions, lessons, gaps |
| `04-build-plan.mmd` | The hackathon build plan, prioritised by the judging criteria |
| `05-hitl-map.mmd` | Where the human sits in the pipeline, and why |
| `06-web-app.mmd` | The current Next.js app: routes, components, shared globe, data modules, planned backend |

## Core ideas in one paragraph
Dixi turns customer feedback from every market into requirements for the next BMW, and keeps the reason for every decision. Signals sit in three layers: **L1 principles** (hard rules per market, owned by people), **L2 evidence** (customer studies, owner feedback, sales, quality data) and **L3 signals** (social media, search trends, concept tests). Each model has its own weights: social signals count more for an entry model than for a flagship. AI drafts most requirements as SMART targets; a product manager keeps, edits, postpones or rejects each one at defined gates. Every decision is stored with its evidence snapshot, so anyone can trace a requirement back to the comments behind it. Dixi also shows what it doesn't know: missing markets, thin samples and conflicting signals.

See also: `../tech-stack/` (technology choices) and `../backend/` (planned API and agents).

# Dixi tech stack

Status as of 10 Oct 2026. ✅ = in use · 🟡 = planned · ⚪ = considered, not chosen.

## Frontend: `web/` ✅
| Layer | Choice | Version | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Framework | **Next.js** (App Router, Cache Components, Partial Prefetching) | 16.4.0 | Server Components by default; static + streamed pages; the team knows it |
| UI runtime | **React** | 19.3.0 | |
| Language | **TypeScript** | 5.x | Typed data contracts shared by every view |
| Styling | **Tailwind CSS** | 4.x | Colour tokens defined once in `web/src/app/globals.css` and exposed as utilities |
| 3D globe | **react-globe.gl** + **three.js** | 2.38 / 0.186 | Country polygons (market highlights) and HTML popups anchored to coordinates; plain dot globes can't colour whole countries |
| Map data | **world-atlas** (110m) + **topojson-client** | 2.0 / 3.1 | Small, public-domain country shapes (Natural Earth) |
| Icons | **lucide-react** | 1.x | |
| Fonts | **Geist Sans / Geist Mono** via `next/font` | | Clean, free, ships with Next.js |
| Tooling | pnpm 10, Node 26, ESLint 9 | | |

Run it: `cd web && pnpm install && pnpm dev` → http://localhost:3000. Note: Next.js 16 has breaking changes; read `web/AGENTS.md`.

## Backend: `backend/` 🟡
| Layer | Choice | Why | Alternatives |
|---|---|---|---|
| API | **FastAPI** (Python) | Same language as the agents; async; OpenAPI for the frontend | Next.js route handlers only |
| Agents | **Pydantic AI** (v2) + Logfire tracing | Typed structured outputs = our data contracts; tracing gives traceability | ⚪ OpenAI Agents SDK (simplest if OpenAI-only), ⚪ LangGraph (explicit graphs, more boilerplate) |
| Database | **Supabase** (Postgres, auth, storage, realtime) | One store for evidence, requirements, decisions, lineage and memory; realtime updates the dashboard | Neon + S3 |
| Vector search | **pgvector** in Supabase (HNSW + full-text, hybrid via RRF) | Enough for ~100k–1M items; one service less | ⚪ Qdrant (only if pgvector is not enough) |
| LLMs | **OpenAI**: small tier for labelling (Batch API), flagship for requirement drafting | Structured outputs; embeddings `text-embedding-3-small` at 512 dims | Anthropic, Gemini (Pydantic AI is model-agnostic) |
| Images | **OpenAI image models** (`scripts/generate-image.mjs`) | Multi-image edits for compositing; every image gets an AI-generated sidecar | FLUX.2 on fal.ai |
| Video (optional) | **fal.ai** (Kling / Veo image-to-video) | OpenAI shut down its Sora video API on 24 Sep 2026 | — |
| Fine-tuning | ⚪ **Not planned** | LLM labelling checked against a hand-labelled sample is faster and explainable | Later: a small classifier distilled from LLM labels |

## Data sources (for a production version)
| Source | Use | Constraint |
|---|---|---|
| Customer studies, owner feedback, sales, quality data | L2 evidence | Provided by BMW; never stored in this repo |
| YouTube Data API | Comments on model reviews per market | 10,000 units/day quota |
| Google Trends | Search momentum per market | Official API in alpha; SerpApi as an alternative |
| Reddit | Owner discussions | App approval; commercial use needs a contract |
| Chinese platforms (Autohome, Dongchedi, Weibo, Xiaohongshu) | China voice | No easy official APIs; vendors or enterprise listening tools |
| Commodity prices (World Bank Pink Sheet, FRED) | Cost signals | Monthly, free; lithium/cobalt need a paid source |

## Traceability and compliance
- **Entire** (entire.io): agent sessions linked to commits, required by the hackathon. `entire enable --agent claude-code`.
- **EU AI Act Art. 50** (since 2 Aug 2026): label AI-generated images and video.
- **GDPR**: store post text and metadata only, hash author IDs, no training on scraped data.
- **Secrets**: `.env` at the repo root, git-ignored. Never commit keys.

# AGENTS.md: Dixi · EHL Hackathon 2026 · BMW "AI for Product Decision Making"

This is the single source of instructions for every coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, …). `CLAUDE.md` only imports this file, so edit this file and nothing else.

## 0. First thing every session: personal memory
- Read `memory.md` in the repo root. It holds **this user's** saved context: decisions, preferences, open threads. It is git-ignored and personal, so each teammate has their own.
- **If `memory.md` does not exist, create it** from the template below before doing anything else.
- When the user tells you something worth keeping (a decision, preference, credential *location* (never the secret), deadline or contact), append it to `memory.md` with the date. Keep entries short. Update stale entries instead of duplicating them.

```markdown
# memory.md (personal, git-ignored, never commit)
_Owner: <name> · created <YYYY-MM-DD>_

## Preferences
- 

## Decisions
- 

## Open threads / todo
- 

## Useful facts
- 
```

## 1. Log important prompts
- Save every substantial instruction from the user (a new feature, direction change or product idea) **verbatim** as a new file in `prompts/`, named `NN-short-slug.md`, numbered after the last file. **Redact secrets** (API keys) before saving.
- Add one line at the end: **Result:** what was produced.
- `prompts/` is local only (git-ignored).

## 1b. Every source document gets an overview
- Put each new document (PDF, slides, report, link, transcript) in `data/sources/` and write `data/sources/overviews/<slug>-overview.md`: what it is, why it matters, key facts with page/slide numbers, how to use it in the product, gaps.
- `data/` is local only (git-ignored).

## 2. Project context
- **Challenge:** derive, justify and prioritise customer requirements for a BMW successor vehicle (1/5/7 Series; Europe, China, USA; 3–5 years ahead). The product manager stays in control, every decision is traceable, evidence and assumptions stay separate, and conflicts are shown, not averaged away.
- **Judging rubric:** decision and scoring logic · workflow and human decisions · traceability and auditability (incl. postponements) · quality, usability and feasibility · innovation, scale and business impact · plus "we reward honesty" (surface missing evidence, conflicts and uncertainty). Logic, workflow and traceability come first when deciding what to build.
- **Product: Dixi**, named after the Dixi 3/15, BMW's first car (1928). A principled, weighted, traceable requirement engine: three layers (L1 principles, L2 evidence, L3 signals), source weights per model, human gates G1–G4, an editable decision memory, lineage from comment to requirement, and "what we don't know" gap cards. Architecture: `docs/architecture/`.
- **Mandatory:** the repo must use **Entire** (entire.io): `entire enable --agent claude-code`, connect the repo on entire.io, turn on Runners and Trails. Submissions without Entire are rejected. If the repo is public, agent transcripts are public too: never paste secrets into a session.

## 3. Repo map
**Only these paths are committed.** `.gitignore` is an allow-list: everything else at the root stays local.

| Path | In git | What |
|---|---|---|

# Developer requirements

Everything you need to work on the Dixi repo. Commands are for macOS (Homebrew); Linux/Windows notes where they differ.

## 1. Accounts and access
| What | Why |
|---|---|
| **GitHub** account with access to `peresramirez/Dixi`, and an **SSH key** added to GitHub | Clone and push (`git@github.com:peresramirez/Dixi.git`) |
| **Entire** account (entire.io), signed in with GitHub | Required by the hackathon: every agent session is linked to commits. Submissions without Entire are rejected |
| **Supabase** account (supabase.com) | Database, auth, storage and vector search for the backend |
| **Vercel** account (vercel.com) | Hosting for the web app (preview + production) |
| **OpenAI API key** | Agents and image generation (`scripts/generate-image.mjs`). Ask the team; never commit it |

## 2. Tools to install
| Tool | Version | Install | Check |
|---|---|---|---|
| Git | any recent | `brew install git` | `git --version` |
| Node.js | **22 or newer** (team uses 26) | `brew install node` or [nvm](https://github.com/nvm-sh/nvm) | `node -v` |
| pnpm | **10** | `corepack enable && corepack prepare pnpm@10 --activate` (or `brew install pnpm`) | `pnpm -v` |
| Python + uv | Python 3.12+, uv | `brew install uv` (uv manages Python) | `uv --version` |
| Docker Desktop | recent | [docker.com](https://www.docker.com/products/docker-desktop/) | `docker info` (needed for local Supabase) |
| **Supabase CLI** | latest | `brew install supabase/tap/supabase` (Linux/Windows: see [Supabase CLI docs](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/cli)) | `supabase --version` |
| **Vercel CLI** | latest | `pnpm add -g vercel` (or `npm i -g vercel`) | `vercel --version` |
| **Entire CLI** | latest | `brew tap entireio/tap && brew trust entireio/tap && brew install --cask entire` (Linux: `curl -fsSL https://entire.io/install.sh \| bash`; Windows: `scoop bucket add entire https://github.com/entireio/scoop-bucket.git && scoop install entire/entire`) | `entire version` |
| A coding agent | Claude Code, Codex or Cursor | — | Reads `AGENTS.md` / `CLAUDE.md` |

## 3. First-time setup
```bash
git clone git@github.com:peresramirez/Dixi.git
cd Dixi

# secrets (repo root, git-ignored)
printf 'OPENAI_API_KEY=<ask the team>\n' > .env

# web app
cd web && pnpm install && pnpm dev     # http://localhost:3000
cd ..
```

### Entire (once per machine, once per repo)
```bash
entire login
entire enable --agent claude-code      # or --agent codex / cursor; installs git + agent hooks and .entire/
```
Then in **entire.io**: connect the repository (Configure GitHub App), and under **Settings** turn on **Runners**, **Trails** and **Auto build on push**. Repo owners add the default runners once:
```bash
entire runner setup -y
git add .entire/runners && git commit -m "Configure trail runners"
```
⚠️ If the repository is public, Entire's agent transcripts are public too. Never paste secrets into an agent session.

### Supabase (when the backend starts)
```bash
supabase login
supabase init                          # creates supabase/ (config + migrations)
supabase start                         # local Postgres + Studio; needs Docker running
supabase link --project-ref <project>  # connect to the hosted project
```

### Vercel (web hosting)
```bash
vercel login
cd web && vercel link                  # project root = web/
vercel env pull .env.local             # pull env vars for local dev
```
Set the Vercel project's **Root Directory** to `web`.

## 4. Environment variables
| Variable | Where | Used by |
|---|---|---|
| `OPENAI_API_KEY` | repo-root `.env` | `scripts/generate-image.mjs`, backend agents |
| `OPENAI_IMAGE_MODEL` *(optional)* | repo-root `.env` | image script model override |
| `NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL`, `NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY` *(planned)* | `web/.env.local` / Vercel | web app → Supabase |
| `SUPABASE_URL`, `SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY` *(planned)* | backend `.env` | backend → Supabase (server only, never in the browser) |

All `.env*` files are git-ignored.

## 5. Daily commands
| Task | Command |
|---|---|
| Run the web app | `cd web && pnpm dev` |
| Type-check / lint / build | `pnpm exec tsc --noEmit` · `pnpm lint` · `pnpm build` (in `web/`) |
| Generate an image | `node scripts/generate-image.mjs --prompt "…" --out web/public/images/name.png` |
| Start a Trail | `entire trail create --title "…"` |
| Local database | `supabase start` / `supabase stop` |
| Deploy a preview | `cd web && vercel` |

## 6. Repo rules (short)
- Only `web/`, `backend/`, `docs/`, `tech-stack/`, `branding/`, `scripts/`, `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md` are committed (`.gitignore` is an allow-list).
- No customer data, private documents or secrets in the repo.
- Next.js 16 has breaking changes: read `web/AGENTS.md` before using a Next.js API.
- Full agent rules: `AGENTS.md`.

input.content:
Hear every market. Decide with a reason.

--- **Dixi** helps BMW product managers decide what the next car should offer. It listens to customers in every market, weighs what they say, and turns it into clear requirements. Every requirement keeps the reason it was chosen. *Named after the Dixi 3/15, BMW's first car (1928).* ## How Dixi thinks: three layers Not every signal counts the same. Dixi sorts everything it hears into three layers, from strongest to weakest. | | Layer | What goes in | How much it counts | |---|---|---|---| | 🟦 | **L1 · Principles** | Hard rules per market, owned by a named manager. *Example: "In Japan, the car must fit multi-storey car parks."* | Strongest. A requirement that breaks a principle is flagged. | | 🔵 | **L2 · Evidence** | Customer studies, owner feedback, sales, quality reports. | The main engine. Weighted by how reliable each source is. | | 🩵 | **L3 · Signals** | Social media, search trends, concept tests. | Weakest. A tie-breaker, never the decider. | ## From a comment to a requirement, in five steps 1. **Listen.** Collect what customers say, market by market. 2. **Sort.** Put each piece into its layer: principle, evidence or signal. 3. **Weigh.** Each car has its own weights. Social media matters more for a young buyer's 1 Series than for a 7 Series. 4. **Decide.** AI drafts the requirement with a measurable target. A product manager **keeps, edits, postpones or rejects** it, and always gives a reason. 5. **Remember.** Every decision is saved with its evidence. Anyone can trace a requirement back to the comments behind it, years later. ```mermaid flowchart LR A[Customer comments
in every market] --> B{Sort into layers} B --> L1[L1 Principles] B --> L2[L2 Evidence] B --> L3[L3 Signals] L1 & L2 & L3 --> W[Weigh per model] W --> D[AI drafts
the requirement] D --> H{{Product manager
keeps · edits · postpones · rejects}} H --> M[(Decision memory
with the reason)] ``` **Dixi is honest about what it doesn't know.** Missing markets, thin samples and conflicting signals are shown to the product manager, not hidden. ## Run it ```bash cd web pnpm install pnpm dev ``` Open http://localhost:3000. Full setup (Supabase CLI, Vercel, Entire): [`docs/requirements.md`](docs/requirements.md). ## What's in the repo | Folder | What | |---|---| | [`web/`](web/) | The app: landing page with a live market globe, and the dashboard | | [`backend/`](backend/) | API and AI agents (planned) | | [`docs/`](docs/) | Setup, architecture diagrams, tech stack | | [`branding/`](branding/) | Logo, colours, brand guide | | [`scripts/`](scripts/) | Image generation | --- Built for the BMW challenge "AI for Product Decision Making" at the EHL Hackathon, Munich, October 2026. Dixi is a hackathon project and is not affiliated with BMW.

# Workflow voice note (Javier, 10 Oct 2026, 20:51), overview

## The workflow, step by step
1. Landing page → "Go to dashboard" → globe → **pick a market**.
2. **Pick a series** (1/5/7).
3. The **AI analyses** everything known about that car in that market: user feedback, trends, what people talk about, likes, dislikes and wishes. These become the candidate customer requirements (possible features).
4. **Fixed categories:** Exterior, Interior, Digital, Powertrain. The AI compresses the feedback into specific requests and categorises each one. *Example:* many people ask for autopilot → "Autopilot", category Digital (no extra sub-category needed).
5. **Feature request list:** the PM filters by category and **urgency**, meaning how many people ask for it (e.g. 30–50 requests means high priority).
6. The **PM decides** which requests to take and which to leave out.
7. **Build:** the AI generates different **car profiles**. Each profile has its own page showing the user requirements and *why* the agent chose it: company fundamentals (L1) plus trends and feedback (L2).
8. **Optional:** post the profiles on social media and measure which one performs better. This gets a small weight in the decision and shows on the dashboard.
9. **Competitors** appear on the profiles, because the trend analysis in L2 includes the competition.

| Layer | Before | Now (voice note) |
|---|---|---|
| L1 | Principles per market, owned by managers | Same: BMW principles and fundamentals |
| L2 | Studies, feedback, sales, quality | Feedback **+ trends + competitors** |
| L3 | Social, trends, concept tests | **Social media response to the generated profiles** (which profile performs better), low weight |

# BMW Hackathon Dataset: Data Report

*EHL hackathon, BMW challenge "AI for Product Decision Making". Analysis date: 2026-10-10.*
*Source folder: `data/bmw/` (originally `BMW-Data/`; read-only, nothing modified). Derived tables in `data/analysis/`.*
*Derived tables (`us_summary.csv`, `cs_cneu.csv`, `kw_themes.csv`, `us.csv`, `options.json`) are in `data/analysis/`.*

> Notation: **[inferred]** marks an interpretation that the data does not state outright. "IDs" means unique feedback records. Feedback files are in long format (one row per classification), so **row counts overstate volume**. All theme counts below use unique IDs unless stated otherwise.

---

## 0. Executive overview

| File | What it is | Size | Models | Markets covered |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `F70_feedback_hackathon.xlsx` | Classified customer verbatims | 4,076 rows / 2,128 IDs | F70 (1 Series), ICE only | GB, JP, SE, FR, AU, DK, FI, KR, ZA (no US, no CN) |
| `G60_feedback_hackathon.xlsx` | Classified customer verbatims | 5,005 rows / 4,000 IDs | G60 (5 Series sedan), ICE/BEV/PHEV | 90% US, plus KR, JP, GB, Nordics, CA (no CN) |
| `G70_feedback_hackathon.xlsx` | Classified customer verbatims | 4,690 rows / 4,000 IDs | G70 (7 Series), ICE/BEV/PHEV | 95% US, plus KR, JP, GB, CA (no CN) |
| `F70_G60_G68_G70_customer_studies.xlsx` | Aggregated satisfaction surveys (2025) | 2 sheets | F70, G60, G68, G70 | CN + EU (sheet 1), US (sheet 2) |
| `sales_volumes.xlsx` | Volumes 2024, 2025, 2030 | 3 sheets | F70, G60+G68, G70 | EU, CN, US, RoW |
| `F70/G60/G70_OptionList.PDF` | German price lists, July 2026 | 23/28/27 pages | F70, G60, G70 (no G68) | Germany only (EUR incl. 19% VAT) |

Key facts:
- **There is no China verbatim data at all.** China is covered only by the CN_EU customer study (G68, G70) and by sales volumes.
- **There is no US data for F70**, which matches sales (F70 US volume = 0, CN = 0).
- Feedback has **no date column**. Customer studies are labelled 2025. Sales cover 2024, 2025 and 2030 (2030 is presumably a forecast **[inferred]**). Option lists are dated July 2026.
- All verbatims are in **English**. Many are clearly translations (JP/KR/SE originals), and Source A text is fully lower-cased **[inferred: pre-processed/translated]**.

---

## 1. Feedback files (`F70_`, `G60_`, `G70_feedback_hackathon.xlsx`)

### 1.1 Structure
Each workbook has a single sheet, `Feedback_Explorer`, with 12 columns and an identical schema. All columns load as strings.

| Column | Meaning | % null F70 / G60 / G70 | Example values |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ID` | Feedback record ID, `<model>-NNNN`. **Repeats across rows** (one row per classification) | 0 / 0 / 0 | `F70-0002`, `G60-1454` |
| `Source` | Channel, anonymised | 0 / 0 / 0 | `Source A`…`Source D` |
| `Brand` | Always `[BMW]` (list-as-string) | 0 | `[BMW]` |
| `Sales Description` | Model family, list-as-string | 0 | `[BMW 1 Series]`, `[BMW 5 Series]`, `[BMW 7 Series]` |
| `Country` | ISO-2 country | 0 | `GB`, `US`, `JP`, `KR` |
| `Derivate (e-code)` | Model code, constant per file | 0 | `F70`, `G60`, `G70` |
| `Engine Type` | Powertrain | 0 | `ICE`, `BEVE` (= BEV), `PHEV` |
| `Feedback Type` | Sentiment/intent class | 26.7 / 14.6 / 14.5 | `Likes`, `Difficult to Use`, `Defect`, `Wants`, NaN |
| `Customer Feedback` | Verbatim text, 15 to 4,260 chars (median approx. 140 to 150) | 0 | see quotes below |
| `Vfc level2 3 Name` | Concatenated `"<L2> : <L3>"` | 0 / 4.0 / 4.3 | `Touch screen, operation : Size not user friendly` |
| `Vfc level2 Name` | Component/topic taxonomy (226 distinct overall) | 0 / 4.0 / 4.3 | `Drivetrain`, `Seats`, `Electric Range`, `no_class_found` |
| `Vfc level3 Name` | Symptom/aspect (84 distinct overall) | 26.7 / 14.5 / 14.3 | `Like: function`, `Not user-friendly`, `Malfunction` |

"VFC" is presumably BMW's vehicle function/fault classification taxonomy **[inferred]**.

### 1.2 Volumes and composition

| | F70 | G60 | G70 | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rows | 4,076 | 5,005 | 4,690 | 13,771 |
| Unique IDs | 2,128 | 4,000 | 4,000 | 10,128 |
| Rows per ID (mean / max) | 1.92 / 11 | 1.25 / 18 | 1.17 / 17 | |
| Distinct L2 topics | 120 | 221 | 211 | 226 |
| Distinct L2:L3 combos | 336 | 953 | 854 | |

**Source by model (unique IDs).** The channel interpretations are **[inferred]** from text style.

| Source | F70 | G60 | G70 | Feedback Type coverage | Apparent nature |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | 2,128 | 854 | 695 | All types + unclassified | Owner reviews/ratings, multi-country, lower-cased, translated (JP uses "・" bullets) |
| B | 0 | 2,626 | 2,853 | Likes/DTU/Wants/Defect (never NaN) | US customer-care/contact-centre notes ("Customer stated… Writer advised…") |
| C | 0 | 384 | 314 | DTU/Defect, or NaN | US quality survey (IQS-style "I had a [very minor…very serious] problem with X" plus NPS-reason and "one comment" prompts) |
| D | 0 | 136 | 138 | Always NaN, no VFC | US appeal survey (APEAL-style "the one thing I love most / could be most improved about…") |

**Country (unique IDs), grouped into markets.**

| | Europe (GB, SE, FR, DK, FI, NO, LV, ES) | US | Other (JP, KR, AU, CA, ZA) | CN |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| F70 | 1,433 (GB 1,293) | 0 | 695 (JP 672) | 0 |
| G60 | 111 | 3,610 | 279 (KR 205, JP 53) | 0 |
| G70 | 19 | 3,792 | 189 (KR 137, JP 40) | 0 |

There is no Germany (DE) in any file. The European voice comes almost entirely from GB, and only for F70.

input.prompt:
Write a Python script at /Volumes/PJ/peresjav/hackathons/ehl-final-minuch-2026/scripts/build-pipeline-data.py and run it. It reads BMW's hackathon dataset (local, git-ignored) and writes /Volumes/PJ/peresjav/hackathons/ehl-final-minuch-2026/web/data-local/pipeline.json, which must match the TypeScript type `PipelineData` in web/src/lib/pipeline/types.ts. Read that file first; it is the contract.

Rules, which are strict:
- Run Python only as `uv run --with pandas --with openpyxl --with pypdf python -I scripts/build-pipeline-data.py` (add other packages with --with if needed). Don't install anything globally.
- The script itself must contain NO BMW data, quotes or numbers. It only reads `data/` and writes `web/data-local/`. It will be committed to git (scripts/ is tracked), so keep it generic.
- Do not print customer verbatims at length in your final report. Summarise counts only.
- Don't touch git, don't touch other files except: the script, the output JSON, and append `/data-local/` to web/.gitignore (with a comment line "# local BMW-derived data (never commit)").
- No OpenAI or other external API calls. Clustering is deterministic.

Inputs (repo root /Volumes/PJ/peresjav/hackathons/ehl-final-minuch-2026):
- data/DATA-REPORT.md: a detailed report of the dataset. Read sections 0–1 and anything about customer studies, sales and option lists first; it explains every column and quirk.
- data/bmw/feedback/{F70,G60,G70}_feedback_hackathon.xlsx: sheet Feedback_Explorer. Long format, so ID repeats; count UNIQUE IDs. Columns include ID, Source, Country, Feedback Type (Likes / Difficult to Use / Defect / Wants / NaN), Customer Feedback, Vfc level2 Name, Vfc level3 Name.
- data/bmw/customer-studies/F70_G60_G68_G70_customer_studies.xlsx: CN+EU sheet (0–10 scale?) and US sheet (check the scale). The derived data/analysis/cs_cneu.csv and us_summary.csv show the shapes. G68 is the China long-wheelbase 5 Series; map G68 to series G60 for market CN.
- data/bmw/sales/sales_volumes.xlsx: 2024/2025/2030 by market (EU, CN, US, RoW). G60+G68 maps to G60.
- data/bmw/option-lists/*.PDF and data/analysis/options.json (already extracted: {main, sub, name, code, price "1.600,–", line}). Use options.json if it's good enough, otherwise re-extract with pypdf. Some entries have bad names (e.g. "Nicht in Verbindung mit …" is a footnote, not a name), so clean those or drop them. Parse the price to a number in EUR; "–,–" means null. Keep up to about 120 useful options per series, deduplicated by code.

Market mapping: GB, SE, FR, DK, FI, NO, LV, ES, DE and other European ISO codes → "EU"; US → "US"; JP → "JP"; CN → "CN"; everything else → "OTHER".

Clustering into FeatureRequest:
- Use rows whose Feedback Type is Wants, Difficult to Use or Defect (and NaN rows from sources C/D only if they clearly carry a VFC topic). Group by `Vfc level2 Name` (skip no_class_found/empty). Optionally merge small topics into a sensible parent. Use the kw_themes.csv themes in data/analysis as inspiration for PM-friendly titles.
- For each series, keep the top ~18–25 clusters by unique IDs (min ~8 mentions).
- title: short, PM-friendly, written as a request ("Simpler iDrive menus", "Softer ride over rough roads", "Better phone connectivity"). Write a hand-made mapping dict from VFC level-2 topic to (title, category, summary) for the topics that actually appear, plus a fallback such as f"Improve {topic.lower()}". It's fine for this mapping dict to live in the script (it's taxonomy names, not customer data).
- category: one of Exterior, Interior, Digital, Powertrain (e.g. drivetrain/engine/battery/range/charging/suspension/brakes → Powertrain; infotainment/iDrive/connectivity/apps/assistance/ADAS/navigation → Digital; seats/climate/materials/storage/noise → Interior; paint/body/lights/doors/wheels/design → Exterior). Use your judgement and be consistent.
- summary: one sentence, built from the dominant level-3 aspects and the type split.
- types: counts of unique IDs per type (wants / difficult / defect).
- byMarket, sources (Source A..D with counts), taxonomy (the VFC level2 names, plus the top level3 names, as "L2 : L3" strings, max 4).
- quotes: up to 3 short verbatims (40–220 chars, cleaned, sentence-cased), preferring "Wants" rows and varied markets.
- relatedOptions: match up to 3 options from that series' option list by keyword (German/English keyword lists per cluster, e.g. Sitz/seat, Head-Up, Parking/Park, Fahrwerk, Klima/Standheizung, Soundsystem/Harman/Bowers, Driving Assistant, Glasdach/Panorama). Empty array when nothing fits; don't force bad matches.
- id: f"{series}-R{nn}".
- strengths: top 6 Likes topics (title + mentions).
- feedbackByMarket: unique IDs per market across all feedback types.
- studies: per series and market, the attributes with scores (the CN/EU sheet is per model column; US sheet: convert to 0–10 by ×10/7 if it's a 1–7 mean; state your choice in a comment). Keep up to ~12 attributes per market.
- sales per series.
- origin "bmw", generatedAt ISO timestamp, series name "1 Series"/"5 Series"/"7 Series".

Validate: load the JSON back and check that every request has all fields, that the categories are valid, and that every series has at least 10 requests. Print a compact summary: per series, the number of requests per category, the top 5 titles with mentions, and the number of options and related-option matches.

Final report (short): the script path, how to run it, the output size, the summary table, and any data caveats you found (e.g. which markets have no verbatims).

content.text:
The pipeline works end to end with BMW's data at **http://localhost:3000/dashboard/us/5-series**. On Japan vs UK: you're partly right.

**What the data says about markets:**
- **The official markets are Europe, China and USA.** Sales and customer studies only use Europe, China, USA and "Rest of World". Neither Japan nor the UK is a separate market there.
- **Japan came from the BMW expert conversation, not the data.** It was their "7 Series in Japan should be smaller" example. In sales, Japan sits inside Rest of World, and it only has comments for the 1 Series (672). The 5 and 7 Series have only 53 and 40.
- **The UK is the real voice of Europe in the comments.** 1,293 of about 1,430 European 1 Series comments are from the UK. But in sales and studies the UK is counted inside Europe.

So Japan shouldn't be the fourth market. You have two clean options:
1. **Three markets: Europe, China, USA** (my recommendation). This matches BMW's sales and studies. The app would note that the UK makes up most of Europe's comments.
2. **Replace Japan with the UK.** The catch: Europe without the UK has only about 140 comments for the 1 Series, and UK sales and studies don't exist on their own.

Tell me which one and I'll change the globe, landing page and dashboard.

**How the pipeline behaves:**
- **Start:** pick a market on the globe, then a series. The cards show the real car photos and how many comments that market has.
- **AI analysis:** a short animation shows the steps: principles (L1), comments, customer studies, sales and the price list (L2), grouping into requests, sorting into the four categories, urgency. The grouping itself is done beforehand by a script; nothing calls an AI model live yet.
- **Your decisions:** 25 feature requests per series, which you can filter by category and urgency.
  - Each request shows its mentions in this market, how they split into wishes, hard-to-use and defects, and matching options from the German price list (July 2026) with code and price.
  - "Evidence" opens the market split, the feedback channels, BMW's own category and three customer quotes.
  - **Reject opens the box you asked for:** you pick a common reason or write your own, and a reason is required. It's saved under Decisions with who and when, and it shows on every profile page.
- **Build profiles:** three profiles (Fix the basics, Tech-forward, Comfort & craft), each with a score split into principles and evidence.
  - Each profile page shows draft targets, the related options and their total price, why the agent chose it, the principles, competitors, and all decisions including rejects with their reasons.
  - **Social test:** optional and simulated. It moves the score by at most 2–20% depending on the series.
- **Markets with no comments:** for example China, or the 1 Series in the USA. A "What we don't know" warning appears and the list falls back to all markets.

**Things to know:**
- **BMW's data stays out of git.** The script `scripts/build-pipeline-data.py` writes it to `web/data-local/`, which is ignored. Vercel and fresh clones get made-up example data instead.
- **Two data problems from the extraction:**
  - **Top powertrain request is probably inflated:** some 1 Series "complaints" in BMW's data are actually praise.
  - **5 and 7 Series are mostly US customer-care notes:** 90–95% of their comments come from there, so "hard to use" dominates their requests.
- **Photos:** six real photos from Wikimedia Commons, all CC BY-SA. Each one shows its photographer and links to its Commons page, which the licence requires.
- **Placeholders:** the principles, the competitor notes and the social test are example content for now.
- **Not finished:**
  - Decisions are stored only in your browser, not in a database yet.
  - With few kept requests, the three profiles look alike.
- **Not committed:** do that from a fresh session, as before.

input.prompt:
You are the "research agent" for Dixi, a hackathon tool that helps BMW product managers decide requirements for the successors of the BMW 1 Series (F70), 5 Series (G60) and 7 Series (G70) in Europe (EU), the USA (US) and China (CN). Today is 2026-10-10.

Task: research public sources and write `/Volumes/PJ/peresjav/hackathons/ehl-final-minuch-2026/web/src/lib/pipeline/market-signals.ts`, exporting `export const MARKET_SIGNALS: MarketSignal[] = [...]` (import the type with `import type { MarketSignal } from "./types";`). Read the `MarketSignal` interface at the end of `web/src/lib/pipeline/types.ts` first; it is the contract.

Two kinds of signal:
1. **competitor**: a feature or quality customers or reviewers clearly *like* in a direct competitor.
   - 1 Series: Mercedes A-Class, Audi A3, VW Golf, Tesla Model 3/Y (EU), BYD Dolphin/Seal, MG4.
   - 5 Series: Mercedes E-Class (incl. long-wheelbase China), Audi A6/A6 e-tron, Tesla Model S/3, Genesis G80, and in China NIO ET7/ET5, Li Auto, Xiaomi SU7, BYD Han, AITO.
   - 7 Series: Mercedes S-Class/EQS, Audi A8, Lexus LS, Genesis G90, and in China NIO ET9, Maextro S800, Hongqi, Yangwang.
   - Examples: Mercedes MBUX Hyperscreen and voice assistant, Tesla over-the-air updates and app, Xiaomi SU7's phone ecosystem integration, NIO battery swap, Genesis value and warranty, Lexus reliability, Chinese EVs' rear-seat entertainment and zero-gravity seats.
2. **trend**: a market trend 2025–2026 relevant to these cars. Examples: return of physical buttons (Euro NCAP 2026 rules), 800 V fast charging, L2+/L3 hands-off driving (China NOA, US hands-free), in-car AI voice assistants (LLMs), software-defined vehicles and OTA, plug-in hybrid/EREV growth in China, rear-seat luxury in China, subscription backlash, US tariffs and price sensitivity, big screens vs distraction, Google built-in/CarPlay demand in the US, e-SIM connectivity.

Requirements:
- **24–36 signals in total**, balanced. Every series gets at least 8 that apply to it, and every market at least 6. Mix competitor and trend roughly 50/50 and cover all four categories (Exterior, Interior, Digital, Powertrain).
- Use the **exa MCP tools** (`mcp__exa__web_search_exa`, `mcp__exa__web_fetch_exa`; load them via ToolSearch with "select:mcp__exa__web_search_exa,mcp__exa__web_fetch_exa"). Power, Consumer Reports, CnEVPost, Reuters, Euro NCAP, manufacturer press, McKinsey/Deloitte consumer studies.

- `detail`: ≤ 20 words, concrete, with a number when there is one.

- `relatesTo`: the exact titles from the list below whose customer feedback asks for the same thing. 0–3 per signal; exact strings only. This drives highlighting in the UI, so be accurate rather than generous.
- `id`: "S01", "S02", …

content.text:
The list now has competitors and trends, a wishlist, drag-to-prioritise and compact rows with a details icon. I clicked through the whole flow in a headless browser with no errors, and the architecture diagram is updated. Reload **http://localhost:3000/dashboard/eu/1-series** to see it.

**Competitors & trends**
- A research agent found 32 signals, each linked to its source: 17 features people like in competitors (Mercedes, Genesis, Lexus, NIO, Xiaomi, Maextro…) and 15 trends.
- Strongest examples:
  - Euro NCAP 2026 rewards physical buttons again.
  - In China, the Maextro S800 outsold the 7 Series in Jan–Apr 2026.
  - 43% of US buyers want hands-free highway driving.
- They sit in a panel above the requests. It shows the top 4 by default, with "Show all".
- Customer requests that match a signal are highlighted and carry a badge, e.g. "Physical buttons are back".
- Click a signal's link icon to show only the matching requests. The "Backed by market" filter does the same for all signals at once.
- **Caveat:** the agent took its facts from search-result text rather than opening each page. A few signals rest on older or second-hand sources; I can list them.

**Wishlist**
- The star on any competitor feature or trend adds it to your wishlist.
- Wishlist items go into the profiles whose theme fits: Tech-forward takes Digital and Powertrain items, Comfort & craft takes Interior and Exterior.
- They're logged in Decisions and shown on the profile page.

**Priority**
- Drag a row by its handle to move it, or focus the handle and use ↑ ↓. The number on each row is its position, and there's a "Reset priority" button.
- Profiles pick and list requirements in your order, show "#1, #2…", and score higher when they include your top priorities.

**Smaller list**
- Each request is now one compact row: category icon, title and urgency flames.
- Small icon counts follow: mentions, wish it, hard to use, defect, and related options.
- Then ✕ / ✓ and an **info icon** that opens a side panel with all the details. There's no dropdown any more.

**Diagram:** `docs/architecture/07-pm-workflow.md` now includes the research agent, the feedback ↔ competitor/trend linking, wishlist, priority order and how they feed the build. It renders without errors.

Still open:
- **Markets:** the data has only Europe, China and USA, so do you want three markets (my recommendation) or the UK instead of Japan?
- **Storage:** decisions, wishlist and priority are saved only in your browser for now.

Base directory for this skill: /Volumes/PJ/DevCache/claude-tmp/claude-501/bundled-skills/2.1.296/a56f9c133e66c7c6bdf3d9b71d6e5351/dataviz

# Data Visualization

A chart is **read by people and executed by you**. This skill turns "make it look
good" into a procedure with checks, so the result is right by construction rather
than by taste.

**The method here is design-system-agnostic.** Nothing in the procedure, the form
heuristic, the six checks, or the mark specs is specific to one product. A design
system supplies a small set of *parameters* (its ramps, a categorical order, a
diverging pair, a status palette, a texture, its surfaces, its filter components);
the method consumes them unchanged. A **validated default palette** is the
reference instance, fully specified in `references/palette.md`. To target your
brand, read that file's structure and substitute its values - touch nothing else.

> The single most important habit: **the color part is computable, so compute it.**
> Never eyeball whether a palette is colorblind-safe - run `scripts/validate_palette.js`.

## The procedure - do these in order

Color comes LAST. Most bad charts pick colors first.

1. **Pick the form.** What is the data's job - magnitude, identity, polarity, a
   single headline, change-over-time? The job picks the chart type, and sometimes
   the answer is *not a chart* (a stat tile or hero number). -> `references/choosing-a-form.md`
2. **Assign color by the job it does.** Categorical (identity), sequential
   (magnitude), diverging (polarity), or status (state) - each has one rule.
   Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled. -> `references/color-formula.md`
3. **VALIDATE the palette - run the script, don't reason about Delta E.**
   `node scripts/validate_palette.js "<hex,hex,...>" --mode light` (relative to
   this skill's base directory - or load it as `<script type="module">` in the
   chart's own page, where it reads
   `data-palette` off `<body>` and logs a `console.table` report). It returns
   pass/fail on the lightness band, chroma floor, adjacent-pair CVD separation,
   the normal-vision floor, and contrast. Fix anything that FAILs before continuing. Re-run for
   `--mode dark` with that mode's surface.
4. **Apply mark specs & spacers.** Thin marks, 4px rounded data-ends anchored to
   the baseline, 2px lines, >=8px markers, a 2px surface gap between fills (stacked
   segments and adjacent bars alike) and a 2px surface ring on overlapping marks,
   selective direct labels. -> `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`
5. **Add the hover layer - by default.** An HTML/SVG chart *is* interactive; ship
   a crosshair+tooltip on line/area and a per-mark hover tooltip on bar/dot/cell.
   The only form that skips it is a bare stat tile with no plot. Hit targets bigger
   than the mark; filters in one row above the charts. -> `references/interaction.md`
6. **Final accessibility pass.** For >= 2 series a legend is always present and <= 4
   are also direct-labeled (a single series needs no legend box - the title names
   it), so identity is never color-alone; a table view exists; dark mode is **selected** - its own
   steps from the same ramps, validated against the dark surface, not an automatic
   flip; texture is available for the CVD/print/forced-colors case.
7. **Render it and look at it.** The validator checks color, not layout - open or
   screenshot the output and eyeball it for label collisions, geometry, and overflow
   before calling it done.

Then check the result against **`references/anti-patterns.md`** - it is the catalog
of what goes wrong. If your chart matches an entry, it's wrong.

## Non-negotiables (true in every design system)

- **Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled.** A 9th series is never a
  generated hue - it folds into "Other," small multiples, or composite encoding.
- **One axis.** Never a dual-axis chart (two y-scales). Two measures of different
  scale -> two charts, small multiples, or indexed to a common base. *(This is the
  #1 chart mistake - see anti-patterns.)*
- **Color follows the entity, never its rank.** A filter that changes the series
  count must not repaint the survivors.
- **Sequential = one hue, light->dark. Diverging = two hues + a neutral gray
  midpoint.** Never a rainbow; never a hue at the diverging midpoint.
- **Run the validator before shipping any categorical palette.** CVD Delta E >= 8 is the
  target (OKLab ×100); 6-8 is a floor that is legal ONLY with secondary encoding. A
  normal-vision floor below 15 is a hard FAIL - full-color readers can't tell the
  pair apart; re-step it on the adjacent pairlist (secondary encoding does not excuse
  this one); under `--pairs all` cut series or facet instead - see check 4. A contrast WARN
  obligates visible labels or a table view - it is not dismissable.
- **Thin marks; a legend always present for >= 2 series (none for one), with
  selective direct labels (never a number on every point); recessive grid/axes.**
- **Text wears text tokens, never the series color** - values, labels, and legends
  stay in primary/secondary/muted ink; a colored mark beside them carries identity.
- **Status colors are reserved** (good/warning/serious/critical) and never reused
  for "series 4"; they ship with an icon + label, never color alone.

## Plugging in a design system

The method is invariant; only these parameters change per system. The reference
instance - every value filled in - is `references/palette.md`.

| Parameter | What the system provides |
|---|---|
| **Ramps** | the hue scales (named steps) the palette draws from |
| **Categorical theme** | the fixed hue order (a named theme); default + alternates |
| **Sequential hue** | the default single hue for magnitude |
| **Diverging pair** | two warm/cool poles + a neutral midpoint |
| **Status palette** | good / warning / serious / critical - steps distinct from categorical |
| **Texture fill** | one directional hand-drawn fill, used at 45° / 135° |
| **Surfaces** | light & dark chart-surface colors (the validator needs these) |
| **Filter controls** | date-range & dimension controls (behavioral spec in `interaction.md`) |

To onboard a new system: fill those rows, feed its ramps to the validator, and let
it snap each slot to the nearest passing step. Structure and rules stay as written.

## Reference files

| File | What it answers |
|------|-----------------|

content.text:
I've redone the page header, added feedback when you move rows, and made **Build profiles** end the pipeline in a profiles dashboard with Profiles and Analytics tabs. I clicked through the whole flow in a headless browser with no errors, and the profile page exports as a clean 3-page A4 PDF. Reload with **Cmd+Shift+R**: the dev server had been serving old styles, so I cleared its cache and restarted it.

**Header and photos**
- The top of the page is now a dark banner. The car photo fills the right side and fades into navy behind the text.
- It shows three stat chips: customer comments, feature requests, and competitors & trends.
- The photo credit is smaller but still visible and linked, as the photo licence requires.
- The profile page uses the same banner with the second photo (rear or interior).

**Moving rows in the list**
- While you drag, the row you're moving dims and gets a dashed outline.
- A blue line with a dot shows where the row will land, above or below the row under your cursor.
- The other rows slide smoothly into their new places.
- The row you moved flashes blue for about a second. This also works when you move it with ↑ ↓.

**When the build is done**
- The pipeline is marked complete and you land on the **Profiles dashboard**.
- **Profiles tab:** three cards, each with its score bar, its requirements with category icons and your priority numbers, and its wishlist items.
- **Analytics tab:** you launch a 14-day social test.
  - **Leader:** a card names the profile tracking best, with its lead in points.
  - **Per profile:** reach, engagement, positive reactions and a week-2-vs-week-1 trend.
  - **Chart:** daily engagement per profile, with hover details and a table view. Each profile keeps the same colour everywhere, and the colours were checked for colour-blind readers.
- The test result also updates each profile's score, at the small social weight for that series.
- **The social test is simulated**, and the page says so. There are no real posts behind it yet.

**Profile page**
- From top to bottom:
  1. The banner.
  2. Four key numbers: requirements, customer mentions covered, today's option prices, and wishlist items.
  3. The requirements in your priority order, each with a draft target and the related options.
  4. Why the agent chose this profile, next to the L1 principles.
  5. Competitors & trends, with their sources.
  6. The decision trail, including reject reasons.
  7. A short line on where the evidence comes from.
- **Download PDF** opens the print dialog; choose "Save as PDF". The navigation is left out, and the report gets its own header with the series, market, profile and date.

The architecture diagram `docs/architecture/07-pm-workflow.md` now covers the dashboard, both tabs and the PDF, and it renders without errors.

The left sidebar is gone from the market page and now appears only after the profiles are built. The market page shows just the series choice, as new photo cards. Types and lint pass, and I checked both pages in a headless browser.

**Analytics fix:** the "Tracking best" card used a combined score, which made it look like it contradicted the chart. It now says it ranks by **social score** (half engagement rate, half share of positive reactions), and each profile card shows that score.

content.text:
Fixed. I tested it with real mouse events: dragging row 5, "More comfortable, better-equipped seats", up the list moved it to position 2, and the rows below moved down by one. No console errors, and types and lint pass.

**Cause:** the list used the browser's built-in drag-and-drop on the handle button. In Chrome, the page re-rendering at the start of the drag can cancel it, so rows didn't move. I replaced it with my own pointer-based dragging, which also works with a trackpad and on touch screens.

**How it works now:**
- Press and hold the **⋮⋮ handle** (left of the number) and drag. The row lifts with a blue outline and shadow and follows your cursor.
- A blue line shows where it will land.
- Near the top or bottom of the window the page scrolls by itself, so you can move a row a long way.
- On release, the rows slide into place, the moved row flashes, and the new order is saved and used for the profiles.
- Keyboard still works: click the handle, then use ↑ ↓.

I did all three: the profile page now follows BMW's catalogue layout, the profile cards match the series cards, and every build is saved as a session you can reopen. I tested build → profile → Sessions page → reopen in a headless browser with no errors, and types pass. Reload with **Cmd+Shift+R**.

**What I took from BMW's catalogues** (5, 1 and 7 Series, July 2026):
- **Cover:** a full-bleed photo with a big light "BMW 5 / LIMOUSINE" title and the month at the bottom.
- **Section titles:** uppercase with a full stop, like "FAHRZEUGPREISE." and "SONDERAUSSTATTUNGEN.".
- **Tables:** grey band headers and hairline rules.
- **Equipment matrix:** model columns with turned headers, ■ for standard and □ for optional, plus option code and price written like "1.900,–".
- **Legend:** a short key at the foot of every page.

**The profile page now follows that layout:**
1. **Cover:** the car photo with "BMW 5" in large light type, "PROFILE A · COMFORT & CRAFT", the tagline, and market · month · session at the bottom.
2. **PROFILE AT A GLANCE.** Two tables with grey bands: Score (L1, L2, L3, total) and Scope (series, requirements, customer mentions covered, wishlist, total price of related options).
3. **REQUIREMENTS.** The catalogue matrix:
   - Grouped by Exterior, Interior, Digital, Powertrain and Wishlist, in your priority order (#1, #2…).
   - Each row has its draft target, plus the option code and its list price where an option matches.
   - One column per profile shows ■ in this profile, □ in another profile, or – not included, so you can compare all three at once.
4. **WHY THIS PROFILE.** and **PRINCIPLES.** side by side.
5. **COMPETITORS AND TRENDS.** with source links.
6. **DECISION TRAIL.** with reject reasons, who and when.
7. **Legend and evidence note** at the foot, as in BMW's lists.

Download PDF still prints this layout to A4.

**Profile cards:** these are now dark cards like the series picker:
- The car photo is tinted in each profile's colour, with a "PROFILE A" badge and a white "Best fit" badge on the winner.
- Below it: the name, a score bar, the top requirements with category icons and priority numbers, any wishlist items, and a white "Open profile" button.

**Sessions:**
- Every **Build profiles** saves a session: its profiles, decisions, priority order and social test results. They're kept in your browser for now, up to the last 30.
- **Three ways in:**
  - A **Sessions** link in the top bar, on every dashboard page.
  - A **Sessions** item in the dashboard sidebar. Sessions for this car and market open in place; others take you to their own page.
  - A link per session (`…/5-series#session=S-…`) that reopens it directly.
- The dashboard header shows which session you're looking at.
- **Edit requests** loads that session's decisions, and building again creates a new session.

I also updated `docs/architecture/07-pm-workflow.md` with sessions and the catalogue-style profile page. It renders without errors.

- **Storage:** sessions only live in your browser until we connect Supabase.
- **Markets:** still waiting on your answer: three markets (Europe, China, USA), or the UK instead of Japan?

content.text:
There's now a real dashboard with your earlier generations, the pipeline itself works as before, and the analysis steps use plain names instead of L1/L2/L3. I tested it end to end in a headless browser: building a profile opened its own generation page, `/dashboard` listed it, and reopening it worked. No errors, and types and lint pass.

**The dashboard**
- **`/dashboard`** opens on the **Generations** tab:
  - Four numbers at the top: generations, car × market combinations, decisions logged, and the top-scoring profile so far.
  - One card per earlier generation, showing the car photo, series and market, date, best profile and its score, kept/rejected/wishlist counts, and whether a social test was run. A delete button appears when you hover.
- **New analysis** (tab, or the blue button in the top bar, at `/dashboard/new`) shows the globe → series → pipeline you already have.

**After a build**
- The pipeline saves the result as a **generation** and opens its own page:
  - The car banner with the generation number and date, and the numbers of profiles, kept, rejected and wishlist items.
  - A sidebar with **Profiles**, **Analytics** (social test) and **Decisions**. Profile pages open in the catalogue style with the PDF download.
  - **Edit and rebuild** reopens the pipeline with that generation's decisions and priority already loaded. Building again creates a new generation, so earlier ones are never overwritten.
- "All generations" takes you back to `/dashboard`.

**Analysis wording** (the screen shown while analysing):
- **BMW principles:** "Retrieving the fundamentals and principles for the 7 Series".
- **Market evidence:**
  - Reading customer comments and feature requests.
  - Adding customer studies, sales and price-list options.
  - The research agent scanning competitors and trends.
- **Building the list:** grouping, linking to competitors and trends, sorting into categories, scoring urgency.

# Scoring and decision memory Every decision (keep, reject with a reason, wishlist) is saved with **who** and **when**, together with how many customers asked at that moment. Later generations read this **decision memory**, so the AI does not push a request that was already rejected, unless the market has changed. The ranking rule and its weights are set by the team in **Dashboard → Settings** (`/dashboard/settings`). ## The score (0–100, shown on every feature request) | Part | What it measures | Default weight | |---|---|---| | Demand | Customers asking in the chosen market, log-scaled against the top request | 60 % | | Market backing | Competitor features and trends (research agent) that support the request | 25 % | | Principle fit | The request's category matches the series' focus (BMW principles) | 15 % | ``` base = 100 × (wD·demand + wB·backing + wF·fit) / (wD + wB + wF) strength = 0.5 ^ (days since the decision / half-life) default half-life 365 days growth = (mentions now − mentions at decision) / mentions at decision rejected before: score = base × (1 − penalty × strength) default penalty 60 % … unless growth ≥ resurface threshold → "Resurfaced", score = base default +30 % kept before: score = base + 10 × bonus × strength default +5 points optional: hide rejected requests instead of ranking them lower memory scope: same market (default) or all markets ``` The PM's drag order always wins over the score. The score sets the default order and is shown so the PM can see why. ## Flow ```mermaid flowchart LR %% How past decisions shape the next generation. classDef human fill:#fdecea,stroke:#e22718,color:#121722,stroke-width:2px classDef store fill:#0f3d75,stroke:#0f3d75,color:#ffffff classDef ai fill:#e8f0fc,stroke:#1c69d4,color:#121722 classDef cfg fill:#eef1f6,stroke:#5b6676,color:#121722 subgraph G1 ["Generation 1"] pm1{{"PM decides

content.text:
Rejected requests now lose priority in later generations unless demand grows, the weights are adjustable in a new Settings page, and the architecture docs describe it all. I tested it in a headless browser: the 5 Series request rejected in the first generation ("Simpler iDrive menus and touchscreen", 81 customers asking) came back last of 25 in the next analysis, with a red "Rejected 10 Oct 2026" badge and a score of 33 instead of about 80. Types and lint pass.

**Decision memory and scoring**
- **What's saved:** every keep and reject records who, their role, when, the reason, and how many customers were asking at that moment. Each build keeps a copy of its decisions as a generation.
- **Next analysis:** for the same series (and the same market by default), Dixi reads those past decisions.
  - **Score:** every feature request shows a score from 0 to 100, built from demand (60%), backing from competitors and trends (25%) and fit with BMW principles (15%). The score sets the default order; your drag order still wins.
  - **Rejected before:** the score drops by 60% and the card shows a red "Rejected <date>" badge. The details panel shows who rejected it, when, why, and how many customers were asking then.
  - **Fading:** the penalty halves every 365 days, so old rejects count less over time.
  - **Resurfaced:** if demand has grown 30% or more since the reject, the penalty is lifted and an amber "Resurfaced +X%" badge appears.
  - **Kept before:** a small bonus and a green badge.
  - **Optional:** hide earlier rejects instead of ranking them lower.

**Settings** (the sliders icon in the top bar, `/dashboard/settings`): sliders for the three weights, the reject penalty, the keep bonus, how fast decisions fade, and the resurfacing threshold. You can also choose same market or all markets, switch hiding on or off, and reset. A live example shows how one request scores in each situation, and the formula is written out.

**Trace on the profile page:** each requirement in the requirements table has an **ⓘ** icon. It opens a side panel with the full path: customer feedback (mentions, channels) → competitors and trends behind it → the decision (who, role, when, why, priority, customers asking then) → placed in this profile. Below that are the evidence, sources, matching options and customer quotes. The icon is left out of the PDF.

**Empty space in the table:** that came from the tall turned profile names in the header. The columns are now **A / B / C** with colour dots, and the full names are in a short key above the table.

**The page issue:** I couldn't reproduce it. The Next.js overlay showed "no issues" at every step of a full run. It was most likely the Settings-page error I fixed during this work, which stays in the overlay until a reload. If you still see it after **Cmd+Shift+R**, send me a screenshot.

**Architecture docs:**
- **`09-scoring-and-memory.md` (new):** the formula, a diagram of how past decisions shape the next generation, and today versus the backend plan.
  - In the backend, the AI agent calls `get_decision_memory(series, market)` before proposing requests. It doesn't re-propose a reject unless it resurfaced, and then it quotes the old reason.
  - Matching will also use text similarity, so a reworded request is still recognised. Today it matches on the same series and the same request title.
- **Also updated:** `03-data-model.md` (customers asking at decision time, scoring settings), `07-pm-workflow.md` (memory, score and settings feed the list, plus the trace icon), `docs/README.md`, and `backend/README.md` (decision memory listed as a must-have for the agents).
